Measured from manifest.snapshot.json: ALL 4 slash_common commands are kind=`both` — diagnostic/diagnostics, help/help, settings/settings, setup/setup — so each one marks its own capability survivable before it can be found missing. 4 of 4 self-satisfying. Zero PanelActionSpec/SelectorSpec carries slash_common. Of the 386 prefix-kind commands, ZERO carry the tag, so the named failure class ("essential capability reachable only by prefix") has an empty tagged population and the gate can only red for a configuration no author has ever written. I reproduced the row's own evidence — `python3 tools/check_intent_survival.py` → `check_intent_survival: OK (49 manifest(s) walked)`, real exit 0 — but green here is guaranteed, not earned.

The population is mislabelled and the headline count is wrong. Measured: `grep -rho "delete_after=" --include=*.py disbot/cogs/` = 106, NOT 113. `disbot/` = 131, which is correct. The per-duration breakdown the row attributes to disbot/cogs/ is in fact the disbot/-WIDE distribution: disbot/ gives 10s=63, 8s=17, 5s=16, 15s=9, 7s=3, 60s=2, 20s=2, 12s=1 (sum 113 = the 131 total minus 18 non-literal `delete_after=<expr>`), while disbot/cogs/ alone gives 10s=56, 8s=15, 5s=16, 15s=8, 7s=3, 60s=2, 20s=2, 12s=1. So "113 counted delete_after= sends in disbot/cogs/" is the count of numeric-literal delete_after across ALL of disbot/, presented as the cogs/ population — a sample-vs-population substitution of exactly the kind this lane exists to catch.

The counts are exact (independently recomputed from manifest.snapshot.json: 413 commands, defer_mode null=399, 'none'=13, 'auto'=1) and the quote is verbatim at resolve.py:265-272 — but the claim they support is false. "cannot be missed by an author forgetting to defer" is refuted by the very line that consumes this function: resolve.py:364 `defer_mode = _spec_field(req, "defer_mode", None) or _surface_default_defer(req)` — the author's declaration WINS over the surface default, and 13 commands use it to declare `none`, 12 of them on slash- or both-kind commands routing to HANDLERS (setup, setup-hub, setup-advanced, setup-status, setup-reset, setup-skip, setup-unskip, utility, myprofile, uxlab, settings, server-management) where `_surface_default_defer` would have returned AUTO. Those 12 are authors explicitly suppressing the automatic ack on the interaction surface. Second hole in the quote itself: SLASH + PanelRef returns DeferMode.NONE, and 6 of 18 slash commands (71 of 413 overall) route to a panel — so a slow panel render on slash has no defer and no guard. No checker anywhere asserts that any interaction-delivered route acks; enforcement_locus is a default value, not a source_guard.

The headline is false in the default configuration. `DEFAULT_DM_ON_ACTION = False` at disbot/services/moderation_config.py:45, with :46 stating "The notify-the-member DM is gated by the master ``dm_on_action`` switch AND a per-action switch", :136 `dm_on_action: bool = DEFAULT_DM_ON_ACTION`, and disbot/services/moderation_service.py:290 "No-op unless the master ``dm_on_action`` switch is enabled **and** *action* ...". So in an unconfigured guild a member who is warned, timed out, kicked or banned gets NO DM at all — which is precisely the failure the row says is prevented ("a member being silently punished with no notification and no stated reason"). The mechanism is opt-in and off by default; the row states it as unconditional behaviour.

The 217 counts classes that INHERIT the constructor call, not classes the call does anything for — a reach claim built on an inheritance measurement. `attach_standard_nav` (disbot/views/navigation.py:407-432) is a NO-OP unless four conditions hold: `subsystem = getattr(view, "SUBSYSTEM", "") or ""` / `if not subsystem or not getattr(view, "STANDARD_NAV", True): return` (:422-424); `meta = SUBSYSTEMS.get(subsystem)` / `if meta is None: return` (:425-427); `if _self_navigates(view): return` (:431-432). Its own docstring says so: "a no-op for views without a ``SUBSYSTEM`` (confirmations, transient sub-views) or with ``STANDARD_NAV = False``". Measured over disbot/: only 67 class-level `SUBSYSTEM =` assignments exist repo-wide, 8 `STANDARD_NAV = False` opt-outs, and the SUBSYSTEMS registry holds 43 entries — so the effective reach is at most ~59 of 280 (≈21%), not 217 (77.5%). "with zero per-view code" is refuted by the same lines: declaring `SUBSYSTEM` IS per-view code. And "812 classes parsed under disbot/" is wrong — an AST walk of every .py under disbot/ parses 1434 classes (the 280 View-descendants and 218 BaseView-descendants both reproduce exactly). CONTRADICTS ITSELF: at ~21% effective reach the conclusion inverts — superbot's inheritance-default reaches LESS of its surface than the 30.6% the row attributes to superbot-next's renderer-injected nav, not 2.5x more.

Every raw number reproduces — disbot/views/ = 250 files / 64,872 LOC over 280 View classes = 231.7; sb/domain/*/panels.py = 41 files / 23,802 LOC over 314 panels = 75.8 — but the two denominators measure different things, so the ~3x ratio is an artifact. superbot's `disbot/views/` holds the View classes AND their button/select callbacks (the callbacks are methods on the View). superbot-next splits the callbacks out: `sb/domain/*/handlers.py` is 24 files / 9,480 LOC carrying 232 `@handler` definitions — the action callbacks for those same panels — and is excluded from the row's denominator. Include them and it is 33,282 LOC / 314 panels = ~106 LOC per surface, a ~2.2x reduction, not ~3x. (I checked the other direction and it is fair: the renderer_override bodies DO live in panels.py — `admin.render_hub` is registered at sb/domain/admin/panels.py:271 — so 218 hand-written renderers are inside the counted files.) Separately, the row has an EMPTY prevents_failure and effect_asserted=false with locus=source_guard, and its consumers=314 is a count of panels, not of consumers of any mechanism — so it does not clear the survival rule on its own fields even before the ratio is corrected.

Citation failure, and the row knows it. The FILE/QUOTE pair cites disbot/services/economy_service.py:1-20 and quotes `import logging` / `from dataclasses import dataclass` — two lines that say nothing about acyclicity and are not evidence for ANY of the five figures the claim rests on (182 statements, 148 edges, 93 modules, 0 mutual pairs, 0 cycles>=3). The row labels its own citation "(representative of the 93 sibling-importing modules measured)" — a sample explicitly standing in for a population, which is the exact substitution this lane refutes. I did not re-run the cycle detection, so I am not asserting the DAG claim is false; I am asserting the row as filed carries no verifiable evidence for it. Scope error on top: the 59-cog layer figure counts only `cogs.*` cross-family statements (9 across 7 edges), excluding cogs->services, cogs->views and services->utils edges, so "the graph is still a DAG" is scoped to two intra-layer subgraphs, not to disbot/.

The count is wrong by more than 3x and two of the four named uses do not exist. Quote verbatim at sb/domain/operator_spine.py:123-131, but `grep -rho "pending_handler(" --include=*.py sb/` returns 14 occurrences, one of which is the definition — so 13 live call sites, not 4: sb/domain/admin/cogmgr.py:327, sb/domain/admin/handlers.py:149, sb/domain/fishing/service.py:1613, sb/domain/mining/service.py:1341, and NINE in sb/domain/ux_lab/handlers.py (:50 buttons_wing, :51 selects_wing, :52 modals_wing, :53 embeds_wing, :54 components_v2_wing, :56 pil_cards_wing, and three more in the same block). There are ZERO btd6 call sites, so the named `btd6.cmd_strat_pending` and `btd6.strat_pending_view` are not pending_handler uses at all. The distribution also inverts the row's framing: 9 of 13 uses stub out the wings of a single demo subsystem, which is "a declared control that does nothing when clicked" at scale — the very failure the row says the primitive prevents — differing from a dead button only in that it says so.

lanes.lane: M1 — superbot (5e3a667b), PRODUCT: setup and server management

lanes.headline: Superbot's setup surface is TWO coherent journeys wearing four front doors: a genuinely well-built access/lockout spine (bootstrap bypass + two-tier setup_access + live authority re-check) that a successor should port almost verbatim, bolted to an accumulated provisioning layer whose flagship preview→confirm panel pair has ZERO production callers, whose confirmation gate is bypassed at 3 of 3 call sites, and whose guild-teardown is a hand-maintained 23-step list against 74 guild-scoped tables — leaking staged setup drafts across bot re-invites.

strengths.claim: The lockout escape hatch is real and centralized: resolve_command_access admits any bootstrap command run by a guild operator or bot owner BEFORE reading the per-guild policy row, so an operator who sets access mode to selected_channels or disabled_except_bootstrap can always still reach !setup / !settings / !admin / !help / !diagnostics from any channel. Counted 6 call sites of resolve_command_access outside its own module across 4 modules (bootstrap_access_cog.py:146 prefix guard, :200 slash tree gate, cleanup_cog.py:199, diagnostic_embeds.py:2372 and :2434, access_projection.py:342).
strengths.prevents_failure: self-lockout: an operator restricts commands to selected channels and then cannot reach any configuration command to undo it
strengths.guard_population: A hardcoded frozenset of 28 command names (BOOTSTRAP_COMMANDS, lines 41-68) widened by space-root and hyphen-root matching. Non-empty and it is the REAL command names, not a model — but it is a hand-maintained allowlist, so the population is exactly what someone remembered to type. See M1-D05.
strengths.simpler_than_counterpart: superbot-next has no equivalent admission resolver at this pin (not checked in this lane)
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port the shape verbatim: bootstrap classification -> operator check -> policy read, in that order. But DERIVE the bootstrap set from a per-command declaration (a decorator or command metadata flag) instead of a hand-typed frozenset, so a new admin front door cannot be forgotten.

strengths.claim: test_no_silent_auto_create.py is a guard over the REAL artifact and it is green: it AST-scans all 883 production .py files under disbot/ (counted) for guild.create_text_channel / create_voice_channel / create_category / create_category_channel / create_role / *.create_thread, with a 6-file allowlist, and additionally pins that services/resource_provisioning.py itself contains zero such calls. 4 tests, measured EXIT=0. CI runs `pytest tests/ -v -n auto` on any code change.
strengths.prevents_failure: a new cog silently creating a Discord channel or role outside the audited pipeline, so the creation never reaches resource_provisioning_audit and the operator has no record of what the bot made in their server
strengths.guard_population: 883 real production .py files under disbot/ (measured). CANNOT be empty — _iter_production_py_files() rglobs the shipped tree, and test_allowlist_entries_exist separately asserts every allowlisted path still exists on disk, so a rename cannot silently widen it. This is the artifact, not a model of it.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port this guard first, before writing any provisioning code — it is the cheapest thing in the repo that keeps a resource-creating bot auditable, and it is one of the very few guards here whose population is provably the real tree.

strengths.claim: services/setup_access.py is a single 158-line typed surface that draws a real two-tier line: is_setup_admin (owner OR Discord administrator OR delegated admin) may VIEW and run readiness scans; can_apply_setup (owner OR delegated admin only — plain administrators excluded) may WRITE. Counted 4 distinct consumer modules reading it: cogs/setup/_wizard_entry.py (4 call sites), cogs/setup_cog.py (setup_depth_slash + _toggle_skip), views/setup/wizard.py:409, views/setup/recovery.py; services/readiness_repair.py uses the *_by_id variants.
strengths.quote:
def can_apply_setup(
    member: discord.Member,
    session: SetupSession | None = None,
) -> bool:
    """True iff ``member`` may APPLY setup repairs / wizard steps.

    Tighter than :func:`is_setup_admin`: only owners and
    delegated admins. Administrators with no delegation get read-only
    access — they can still run the readiness scan but the wizard
    refuses to write on their behalf so the owner stays in control
    of capability-significant changes.
strengths.prevents_failure: a plain Discord administrator (a role often handed out freely) silently applying capability-significant server-wide setup changes on the owner's behalf
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port the two-tier read/write split and the sync cache-only discipline (no DB, no API calls — safe from any view callback). The delegation list living on the setup session row rather than on a Discord role is the right call and should survive.

strengths.claim: ServerManagementHubView re-evaluates the administrator floor LIVE on every interaction rather than locking the panel to its invoker, which is what makes one builder safely back two surfaces: the persistent anchored !servermanagement panel (restored across restart via message_anchor_manager.restore_anchors) and the ephemeral /server-management slash. Counted 2 consuming surfaces of build_server_management_hub in server_management_cog.py (lines 52 and 89) plus a third via build_help_menu_view for the help router.
strengths.quote:
async def interaction_check(self, interaction: discord.Interaction) -> bool:
        if interaction_is_admin(interaction):
            return True
        await interaction.response.send_message(
            "❌ You need **Administrator** permission to use the Server "
            "Management hub.",
            ephemeral=True,
        )
        return False
strengths.prevents_failure: a persistent admin panel outliving the admin role of whoever opened it — after a restart the anchored message is still clickable, and an ownership-only gate would let a demoted member keep operating it
strengths.successor_recommendation: Make authority-re-check-at-click the DEFAULT for every persistent panel in the successor, not a per-panel opt-in. Superbot has both patterns (ownership-locked BaseView and authority-gated) and the choice is per-panel prose; that is a bug factory at 314 panels.

strengths.claim: The setup-copy jargon ratchet is a well-shaped guard over the real view source: check_setup_copy.py AST-walks every *.py under disbot/views/setup/, and the invariant test enforces TWO assertions instead of a line-numbered baseline — a count ceiling (_BASELINE_TOTAL = 133, and the current count is EXACTLY 133, i.e. zero headroom) and a file-set guard that fails on any finding in a file not already in the 24-file dirty set. Measured: script EXIT=0 with count 133 across 24 files; pytest EXIT=0, 7 passed.
strengths.quote:
Why two assertions rather than a frozen 207-line baseline: line numbers shift
constantly, so a per-line baseline is noise.  The two real regressions we must
catch are (a) an existing file growing *more* jargon and (b) a brand-new setup
section shipping with jargon — a count ceiling catches (a), the file-set guard
catches (b).
strengths.contradicts: The plan this guard enforces calls zero-jargon 'Law 2' and check_setup_copy.py's own docstring calls it a 'ratchet', but the script's default --mode report exits 0 with 133 live violations and it is NOT run in any workflow — the only enforcement is the pytest invariant. A reader of the script alone would wrongly conclude the law is unenforced; a reader of the plan alone would wrongly conclude it is satisfied.
strengths.prevents_failure: a new setup section shipping with Discord-internal vocabulary ('draft', 'binding', 'subsystem', 'operation') in front of a non-technical server owner
strengths.guard_population: Every *.py under disbot/views/setup/ — real shipped view source, currently 24 files with findings out of 33+. Non-empty and not a model. The known hole is the prose heuristic: a string only counts as operator-facing copy if it CONTAINS A SPACE, so a one-word jargon label ('Draft', 'Bindings') as a button label passes silently. The script's own docstring admits this.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port count-ceiling + file-set instead of a golden baseline — it survives refactors. But fix the population hole: extract copy from typed label/description fields (button label=, embed title=) rather than guessing prose by whitespace, so single-word labels are in scope.

strengths.claim: guild_lifecycle.teardown deliberately PRESERVES the forensic audit trail while purging live state: delete_active_bindings_for_guild drops subsystem_bindings but binding_audit_log is retained, and the purge primitive purge_binding_audit_for_guild is documented as never called from teardown. 25 tests in test_guild_lifecycle_teardown.py pin this plus per-step failure isolation (one failing step does not abort the sweep) and idempotency.
strengths.quote:
5. Subsystem bindings     — delete active subsystem_bindings rows (Phase 2);
                                   binding_audit_log rows are PRESERVED by design.
strengths.prevents_failure: a guild leaving (accidentally, or during a support incident) destroying the only record of who bound what, so a re-invited server cannot be reconstructed and abuse cannot be investigated
strengths.guard_population: The retention test asserts that one specific named primitive is never awaited during a mocked teardown. Population = one function name. It is a MODEL of teardown (AsyncMock patches, no database), so it proves the call is not made, not that the rows survive. See M1-D06 for what this population does NOT cover.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep 'purge live state, retain audit' as a first-class rule in the successor's data model — encode it as a table-level attribute (guild_scoped_live vs guild_scoped_audit) so teardown is DERIVED from the schema rather than hand-listed.

strengths.claim: views/setup/recovery.py is a genuine mid-journey recovery surface, not an error dump: a 4-field structured embed (What happened / Why / Recommended / If skipped) plus Continue / Retry / Skip section / Customize / Cancel, where the mutating buttons re-check can_apply_setup against a FRESH session snapshot rather than trusting the snapshot captured when the panel was built. Counted 2 mount sites, both in views/setup/wizard.py (lines 587 and 610).
strengths.quote:
The embed surfaces four operator-facing fields:

* **What happened** — one-line human cause ("I couldn't read the
  channel list").
* **Why** — permission / feature reason ("Manage Channels missing").
* **Recommended** — one actionable suggestion ("Grant Manage Channels
  and press Retry").
* **If skipped** — the consequence ("Logging defaults stay
  unconfigured; you can revisit `/setup-skip`").
strengths.contradicts: recovery.py's own module docstring says 'the section module catches the exception, fills in a RecoveryContext, and mounts a SectionRecoveryView'. Measured: ZERO of the 11 modules in disbot/views/setup/sections/ import SectionRecoveryView, RecoveryContext or views.setup.recovery. The only importer in all of disbot/ is views/setup/wizard.py:434. The documented per-section contract does not exist; a single wizard-level helper does.
strengths.prevents_failure: an operator stranded mid-wizard by a missing bot permission, shown a traceback or nothing at all, with no statement of what broke or what happens if they skip
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port the four-field embed shape and the re-check-on-mutate rule. But make recovery a property of the step RUNNER (one wrapper around every step callback) rather than something each callback opts into — superbot proves the opt-in version reaches 2 of 7 wizard callbacks and 0 of 11 sections.

strengths.claim: Both admission gates surface the resolver's own user-facing reason before returning False, and log a structured deny line with guild/channel/user/command/reason/source/mode — so a policy denial is a visible decision rather than discord.py's silent CheckFailure. Two consumers (prefix _channel_guard, slash _slash_access_check), each with a surface-appropriate delivery (delete_after=10 vs ephemeral), and DM/lifecycle denials deliberately carry feedback=None so the bot stays silent while shutting down.
strengths.quote:
# Surface the resolver's user-facing feedback before returning
        # False — otherwise the CheckFailure raised by discord.py
        # produces no reply and the operator sees the same "invoked
        # but not completed" silent failure that PR-4 was written to
        # eliminate.  Lifecycle / DM denials carry feedback=None on
        # purpose and stay silent.
strengths.prevents_failure: the silent-denial class: an operator types a command, nothing happens, and there is no way for them or for support to tell whether the bot is down, lacks permission, or the channel is not allowlisted
strengths.successor_recommendation: Make 'a denial must produce both a user-visible reason and a structured log line' a contract the successor's gate framework enforces, not a per-gate courtesy. Component interactions currently get neither (see M1-D05).

defects.claim: Staged setup-wizard operations survive a guild leaving and are re-read on re-invite. guild_lifecycle.teardown deletes the setup_session row (step 18) but NEVER touches setup_draft_operations — grep for 'setup_draft_operations' in disbot/guild_lifecycle.py returns 0 hits — and migration 035 declares the table with NO foreign key to setup_session, so nothing cascades. Meanwhile the read path list_rows() filters on guild_id ALONE, ignoring the session_started_at column it selects.
defects.quote:
async def list_rows(guild_id: int) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:

        SELECT id, guild_id, session_started_at, seq, op_kind, subsystem,
               binding_name, setting_name, target_id, target_name, target_kind,
               value_raw, resource_mode, resource_name, existing_id,
               automation_rule_id, automation_rule_name, trigger_kind,
               action_kind, trigger_config_json, action_config_json,
               schedule, timezone, actor_id, label, metadata_json, created_at,
               section_slug, staging_kind, group_id, parent_seq
          FROM setup_draft_operations
         WHERE guild_id = $1
         ORDER BY seq ASC
defects.contradicts: guild_lifecycle.py's module docstring: 'Centralises all cleanup that must happen when the bot leaves a guild, so that no module accumulates permanent per-guild state indefinitely. Every module that owns guild-scoped in-process state must be represented here.' setup_draft_operations is guild-scoped and is not represented.
defects.failure_scenario: An owner runs !setupadvanced, stages draft operations in Final Review (e.g. 'bind mod-log to #staff-logs', 'create role @Moderator'), never presses Apply, and removes the bot. Teardown deletes setup_session; the draft rows stay forever. Months later the owner re-invites the bot and opens !setupadvanced: a fresh session row is created, but list_rows(guild_id) returns the OLD staged operations — pointing at channel and role IDs that were deleted in the interim. Final Review presents them as this session's pending work, and Apply either binds dead IDs or fails mid-batch.
defects.new_failure_class: cross-install state resurrection
defects.successor_recommendation: Every guild-scoped staging table must FK to the session that owns it with ON DELETE CASCADE, and every read must be scoped by session identity, not by guild_id. Do not rely on a hand-maintained teardown list to catch this.

defects.claim: The provisioning pipeline's confirmation gate is unreachable in production: all 3 of 3 production call sites of ResourceProvisioningPipeline().provision() hardcode confirmed=True — services/readiness_repair.py:382-387, services/automation_executor.py:427-432, services/setup_operations.py:1352-1358. The ProvisioningConfirmationRequired exception at resource_provisioning.py:409 can therefore never be raised by any operator-reachable path.
defects.contradicts: resource_provisioning.py's own 'Hard limits for S4.5' section, lines 66-70: 'No silent auto-create.  ``mode='create'`` always requires ``confirmed=True``'. The gate is satisfied by the caller asserting confirmation, not by a human giving it, so it constrains nothing.
defects.failure_scenario: An operator saves an automation rule with action_kind='create_channel'. The scheduler later fires execute_rule with dry_run=False and no human present; _handle_create_channel calls provision(..., confirmed=True) and a real Discord channel is created in the server with nobody watching. The pipeline records it as a confirmed provisioning in resource_provisioning_audit, so the audit log cannot distinguish it from an operator-confirmed creation.
defects.new_failure_class: confirmation laundering — the audit trail records consent that was never given
defects.successor_recommendation: A confirmation gate must consume a token that only a UI confirmation step can mint (a nonce written by the preview call and redeemed once by apply), never a boolean the caller supplies. Otherwise the gate is a comment.

defects.claim: The operator-facing preview→Apply→confirm journey for resource provisioning has ZERO production callers. disbot/views/setup/provisioning/ (450 lines: preview_panel.py 197, confirm_panel.py 219, __init__.py 34) is imported by nothing in disbot/ outside its own package — grep for 'views.setup.provisioning' across disbot/ returns only self-references and the package __init__. Its only other consumers are 11 tests in tests/unit/views/setup/provisioning/test_provisioning_panels.py (384 lines).
defects.quote:
"""Provisioning UI adapters — Track 3 PR 7.

Two panels that surface the
:class:`~services.resource_provisioning.ResourceProvisioningPipeline`
through the standard
:class:`~disbot.views.base.BaseView` shell:

* :class:`~disbot.views.setup.provisioning.preview_panel.PreviewPanelView`
  — renders ``pipeline.preview(...)`` output and offers Apply / Cancel
  buttons.
defects.contradicts: This is a second, independent instance of the pattern the prompt already confirmed twice (superbot-next's golden test over a cleared registry; superbot's help-reachability model). Here the tests are green over a real artifact that no user can reach — 384 test lines and 11 tests proving the behaviour of a panel with no door.
defects.failure_scenario: An operator following the setup wizard to create a mod-log channel never sees the preview panel's 'already bound? name collision? category exists?' warnings, because the only path into provisioning is setup_operations.py:1352, which calls provision(confirmed=True) directly from Final Review's apply loop. The collision warnings the preview computes (resource_provisioning.py:272-345) are produced and discarded — so the operator gets a second #mod-log channel with no warning that one already existed.
defects.successor_recommendation: Delete on port. Then, in the successor, make 'a panel is reachable' a build-time fact: every view class must be registered against a route, and a route-less view fails the build. Do not carry 450 lines of orphaned UI plus 384 lines of tests that certify it.

defects.claim: check_settings_reachability.py certifies reachability from a SOURCE LITERAL, never from the live catalogue, and its verdict is tautological. It reports '19 reachable · 3 exempt · 0 GAP' (measured, EXIT=0) where 'reachable' means only that a `SubsystemSchema(subsystem="X")` call literal appears in cogs/<sub>/schemas.py and visibility_mode != 'internal' — which is also the filter for being examined at all, so a schema-declaring subsystem can never be reported as a gap. Measured divergence from the real rule: after importing all 19 cogs/*/schemas.py modules, all_schemas() returned 0 registered schemas and actionable_settings_groups() returned 0 groups, because registration requires each cog's cog_load to call register_schemas(). defects.claim: The provisioning pipeline has no rollback: when the Discord resource is created successfully but the binding write fails, the channel or role stays in the server unbound and the operator is told to clean it up by hand. This is stated as designed behaviour in the 11-step contract, and the failure is only surfaced as an audit outcome string ('binding_failed', emitted at resource_provisioning.py:538 and :564).

8. Bind the resource through
     :meth:`services.binding_mutation.BindingMutationPipeline.set_binding`.
     Binding failure does NOT roll back the created Discord resource —
     it is audited as ``binding_failed`` so the operator can manually
     re-bind or clean up.
defects.failure_scenario: An owner in Final Review applies 'create #mod-log and bind it to moderation.log_channel'. The channel is created; the binding INSERT fails (pool exhausted mid-deploy, or a unique-constraint race with a concurrent setup session). setup_operations.py:1360 logs a warning and marks the op failed. The owner sees 'failed', re-runs Final Review, and guild_resources.ensure_channel resolves the channel it just made BY NAME and reuses it — so the second attempt appears to work while the first attempt's audit row still says binding_failed. If instead the operator renamed the orphan first, they get a second #mod-log. Either way the server now contains channels the setup flow created and does not know about.
defects.successor_recommendation: Provisioning must be a transaction with a compensating action: write the binding intent first, create the resource second, and on binding failure delete the just-created resource (it is provably unreferenced) or park it in a reconciliation queue. 'The operator can manually clean up' is not a rollback story for a bot whose whole value is not making the owner do server admin by hand.

strengths.claim: Every coin debit in this mass that matters for money-safety composes one primitive — a single conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE coins >= $amount RETURNING coins` (no read-then-write) — via `economy_service.debit_in_txn`/`credit_in_txn`. Counted 7 of this mass's own service files calling it: mining_workflow.py, fishing_workflow.py, farm_workflow.py, skill_service.py, shop_purchase_workflow.py, treasury_service.py, game_wager_workflow.py — spanning mining, fishing, farming, skills, the shop, the treasury, and PvP/tournament wagers. Two of those sites (shop_purchase_workflow, game_wager_workflow) name a real historical production bug this exact mechanism replaced: FIND-RS01, 'double-click → double charge.'
strengths.quote:
async def try_debit_coins(
    user_id: int,
    guild_id: int,
    amount: int,
    *,
    conn: asyncpg.Connection | None = None,
) -> int | None:
    """Conditionally subtract *amount* coins; ``None`` when unaffordable.

    The conditional UPDATE (``coins >= $3``) decides affordability and
    writes in one statement, eliminating the read-then-write race of the
    legacy ``get_coins`` + ``add_coins`` pair.
    """
    row = await pool.fetchone(
        """UPDATE xp SET coins = xp.coins - $3
           WHERE user_id=$1 AND guild_id=$2 AND coins >= $3
           RETURNING coins""",
        (user_id, guild_id, amount),
        conn=conn,
    )
    return row["coins"] if row else None
strengths.contradicts: The pattern itself is sound and widely reused, but is NOT universal in this codebase — see M3-D1 (the reward-cooldown gate uses the legacy read-then-write shape this primitive exists to replace) and M3-D3 (a documented 'public API' function, bet_and_settle, that never adopted it and has the race live inside it). The primitive being good does not mean the mass is uniformly safe.
strengths.prevents_failure: double-charge / double-spend via a read-then-write race on a coin or unique-item debit — named production bug FIND-RS01 ('both shop-panel callbacks previously debited coins and granted the item as two separately-committed legs... racy (double-click → double charge)', shop_purchase_workflow.py:3-6) and the P0-1 wager-mint/short-pay class (game_wager_workflow.py:8-14)
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port this one primitive (conditional-UPDATE debit + the debit_in_txn/credit_in_txn wrapper) as the successor's ONLY coin-mutation path from day one, and make its use structurally mandatory (an AST/import-linter fence, not a convention) so the cooldown-gate exception in M3-D1 cannot recur.

strengths.claim: PvP wagers and tournament entries move through `game_wager_workflow.py`'s escrow-at-accept + idempotent-settle design: `open_pvp_wager` debits both stakes and writes 1 checkpoint row per player in ONE transaction; `settle_pvp`/`refund_pvp` lock those rows `FOR UPDATE` and treat their absence (already consumed) as a no-op. Counted 6 distinct call-site files across 2 independently-built game families: rps_tournament_cog.py, blackjack_cog.py, views/rps/pvp_play.py, views/rps/pvp_challenge.py, views/blackjack/tournament_views.py, views/blackjack/pvp_view.py.
strengths.quote:
* ``settle_pvp`` / ``refund_pvp`` pay the escrowed pot out (to the
  winner, or back to each player on a tie/abort) and delete the escrow
  rows in one transaction.  Both are **idempotent**: they ``FOR UPDATE``
  the escrow rows, and a replay that finds them already gone is a no-op
  — a crash-retry or a double settle can never double-pay.
strengths.contradicts: See M3-D2: the real-Postgres integration suite that would prove this idempotency claim under an actual crash-retry (test_game_wager_workflow_integration.py) unconditionally self-skips in the only CI lane that runs pytest, since DATABASE_URL is never set there. The mechanism itself is source-enforced (the FOR UPDATE + row-deletion runs on every real invocation regardless of tests), but its CI proof is not — do not cite this pattern as 'CI-verified' without also citing that gap.
strengths.prevents_failure: coin-mint via partial-credit after a mid-transaction crash (winner credited, loser's debit skipped) and double-pay via a replayed/duplicate settle call — the two named P0-1 production bug classes the module's own docstring says predate this design
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve escrow-at-accept as the successor's standard shape for any two-party or paid-entry wager, but pair it with a CI lane that actually spins up Postgres for the integration suite (mirror parity-replay.yml's `services: postgres:` block) rather than a lane that silently skips.

strengths.claim: A single, generic restart-safe checkpoint table (`game_state`, migration 015) backs in-flight game sessions across this mass, with the invariant enforced by a real DB constraint, not application logic: UNIQUE(guild_id, user_id, channel_id, subsystem). A companion GC sweep (`game_state_cleanup.sweep_stale_game_state`) auto-refunds any stranded row whose JSONB payload carries a positive `bet` key before deleting it. Counted 6 consumer files spanning blackjack + RPS tournament + the shared wager workflow: blackjack_cog.py, rps_tournament/_persistence.py, blackjack_persistence.py, game_wager_workflow.py, views/rps/pvp_challenge.py, views/rps/pvp_play.py.
strengths.quote:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS game_state (
    id           BIGINT      GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    guild_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    user_id      BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    channel_id   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    subsystem    TEXT        NOT NULL,
    state        JSONB       NOT NULL,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    CONSTRAINT uq_game_state UNIQUE (guild_id, user_id, channel_id, subsystem)
);
strengths.contradicts: Not adopted everywhere in this same mass: casino/poker_table.py explicitly opts out ('v1 uses table play-chips ... In-flight table state is in-memory and not restart-safe by design (ADR-002), exactly like blackjack/RPS') — verified as a deliberate, documented, no-real-money choice rather than an oversight, so not filed as a defect, but it means 'session lifecycle' is not yet a uniform contract across every game in this mass.
strengths.prevents_failure: two concurrent in-flight games silently coexisting for the same (player, channel, subsystem) after a crash, and a stake that is permanently lost when a game is abandoned mid-session (the GC sweep refunds it by convention on the shared `bet` payload key instead)
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve the (guild,user,channel,subsystem)-unique checkpoint table and the bet-keyed auto-refund GC convention verbatim; extend it to any new game that wants restart-safety instead of building a bespoke table per feature.

strengths.claim: Leaderboards are a genuinely working plugin seam: `rank_providers.py` defines an ABC (`RankProvider`, `top()`+`member_rank()` both abstract) and a registry read by exactly 2 host surfaces (leaderboard_cog, xp_cog); this mass supplies 7 independently-registered concrete providers — Mining, Creatures, Fishing, Farm, GameXp, Deathmatch, Rps (plus an 8th, Crafting, adjacent but not separately named in this lane's scope) — none of which required editing either host cog to add.
strengths.quote:
The registry is read via :func:`get_provider` (alias-aware) and
:func:`provider_names`. ``leaderboard_cog`` and ``xp_cog`` are the
two consumers; new categories are added by registering a provider
here, not by editing either cog.
strengths.successor_recommendation: This is the genuine answer to Q2's 'which pattern is separable' for leaderboards specifically: a new game gets ranked visibility by writing one small RankProvider subclass and registering it — worth preserving as the model for how any per-game feature should plug into a shared cross-cutting service, in contrast to M3-D5's world_registry, where the same idea exists but 2 of 3 real examples don't actually follow it.
