defects.claim: The escape-hatch ratchet — declared 'required CI from the first kernel PR through post-cutover, NO EXPIRY' — counts ONLY tier-3 `view:` refs. The snapshot contains ZERO occurrences of '"view:' (counted in manifest.snapshot.json) and the committed baseline is `"per_subsystem": {}, "total": 0`. Meanwhile the tier-2 hatch it explicitly does not count, `renderer_override`, is set on 218 of 314 panels (69%) — 40 in setup, 27 in ai, 13 in fishing, 10 in mining, 10 in utility, 9 in channel, 8 in cleanup, 8 in settings, 7 in btd6, 6 in creature. Ran it: `python3 tools/check_escape_hatches.py` → EXIT=0, 'check_escape_hatches: clean'.
defects.quote:
Tier-3 units counted from the compiled snapshot:
  - every `{"$ref": "view:..."}` occurrence (a ViewRef IS the §2.9 tier-3
    re-homed-legacy-view escape hatch) — its carrying node must declare a
    non-empty `justification`;
  - every node carrying `tier: 3` or a truthy `escape_hatch` marker.
Also red: `sb/domain/<x>/ui/` modules unreachable from any registered ref.
defects.contradicts: sb/kernel/panels/engine.py:2-4 — 'One kernel runtime interprets every grammar-expressible PanelSpec … no per-panel view class.' 69% of registered panels supply their own renderer callable, so the majority of the UI does have a per-panel renderer; the engine is the dispatcher, not the interpreter, for those. It also contradicts the plain reading of a green escape-hatch ratchet: 'clean' here means 'the population is zero', not 'the escape hatches are under control'.
defects.failure_scenario: An engineer opens a PR that adds the 219th renderer_override panel. CI is green and the escape-hatch ratchet prints 'clean', because the ratchet's baseline total is 0 and the only thing it counts (tier-3 `view:` refs) is still 0. Nothing on any surface tells the author, the reviewer, or the owner that the declarative panel grammar has just been bypassed again. The ratchet was built precisely to stop this drift and it cannot see it.
defects.new_failure_class: A 'clean' ratchet reading is now positive evidence of health to any reader, while the drift it was built to stop is at 69% and rising unmeasured.
defects.successor_recommendation: In the successor, the ratchet must count EVERY escape from the declarative path — tier-2 included — and its baseline must be minted from the real compiled population on day one. A ratchet whose baseline is 0 because it counts nothing is worse than no ratchet.

defects.claim: Compiler pass P6's `audit_completeness` predicate keys on a field named `effect`, and ZERO of the 3,552 spec objects it walks have an `effect` attribute (measured with hasattr over the live P1 load of all 49 manifests). The same is true of the `action_cooldown_parity` check five lines below, which is gated on the same `effect == "mutating"`. Both are permanently green over the empty set.
defects.contradicts: tools/manifest_compile.py:17-18 names audit_completeness as one of 'the six predicates' the compiler enforces, and sb/kernel/workflow/compile.py:9-13 describes a spec-side 'audit_completeness' half. The estate reads the compiler as the thing that makes audit non-optional. It does not: 640 declared panel actions and 413 commands pass through P6 and not one of them can trigger this predicate, because no spec class in sb/spec/ declares an `effect` field (there is no `*.effect` key in the snapshot's 318-entry field_roles map).
defects.failure_scenario: A port band declares a panel action whose handler is a HandlerRef that writes the database directly instead of a WorkflowRef. `python3 tools/manifest_compile.py` exits 0, CI is green, the panel ships. The mutation lands with no audit_log row and no audit.action_recorded event, so the guild's audit channel silently misses it — and the one compiler predicate whose job is to catch exactly that never evaluated the action.
defects.new_failure_class: The compiler's green exit is read as 'every mutating declaration is audited'. It means 'no declaration claimed to be mutating', which nothing can.
defects.successor_recommendation: Either add the `effect` field to CommandSpec/PanelActionSpec and make it required, or drop the predicate. A named predicate whose population is provably 0 must fail loudly at compile time ('predicate X evaluated 0 candidates'), not pass quietly.

defects.claim: Two more P6 sub-checks are structurally unreachable. (a) `leaderboard_writer` keys on `_spec_name(spec) == "LeaderboardSpec"`; there are 0 LeaderboardSpec instances among the 3,552 walked objects (LeaderboardSpec does not appear in the snapshot's field_roles at all). (b) `never_strand: panel has no NavigationSpec` tests `navigation is None`, but PanelSpec declares `navigation: NavigationSpec = NavigationSpec()` — a non-None default — so it can never fire; the snapshot carries a navigation node on all 314 panels.
defects.contradicts: The 'never_strand' name and superbot's own inherited contract (disbot/views/navigation.py:53-54: 'the two standard-nav controls auto-attached to every subsystem panel (the "never stranded" contract — owner directive 2026-06-23)'). superbot-next's never_strand does NOT check that a panel offers navigation — it checks that a field with a non-None default is non-None. The owner directive it inherits is not enforced by the predicate that carries its name.
defects.failure_scenario: An author declares a panel with `NavigationSpec(show_home=False, show_help=False)` and no parent. The compiler's never_strand predicate passes (navigation is not None), the panel registers, and it renders with no Back, no Home and no Help — see M9-D05 for four such panels that are reachable by a button today.
defects.new_failure_class: A predicate named after an owner directive gives false assurance that the directive is enforced.
defects.successor_recommendation: Rewrite never_strand to assert what its name says: every non-terminal panel must render at least one navigation affordance, evaluated over the REGISTERED population by actually rendering it (my probe does this in ~30 lines).

defects.claim: The `destructive_confirmation` predicate's population is 2 of 640 declared panel actions (0.3%): 638 of 640 carry `destructive=False` and 638 of 640 carry `confirm=None`. Only 35 of 640 declare a non-empty `audit` string. Both `destructive` and `confirm` are opt-in booleans/objects with no cross-check against what the action's handler actually does.
defects.contradicts: The compiler's framing of destructive_confirmation as one of the six load-bearing semantic predicates. It is load-bearing over two actions. The 175 registered CompoundOpSpecs, by contrast, are 100% audited — so the mutation layer is protected and the CLICK layer that reaches it is protected on 0.3% of its surface.
defects.failure_scenario: A guild admin opens a panel and clicks a button whose handler resets every member's XP (or clears a warning history). The action's author did not set destructive=True, so no ConfirmationSpec is required, no typed challenge is demanded, and the compiler is green. The click executes immediately with no confirm step. Nothing in the declaration or the compiler connects 'this handler deletes rows' to 'this button must confirm'.
defects.successor_recommendation: Derive destructiveness from the op the action routes to (the CompoundOpSpec already declares reversibility and audit_verb) rather than from an opt-in boolean on the button. Then the predicate's population is every action that routes to a destructive op, not the two whose authors remembered.

defects.claim: Measured by rendering all 314 registered panels through the real engine: 150 of 314 render ZERO engine-injected nav components, and 51 of 314 render ZERO components of any kind. Four of those 51 are reachable by a button or select on another panel: community.hub.co_counters → counters.status; fishing.hub.fishing_log → fishing.log; games.world.world_card → games.world_card; community.hub.co_welcome → welcome.status. 148 of 314 panels explicitly declare show_home=False AND show_help=False AND no parent, overriding the NavigationSpec defaults which are both True.
defects.quote:
parent: PanelRef | None = None              # [S]
    home_hub: str = FOLLOW_PARENT               # [S] the routing RULE, not a captured value
    show_help: bool = True                      # [S] the nav:help slot (custom_id verbatim)
    show_home: bool = True                      # [S] the nav:hub:<hub> slot (hub-keyed [S] mint)
    show_rules: bool = False                    # [S]
    extra_routes: tuple[NavRouteSpec, ...] = () # [S]
defects.contradicts: The prompt's confirmed finding that tests/unit/navigation_golden/test_navigation_completeness.py is vacuously green over the empty set — my measurement supplies what that golden would have found had it run over the registry: four button-reachable panels with no way back. It also contradicts the inherited 'never stranded' contract at disbot/views/navigation.py:53-54.
defects.failure_scenario: A member opens the Community hub and clicks 'Counters'. The engine opens counters.status, which renders an embed and zero components — no Back, no Home, no Help. The member has no in-UI route back to the Community hub and must retype a prefix command. Same for the Fishing hub's 'Fishing Log' button, the Games world card, and the Community hub's 'Welcome' button.
defects.successor_recommendation: Make 'renders at least one navigation affordance' a property the engine guarantees for any panel opened as a navigation DESTINATION, with terminal result cards a separately typed thing that cannot be a nav target. Assert it by rendering the registered population in CI.

defects.claim: The durable outbox — 763 LOC across enqueue.py, store.py, relay.py, metrics.py, plus an event_outbox table, dedup keys, a relay lane and a hard in-txn name-guard — serves exactly ONE event. Measured after a full manifest boot: KNOWN_EVENTS holds 25 names, of which 24 are DeliveryClass.BEST_EFFORT and 1 is AT_LEAST_ONCE ('audit.action_recorded'). The UnknownEventError name-guard's population is therefore 1.
defects.contradicts: sb/kernel/outbox/enqueue.py:1-8 presents the outbox as the general no-phantom/no-lost-event spine ('the event exists iff the effect committed'). At this pin it guarantees that for one event out of 25. My own earlier reading that KNOWN_EVENTS held only 1 entry was WRONG — it was measured before load_live_manifests(); the corrected figure is 25 total, 1 durable.
defects.failure_scenario: A member levels up. `xp.level_up` is BEST_EFFORT, so it is emitted through EventBus.emit after commit. The subscriber sb/domain/xp/service.py:_route_level_up raises (channel deleted, permission removed) — EventBus.emit catches it, logs, and returns; or the process restarts between the commit and the post-commit emit. Either way the level-up announcement is lost with no retry and no record, which is precisely the class the outbox exists to eliminate, and the same class superbot has today.
defects.successor_recommendation: Either promote the events that actually must not be lost (xp.level_up, moderation.action_taken, economy.balance_changed) onto the durable lane so the machinery earns its 763 LOC, or delete the durable lane and keep the audit row as the forensic record.

defects.claim: The declared event graph and the running one disagree. All 23 EventSpecs across the 49 manifests declare `expected_subscribers=()` (0 of 23 non-empty) and `observability_only=False` (0 of 23 true) and `audited=False` (0 of 23 true) — so the compiler's `delivery_declared` subscriber fence iterates an empty tuple every time. Meanwhile the running bot has 9 real `bus.on(...)` subscriptions in 5 domain modules (community/spotlight.py, channel/service.py, economy/service.py, server_logging/service.py ×3, xp/service.py) plus one in sb/app/main.py — none of them declared.
defects.quote:
for sub_ref in _get(spec, "expected_subscribers", ()) or ():
                        if not _handler_accepts_reserved_keys(sub_ref):
                            flag(key, locus,
                                 "delivery_declared: effectful subscriber "
                                 f"{getattr(sub_ref, 'name', sub_ref)!r} cannot receive "
                                 "the reserved _outbox_* delivery keys "
                                 "(declare **kwargs or an explicit _outbox_dedup_key)")
defects.contradicts: sb/spec/events.py:20-22 — 'KNOWN_EVENTS is the name -> EventSpec registry the enqueue name-guard and the relay read. It is populated by the manifest build (each subsystem's events facet)'. The name half is populated and real (25 names); the SUBSCRIBER half of the same declarations is empty on all 23, so the manifest cannot answer 'who listens to this event', which is the question a rebuild most needs it to answer.
defects.failure_scenario: Someone renames or retires `xp.level_up` in sb/manifest/xp.py. The compiler is green — no declaration references a subscriber. The bot boots. sb/domain/community/spotlight.py:43 still calls `bus.on("xp.level_up", _on_level_up)` on a name nothing emits any more, so community spotlight silently stops firing, with no error at compile time, boot time or run time.
defects.successor_recommendation: Make subscription a declaration, not a call: if `bus.on(name, handler)` is only reachable through a declared EventSpec.expected_subscribers, the compiler can prove the graph. Today the graph exists only in Python.

defects.claim: Of the 237 distinct field names the 318-entry field_roles map declares, 87 are never given a non-default value anywhere in the compiled snapshot of all 49 subsystems, and 20 more are non-default 3 times or fewer — 107 of 237 (45%). 37 of the 87 belong to spec classes that DO appear (alt_text 0/314, co_open_group 0/314, show_rules 0/314, legacy_view 0/314, thumbnail_ref 0/314, co_use_group 0/640, result_card 0/640, flow_stage 0/640, enabled_when 0/413, help_section_order 0/413, quota_ref 0/413, advanced/bound_binding/co_edit_group/depends_on/keyed_secret/legacy_keys/panel_order/validator all 0/102, active_rows_ref/cache_scope/compensation_ref/is_cache/replay_intent/retire_ref/upcast_ref all 0/74, audited/expected_subscribers/observability_only/redaction_ref/resource_link all 0/23, default_enforce/ground_truth_store/tolerance 0/4, capabilities 0/49, step 0/10). I then grepped sb/kernel + sb/adapters + sb/app for readers of ten of them: quota_ref, result_card, co_use_group, show_rules, panel_order and legacy_keys have ZERO readers anywhere in the kernel, adapters or app.
defects.line_span: field_roles map, 318 entries (parsed with python3 json; not read as text)
defects.quote: "PanelActionSpec.result_card": "S", "PanelActionSpec.co_use_group": "S", "PanelActionSpec.flow_stage": "S", "CommandSpec.quota_ref": "S", "NavigationSpec.show_rules": "S", "SettingSpec.panel_order": "S", "SettingSpec.legacy_keys": "S"
defects.contradicts: The reading that the manifest is 'the declaration of what the bot is'. Nearly half of its vocabulary declares nothing, and six sampled fields are serialized into a 2.2 MB committed artifact, role-tagged by compiler pass P5, and read by no code in the kernel, the adapters or the app.
defects.failure_scenario: An engineer sets `result_card=...` on a panel action, or `quota_ref="ai.daily"` on a command, because the grammar offers the field and the field_roles map tags it [S]. The compiler accepts it, the snapshot serializes it, CI is green — and nothing reads it, so the result card never renders and the quota is never enforced. There is no diagnostic anywhere that a declared, role-tagged, committed field has no consumer.
defects.new_failure_class: A declaration language whose fields can be silent no-ops is more dangerous than no declaration language, because setting a field looks like configuring behaviour.
defects.successor_recommendation: Ship the successor's grammar with a compile-time rule: every declared field must have at least one reader in the kernel, proven by the compiler, or it is not in the grammar. Grow the vocabulary when a consumer exists, never before.

defects.claim: There are 92 module-level `clear_*_for_tests` / `reset_*_for_tests` functions across sb/ (counted by grep), each guarding a process-global mutable dict — 23 module-level registry dicts in sb/kernel alone. Test isolation is therefore a hand-maintained roster that must be duplicated per pytest directory, and the conftest that produced the known-vacuous navigation golden says so in its own docstring.
defects.quote:
"""Clean panel/locale state for the A-3 navigation-completeness golden
(the same reset roster as tests/unit/panels — duplicated because pytest
test dirs are independent top-level packages here)."""
defects.contradicts: The 'one source of truth' framing of the registries. There is one static custom-id table and one panel registry — but there are 92 independent global registries with 92 bespoke reset functions and no single reset entry point, which is what turned an autouse fixture into a permanently green golden over zero panels.
defects.failure_scenario: An engineer adds tests/unit/<newdir>/ and copies the nearest conftest's reset roster, which is missing one of the 92 (say reset_router_for_tests). Tests in that directory now inherit router state from whatever ran before them in the same process; the suite passes or fails depending on collection order, and the failure is attributed to the new test rather than to the missing reset. The already-confirmed instance of this pattern is the navigation golden, which walks a registry its own autouse fixture just cleared and is green over 0 panels forever.
defects.successor_recommendation: One registry container, constructed per test (and per process at boot), passed explicitly. No module-level mutable registries, so there is no reset roster to forget and no way to write a guard over an emptied one.

defects.claim: A failing panel data provider is swallowed and the panel renders anyway. Observed live: rendering all 314 panels logged 'panel provider <name> failed … RuntimeError: Database not initialised' for multiple providers (xp.hub_overview among them) and render_panel still returned a RenderedPanel for all 314 with 0 exceptions raised. There are 197 registered provider refs.
defects.quote:
async def _provider_rows(ref, ctx: PanelContext):
    """Resolve + call a ProviderRef; a broken provider degrades to None
    (the block renders its empty_state), never a crashed panel."""
    if ref is None:
        return None
    try:
        provider = resolve_ref(ref)
        return await provider(ctx)
    except RefUnresolved:
        logger.warning("panel provider %r unresolved", getattr(ref, "name", ref))
        return None
    except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 — a data provider never takes the panel down
        logger.warning("panel provider %r failed", getattr(ref, "name", ref), exc_info=True)
        return None
defects.contradicts: 'a data provider never takes the panel down' reads as a resilience feature. Combined with `EmptyResultSpec.user_message` being ABSENT from the snapshot (0 instances) and `empty_state` unpopulated on the block specs, the degraded render has nothing distinguishing to say — so the user sees a normal-looking panel with a missing section.
defects.failure_scenario: The XP store query fails (transient DB error, migration in flight). The member runs !xpmenu, the hub renders with the rank fields simply absent, and the member reads it as 'I have no XP'. Nothing in the embed, and nothing returned to the caller, distinguishes 'no data' from 'the query failed' — the only trace is a WARNING in the bot log.
defects.new_failure_class: Silent data loss presented as valid state, on 197 provider-fed blocks.
defects.successor_recommendation: Keep the panel alive, but make degradation visible: the block must render a distinct 'couldn't load this' state, and the render result must carry a degraded flag the presenter and the metrics can see.

defects.claim: Measured on two subsystems, the manifest layer is a small share of the feature and buys a modest net reduction, not an order of magnitude. XP: sb/manifest/xp.py is 184 LOC of 2,390 total (7.7%); the whole feature is 2,390 LOC in superbot-next vs 2,989 in superbot (views/xp 1,125 + services/xp_* 846 + cogs 850 + utils/db/xp.py 168) = 20.0% smaller. MODERATION: sb/manifest/moderation.py is 154 LOC of 1,642 (9.4%); 1,642 vs 2,886 in superbot (views 542 + services 1,393 + cogs 815 + utils/db 136) = 43.1% smaller. The 'declarative' panel files are not pure declaration: sb/domain/settings/panels.py is 2,567 LOC containing 73 function definitions and 13 PanelSpec constructions; sb/domain/ai/panels.py is 1,710 LOC / 52 defs / 16 PanelSpecs. Across sb/domain, panels.py files total 23,802 LOC on top of the 5,545 LOC of sb/manifest.
defects.quote:
"""The XP panels (band 4) — the shipped `_XpHubView` declaratively:
the invoker's rank overview (provider-fed fields) + the admin action row
(Give XP / Reset XP as G-10 modals over the audited K7 ops; the shipped
`_GiveXpModal`/`_ResetXpModal` one-form flows), PLUS the shipped visual
card-engine H3 posture: the hub send carries the invoker's rank image
card ``rank.png`` (views/xp/main_panel.py build_response, PR #1413) and
``!rank`` sends the card directly (utils/rank_render.py, PR #1401) —
goldens/xp/sweep_xpmenu + xp_chat_award pin the multipart send shape.
defects.contradicts: The intuitive reading that a compiled-manifest architecture makes a feature mostly declaration. It does not here: the manifest module is 8-9% of the subsystem, and the panel specs live in large hand-written Python modules that mix spec literals with providers and handlers. Whole-repo: superbot disbot/ is 243,961 LOC; superbot-next sb/ is 150,328 LOC for a port that is not complete.
defects.failure_scenario: A rebuild plan budgets on 'declaration replaces code' and sizes the successor at a fraction of superbot. On the two subsystems measured the real saving is 20% and 43%, and the compiler + spec grammar + kernel are 5,545 + 3,535 + 20,486 = 29,566 LOC of new machinery that must be paid for before the first feature ships. A plan built on the wrong ratio under-budgets the port by roughly a factor of two.
defects.successor_recommendation: Budget the successor from these two measured ratios, not from the architecture's promise. And separate spec literals from provider/handler code into different modules so 'how much is declaration' is answerable by counting files rather than by reading them.

defects.area: documentation at the compiler entry point
defects.claim: The docstring of sb/manifest/__init__.py — the package the compiler imports first (pass P1) and the first file any reader opens to learn what a manifest is — states the package is empty. It holds 49 modules totalling 5,545 LOC, and `python3 tools/manifest_compile.py` reports '49 manifest(s)'.
defects.quote:
"""``sb/manifest`` — pure declarations + handler registrations (design-spec §1.1).

Each module declares `MANIFEST = SubsystemManifest(...)` and binds its
callables with the `@handler`/`@panel`/`@engine`/`@workflow`/`@provider`
decorators from `sb.spec.refs`. The compiler (`tools/manifest_compile.py`)
imports every module here (P1), so declaring IS reserving (design-spec §3.2).

EMPTY at K2: subsystem manifests are authored by the port bands (Phase 4).
"""
defects.contradicts: The owner's own standard (2026-09-01) that documentation was 'especially true in /superbot before the EAP was announced' — the OLD bot is the doc baseline. This is the successor's most-read orientation file and its last line is false at HEAD.
defects.failure_scenario: A new session (human or agent) opens sb/manifest/__init__.py to orient before touching a manifest, reads 'EMPTY at K2', and concludes the manifest layer is unbuilt scaffolding — so it goes looking for the real declarations in sb/domain and works there, adding panel specs outside the manifest facet. The compiler stays green because sb/domain/*/panels.py registration is a supported path; the subsystem's declared surface and its real surface drift apart.
defects.successor_recommendation: In the successor, any docstring line that asserts a countable fact about the tree ('EMPTY', 'N subsystems') must be generated or checked, never hand-written. superbot-next already has a checker family that could assert it in one line.

honest_nulls: I did NOT establish what the 218 renderer_override callables actually render. sb/domain/*.py contains 126 calls to render_panel( across 53 files, so SOME overrides re-enter the grammar renderer (the engine docstring at sb/kernel/panels/engine.py:424-427 explicitly anticipates 'a renderer_override that re-calls render_panel(spec, ctx) itself'), but I did not resolve each of the 218 refs to its callable and check. My live nav counts (84/96 with nav, 4 zero-component) are therefore for the GRAMMAR path only. The 218 could be anywhere between 'thin wrappers that still get engine nav' and 'full hand-written views'. This is the single highest-value follow-up in this lane and it is one probe: resolve each renderer_override ref, call it with the probe context, and count nav components in the result.

I did NOT verify whether opening a panel EDITS the originating message or SENDS a new one — that is the presenter port's decision (sb/kernel/panels/engine.py:463 `message_ref = await _presenter(rendered, req)`) and the discord adapter was not exercised because discord.py is absent. So for the four dead-end panels in M9-D05 I can state that the DESTINATION offers no navigation affordance; I cannot state whether the hub message survives behind it.

I did NOT test cog-portability, which the owner named as a hard requirement (2026-08-23). sb/app/plugin_host.py, plugins.lock.json, docs/game-plugin-contract.md and tests/unit/app/test_plugin_boot_real_exemplar.py all exist and I read none of them. Whether an existing superbot cog can be 'slightly altered' to work here is unmeasured by this lane — and note that the answer interacts with M9-D01: a 69% renderer_override rate is either the mechanism that makes cog import easy, or the evidence that the declarative path could not absorb the real cogs. I could not tell which.

The scheduler is nearly unexercised and I chose not to file it as a surviving defect because I could not construct a concrete user-facing failure. Measured: 3 ManagedTaskSpecs declared across all 49 subsystems (games:session_gc, proof:lock_reconcile, role:grants_expiry), and every ManagedTaskSpec grammar field — trigger, catch_up, max_catchup, misfire_policy, grace_s, error_policy, durability, metrics_labels, quiet_hours, tz, start_hour, end_hour, policy, expr, seconds, poll_interval_s, condition, event — is ABSENT from the snapshot. superbot by contrast runs many recurring jobs (disbot/services/automation_scheduler.py et al). The successor should treat the scheduler grammar as unvalidated, not as proven.

The draft pipeline (sb/kernel/draft/, 758 LOC, 7 modules) has exactly ONE domain consumer: sb/domain/setup (8 files). I dropped it as a defect row because the failure I could name is maintenance-shaped ('the next author re-implements it') rather than 'user does X, Y goes wrong', and the survival rule is right to reject that. Recording the count here so a planner can weigh it: a 7-module generic draft/preview/apply/janitor kernel serving one feature.

I did NOT run tools/check_sim_gate.py, check_parity_depth.py, check_namespace.py or the other ~20 checkers in .github/workflows/ci.yml individually — I ran the compiler, check_orphan_pendings, check_escape_hatches and the full pytest suite. So my population claims about guards cover four checkers, not the whole family. Given that two of the four I DID examine turned out to run over empty or near-empty populations (escape hatches: 0; the P6 predicates inside the compiler: 0 and 2), the remaining ~20 deserve the same single question before any of them is quoted as evidence in a rebuild plan: what population does it run over, and can that population be empty?

I did NOT compare superbot's own help-reachability invariant (the prompt says it checks a hand-built MODEL of the hub registry) against superbot-next's equivalent, because superbot-next has no reachability invariant at all — the closest thing is the navigation golden, which is already confirmed vacuous, and the never_strand predicate, which I show in M9-D03 tests a field default rather than reachability. The honest statement is: neither repo currently proves panel reachability over its real artifact.

consumers counts in the strength rows are counted call sites or counted registry members, never estimates: 96 (grammar-path panels, from panel_inventory), 2 (static_route callers: sb/kernel/panels/router.py:104 and the engine's handle_nav), 175 (CompoundOpSpecs in the live REGISTRY), 3 (gate_recompile callers by grep), 1 (ci.yml step for check_orphan_pendings), 273 (test files by find), 32 (domain packages importing the workflow engine by grep), 4 (SettingSpecs with external_side_effects=True).

defects.claim: The AI gateway is presented as "the single never-raises chokepoint for provider calls" and providers/base.py claims its two provider modules are "the ONLY production modules permitted to import external LLM SDKs" — but this boundary is enforced by nothing. Whole-repo grep for real import statements (`^\s*import anthropic\b|^\s*from anthropic\b|^\s*import openai\b|^\s*from openai\b`) across every .py file in the repo returns exactly 2 hits, both inside sb/kernel/ai/providers/ (anthropic_provider.py:59, openai_provider.py:47). Zero outside. That count is real today, but unlike three sibling seams in this SAME codebase (env-var access -> tools/check_config_usage.py, Discord egress -> tools/check_egress.py, Discord surface/import containment -> tools/check_no_skip.py, all three AST-based, stdlib-only, wired into .github/workflows/named-gates.yml's required 'architecture' job), there is no tools/check_*.py anywhere in tools/ (27 checkers enumerated) that scans for a stray `import openai`/`import anthropic` outside sb/kernel/ai/providers/.
defects.quote:
Modules under ``sb/kernel/ai/providers/`` are the ONLY production modules
permitted to import external LLM SDKs (guarded imports; the SDKs are not
installed in CI containers).
defects.contradicts: The M10 prompt's framing ('is the AI gateway genuinely the only path to a provider') implies the answer should be checkable the same way check_config_usage.py makes the config seam checkable. It currently is NOT checkable by any automated gate — it is true only by absence of a violation today, which is exactly the kind of claim this codebase's own convention (4 parallel AST fences for adjacent seams) says should never be left unenforced.
defects.failure_scenario: A future band adds a feature and, to avoid gateway timeout/redaction/audit overhead for a 'quick' call, writes `from openai import AsyncOpenAI` directly inside a domain module (e.g. sb/domain/media/ or sb/domain/btd6/). CI stays fully green — check_config_usage.py doesn't look for SDK imports, check_egress.py only bans Discord-mutation methods, check_no_skip.py only bans Discord surface registration/import. The gateway's redaction, per-guild policy overlay, audit-spine row, safety precheck, and fallback logic are all silently bypassed for that call path, and no red build ever announces it.

defects.claim: pool.py's own docstring declares raw `conn.execute`/`conn.transaction()` and by extension raw `asyncpg` construction 'banned outside sb/kernel/db (spec 05 §7)', and multiple StoreSpec rows declare a `sole_writer` (e.g. CREDENTIAL_ROTATION_STORE, event_outbox's INV-OUTBOX-SOLE-WRITER) — but neither invariant has a checker. `import asyncpg` appears in exactly one file today (sb/kernel/db/pool.py, confirmed by repo-wide grep), and tools/manifest_compile.py only PROJECTS `sole_writer` into the compiled manifest.snapshot.json as inert metadata (`stores_proj[str(table)] = {"sole_writer": _serialize(sole_writer), ...}`) — it never cross-checks that metadata against real write call sites. tools/check_data_lifecycle.py, the one checker that walks StoreSpec rows, only verifies retention/erasure_ref/cache_scope presence, never writer identity.
defects.contradicts: sb/kernel/db/pool.py's own docstring language ('stays banned outside sb/kernel/db') reads as an enforced rule; it is a documentation-only claim with zero machine backing, the same pattern as M10-D1 one layer down the stack.
defects.failure_scenario: A new domain store.py (there are already 11 files outside sb/kernel/db calling pool.fetchall/execute/conn.execute per grep) adds `import asyncpg` and opens its own connection/transaction directly, bypassing pool.py's checked_acquire() dead-connection validation and query-timing observability, and writes to a table another StoreSpec has declared sole_writer for — corrupting the declared single-writer invariant with no CI signal, unlike a stray os.getenv call which check_config_usage.py would catch in the same PR.

defects.claim: The AIScope authority lattice (USER<MODERATOR<ADMIN<SERVER_OWNER<PLATFORM_OWNER<SYSTEM, tools_catalogue.py:49-61) is real, tested code, but it is never driven by the actual per-user Discord authority the button/command path uses (sb.kernel.authority.resolve_authority). Evidence: (a) the only production tool registrations (sb/domain/ai/tools.py, register_btd6_tools, 8 rows) all declare `min_scope=AIScope.USER` — 8 of 8, grep-counted; (b) NLMessage.scope defaults to AIScope.USER (nl_engine.py:81) and the one live construction site, sb/adapters/discord/nl_shell.py:66-80, passes guild_id/channel_id/category_id/user_id/message_id/text/raw_text/is_mention/user_level/user_role_ids/is_fresh_user/author_is_bot/display_name/bot_user_id — 13 keyword arguments, zero of them `scope=` — so every live message is evaluated at the USER floor regardless of the caller's real Discord role/tier, even though user_level/user_role_ids ARE collected (for the separate policy.py reply-eligibility gate) and could feed a scope computation; (c) the only OTHER call site that supplies a non-default AIScope is sb/domain/ai/orchestration_widgets.py:249, which hardcodes AIScope.SYSTEM for an admin dry-run preview embed, not live traffic. Net: 0 of the 2 non-test production call sites that touch AIScope compute it from real per-user authority.
defects.quote:
msg = nl_engine.NLMessage(
            guild_id=int(getattr(message, "guild_id", 0) or 0),
            channel_id=int(getattr(message, "channel_id", 0) or 0),
            category_id=getattr(message, "category_id", None),
            user_id=int(getattr(message, "user_id", 0) or 0),
            message_id=getattr(message, "message_id", None),
            text=text,
            raw_text=content,
            is_mention=is_mention,
            user_level=int(getattr(message, "user_level", 0) or 0),
            user_role_ids=tuple(getattr(message, "user_role_ids", ()) or ()),
            is_fresh_user=bool(getattr(message, "is_fresh_user", False)),
            author_is_bot=False,
            display_name=getattr(message, "display_name", None),
            bot_user_id=bot_user_id,
        )
defects.contradicts: This directly undercuts the M10 prompt's premise that AI tool authority is presently something to characterize as 'constrained, and by what' in a live sense — the constraint mechanism is real but currently disconnected from live data, so the correct finding is 'built but unwired,' not 'constrained by X.' It also means tools_catalogue.py's own docstring claim that 'the model never chooses what it may see' is true only because everything sits at the same floor scope today, not because the lattice is actively discriminating between real users.
defects.failure_scenario: A future band registers a tool at min_scope=AIScope.ADMIN expecting the caller's scope to reflect the user's real Discord permissions. Because nl_shell.py never sets NLMessage.scope above the USER default, that tool is silently excluded for every live user forever (a working-as-designed but confusing dead feature) — or, if a future patch 'fixes' this by wiring scope from an easy-but-wrong signal (e.g. is_mention, or the same user_level used for the unrelated reply-eligibility gate) instead of resolve_authority, ordinary chat users could be handed elevated tool access, since no test in the current suite exercises a non-default live scope at all.

defects.area: AI gateway / guild-policy model safety net
defects.claim: The per-guild model/provider overlay's cross-family safety check (`model_matches_provider`, routing.py:111-122) is a crude prefix test — `model.startswith("claude")` for anthropic, `model.startswith("gpt")` for openai — not a maintained allowlist of real model ids, despite the surrounding comment calling it a 'safety net' against 'a stored model outside the resolved provider's family.'
defects.failure_scenario: A guild's stored default_model is a typo'd or since-retired id, e.g. "claude-typo-999" or "claude-1-nonexistent": the prefix check passes (starts with "claude"), so gateway._overlay_guild_policy does NOT fall back to the per-task default as the code comment says it should — the request proceeds to Anthropic's real API and 404s there, producing a generic provider-fault degrade instead of the intended named 'default_model does not match provider' warning-and-correct path. The gateway still never raises (contained by the outer never-raise contract), so severity is low, but the specific safety net named in the comment does not do what the comment says for this class of input.

lanes.headline: The AI kernel's own internal seams (redaction, routing, audit-spine, fallback, task registry) are genuinely well-built and well-tested — but the two boundaries this lane exists to verify are both true only by absence of a counter-example, not by enforcement: (1) zero direct provider-SDK imports exist outside sb/kernel/ai/providers/ today, yet no checker (unlike the config/egress/no-skip AST fences that already exist in this exact repo) would catch a new one; and (2) the AIScope authority lattice is real and tested in isolation but is never actually fed from a live user's real Discord permissions — every production call site sits at the USER floor by default, and the entire registered tool catalogue (8 rows) is read-only, so the rebuild's headline question ("does an AI side effect reuse the same typed operation a button uses?") currently has no code to answer it with — there are zero side-effect-capable AI tools in the tree.
honest_nulls: Cannot determine whether an AI-triggered side effect would go through the same typed operation a button uses, because zero side-effect-capable AI tools exist anywhere in the current tree. All 8 registered tools (sb/domain/ai/tools.py) are read-only deterministic BTD6 lookups; the file's own docstring says the mutating rows ('the deep-tools + ingestion successor ports, D-0048') haven't landed handlers yet. This is the central question the M10 prompt asks and the codebase genuinely cannot answer it yet — reported as a null rather than forced into a verdict.

Did not verify live GitHub branch-protection settings for superbot-next (whether named-gates.yml's 'architecture'/'manifest-validate' jobs are actually configured as REQUIRED status checks that block merge, versus merely present as workflow jobs) — the repo's own remote carries a live PAT and the task instructions are read-only/never-push, so I did not make any network call against it. named-gates.yml's own file header claims these are 'the owner-armed required-check names' but I could not independently confirm that against live ruleset state.

Did not run the full pytest suite (only the AI/authority/config/db-scoped subset: tests/unit/ai, tests/unit/authority, tests/unit/kernel/test_config.py, test_migrations.py, test_db_pool.py, test_check_config_usage.py, and the gateway/nl_engine files individually — 242+31+14 = confirmed passing across those targeted runs) — a repo-wide run was out of scope for the ~70-call budget and this lane's file list.

Could not exercise check_migrations.py's or check_config_usage.py's DETECTION path against a real violation in situ (only against the tests' own synthetic tmp_path fixtures, which I read but did not re-run standalone) — I ran the checkers against the real tree (both clean, exit 0) and read the unit tests that plant a synthetic violation and assert it is caught, but did not independently construct a fresh violation against the live tree myself to double-check.

Did not trace whether sb/kernel/db/pool.py's checked_acquire() dead-connection revalidation is itself exercised by an integration test against a real Postgres (golden-parity.yml's job, per named-gates.yml comments, is the only required leg with a live Postgres) — asyncpg is not installed in this sandbox and stubbing its connection-pool internals well enough to prove checked_acquire()'s revalidation logic was judged out of scope for the budget.

lanes.headline: superbot-next's proof estate is real and live-enforced (7 required checks, active ruleset, 3,648 green tests, a genuinely strong headless boot-and-wire gate that I fired with a negative control) — but the ACCEPTANCE half of it proves opening bytes, not a working bot: the 533-golden oracle clicks 16 stable custom_ids against 640 declared panel actions, 485 of 533 goldens are one command in / bytes out, 5 of 32 exercised proof mechanisms have a structurally EMPTY population (9 of 32 empty, near-empty or a model), the kernel spine is dispositioned out of 529 of 533 goldens, and chasing byte-parity DID cause the capture-literal convention — sb/domain/admin/cogmgr.py ships a hardcoded 58-entry roster of the OLD bot's cog modules so a golden replays green. The successor should keep the enforcement machinery and the boot-and-wire gate, and must NOT inherit byte-parity as its acceptance oracle.

strengths.claim: The 7 named gates are NOT aspirational: the main-branch ruleset is enforcement="active" and carries exactly 7 required status checks — code-quality, manifest-validate, architecture, sim-gate, golden-parity, check_compat_frozen, pip-audit — read live from the rulesets API at this session's time. This is the one enforcement fact everything else in the lane hangs on.
strengths.quote:
# named-gates.yml — the design-spec §6 REQUIRED-CHECK NAMES, as jobs.
#
# The owner armed the main-branch ruleset with the §6 gate names
# (build-brief §8.1 — "agents author the workflow FILES; owner flips the
# settings"): merges started refusing with N-of-5 required checks
# "expected" because no job carried those names.
strengths.contradicts: golden-parity.yml:10 still carries an OPEN owner step — "👤 OWNER: designate THIS job as the required status check" — for a check the owner has in fact already armed. The workflow files under-report their own enforcement, so a session reading only the files concludes less is required than actually is.
strengths.prevents_failure: a red gate decorates the PR instead of blocking the merge (the exact failure fleet-manager records for its own repo before 2026-08-06)
strengths.guard_population: 7 required contexts over every PR to main; population is non-empty and cannot be emptied without a ruleset edit, which is itself an owner action
strengths.simpler_than_counterpart: superbot has no equivalent required-check spine
strengths.successor_recommendation: Carry the ruleset-armed named-gate pattern verbatim into the successor on day one. It is the cheapest thing in this repo and the only reason any other gate matters.

strengths.claim: tools/check_runtime_smoke.py is the strongest proof layer in the repo: it runs the REAL composition-root calls (gate_recompile, build_runtime, install_live_target_index, register_manifest_panels, arm_subscribe_roster) and measured 49 manifests / 1327 dispatch targets / 314 panels / 137 distinct manifest PanelRefs. strengths.claim: The route-registry boot validator (`routes.validate()`) walks the SAME literal, non-empty, module-level `ROUTES` tuple that both the real bot's `setup_hook()` calls at real boot and the real Home panel renders from -- not a fixture, not a cleared/mocked copy. This is the structural opposite of the two named hollow-guard traps (superbot-next's cleared-registry golden test; superbot's hand-built reachability model).
strengths.quote:
def validate() -> list[str]:
    """Registry self-check, run at boot: keys unique, rows inside Discord's budget.

    Returns a list of problems (empty means healthy) rather than raising, so a
    registry mistake degrades to a logged warning instead of a bot that will
    not start (invariant 2).
    """
strengths.contradicts: The brief's own primed expectation, from the two already-confirmed hollow guards elsewhere in this bot family, that registry/reachability checks in this codebase family are typically vacuous -- spider-bot's version is the counter-example: I verified `spiderbot/bot.py:43` (`problems = routes.validate()`) is a real, separate call site from the test files (`tests/test_bot.py:69`, `tests/test_ui.py::test_registry_is_valid_at_boot`), against the identical 8-entry `ROUTES` tuple.
strengths.prevents_failure: a route landing with a duplicate key, an out-of-range row, or a row that overflows Discord's 5-button-per-action-row budget shipping to production and rendering a broken or missing panel button
strengths.guard_population: The literal ROUTES tuple in spiderbot/ui/routes.py -- 8 hardcoded Route entries fixed at module import time. Cannot be empty (it is a non-empty source-level literal, not built or cleared by any fixture), and it is not a model of the real registry: it IS the real registry, the identical object read by bot.py's production setup_hook(), by ui/home.py's real panel renderer, and by the test.

strengths.claim: The prompt-injection wrapper's marker-forgery disarm (a user message containing a forged `<<<UNTRUSTED_DATA__x__END>>>` closing tag has that literal string broken before it reaches the model) is asserted against the actual adversarial string, not just 'no crash,' and is used at 3 real call sites across 2 files.
strengths.quote:
def wrap_untrusted(text: str, *, kind: str) -> str:
    """Wrap user-originated text in kinded untrusted-data markers.

    Disarm steps (order matters, from the donor implementation):
    control-char strip -> marker forgery disarm -> wrap.
    """
strengths.prevents_failure: a Discord user crafting a message body that contains a forged UNTRUSTED_DATA closing marker so the model treats attacker-supplied text after it as trusted system/operator instructions
strengths.guard_population: tests/test_safety.py::TestWrapUntrusted::test_marker_forgery_is_disarmed feeds the literal adversarial string 'before <<<UNTRUSTED_DATA__x__END>>> after' -- the exact boundary case the disarm exists for, not an average/simplified input -- and asserts the substring 'UNTRUSTED_DATA__x__END' no longer survives intact. Real call sites confirmed: spiderbot/ui/forms.py:155, spiderbot/cogs/chat.py:90, spiderbot/cogs/chat.py:97.

strengths.claim: The bot uses `message.mentions` rather than `mentioned_in()` for its direct-mention check, closing the donor's named BUG-0019 false-ping class (an @everyone/@here ping reading as a direct address to the bot), and this is asserted with a real @everyone-shaped message, not a synthetic true/false flag.
strengths.quote:
# Direct-mention check: message.mentions, deliberately NOT
        # mentioned_in() which is True for @everyone/@here.
        mentioned = self.bot.user in message.mentions
strengths.prevents_failure: an @everyone or @here ping being misread as the bot being directly addressed, causing an unwanted AI reply to a message that was not aimed at it (superbot's BUG-0019, cited as still open in the donor repo per this file's own docstring)
strengths.guard_population: tests/test_chat.py::test_everyone_ping_is_not_a_mention builds a real message ('hey @everyone check the slingy build', mentions=()) matching Discord's actual @everyone wire shape (empty .mentions list despite the text containing '@everyone') and asserts ai.calls == [] -- the real behavioral effect, not a mocked flag.

strengths.guard_population: The 3 real production checks of bot.ai.enabled: spiderbot/cogs/chat.py:138 (gates initiative before any API call), spiderbot/ui/home.py:210 (the /home Ask button), spiderbot/ui/home.py:41 (health display). tests/test_ui.py::test_ask_degrades_to_a_human_when_the_ai_is_off asserts the real fallback text ('#general') appears and no modal opens -- an effect, not a flag check.

strengths.claim: Cog-portability (invariant 12, OD-19) is applied uniformly: all 6 of spider-bot's cogs are plain commands.Cog classes with an async def setup(bot) entry point -- exactly the shape the owner named as a hard requirement so an existing superbot cog can be added or lightly altered on demand.

lanes.headline: The formal CAPTURE-WORLD LITERAL label finds 4 files; the defect class holds at least 12, and the biggest instance is unlabelled: sb/domain/diagnostic/platform_views.py freezes 28 operator diagnostics cards from the OLD bot's runtime and ships them as 33 registered commands wrapped in a LIVE {ts}/{gid}/{ch}/{tier} frame — including a database-health card that always reports "Schema healthy … 103/103" over a 57-migration ladder. It was accepted because the A-16 byte-parity gate (the owner-designated REQUIRED check) makes an honest live read structurally RED, the table was "GENERATED from the goldens" so the guard compares the golden to a copy of itself, and the cited authority (trap 10a) actually prescribes the OPPOSITE disposition — runner-seeded world reconstruction, which the same repo uses correctly in five other places.

strengths.claim: The CORRECT disposition for capture-world state already exists and is used in 5 distinct places: sb/adapters/parity/runner.py seeds capture-world state into the REAL runtime objects per observing case and CLEARS it at every case head (CAPTURE_WORLD_SETTINGS, CAPTURE_WORLD_COUNTERS, CAPTURE_WORLD_WORD_CACHE, CAPTURE_WORLD_WEATHER, CAPTURE_WORLD_CHANNELS — I counted 5 of 5 by grep). Domain source stays live: sb/domain/cleanup/service.py:85-89 still does a real load-on-miss DB read. This is the lane the 12 literal files should have taken.
strengths.quote:
#: Seeded/CLEARED at every case (None ⇒ clear), so
#: gate/report/isolation replay the same trajectory (trap 20:
#: runner-seeded, never accumulated — the ops' own post-mutation
#: invalidation would otherwise leak `test` differently per mode).
CAPTURE_WORLD_WORD_CACHE: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]] = {
strengths.contradicts: The four CAPTURE-WORLD LITERAL headers cite 'trap 10a' as their authority for freezing state into domain source; trap 10a's own precedent (_word_cache) was resolved by THIS lane instead — a runner seed with the domain code left live.
strengths.prevents_failure: Mode-dependent golden bytes / cross-case state leakage, and — the reason it matters for the rebuild — a shipped surface that renders capture state to a real user.
strengths.guard_population: The parity corpus's observing cases, named explicitly per constant (sweep.word_list, sweep.wordmenu, sweep.fish, …). Non-empty by construction — an unseeded case clears rather than leaks. It seeds the REAL objects (the settings table, the module-global cache) not a model of them, which is exactly why it does not have the tautology problem the pinned-literal lane has.
strengths.successor_recommendation: In the successor, make this the ONLY way capture/fixture state may enter a render path: fixture state is injected by the test harness into real runtime objects; production source may contain zero snapshots of the program's own state. Enforce with the guard in R1-D12.

It is the mechanism that produced R1-S2's honesty.

strengths.prevents_failure: Declaring a command whose rendered bytes nothing can source.
strengths.guard_population: One JSON file listing surfaces the capture COULD NOT record. It is a MODEL of 'unsourceable', not the real predicate: a surface can be captured perfectly and still be unsourceable in the successor — which is precisely the 28-card case. The list can also in principle be empty, and an empty list makes the whole discipline vacuous with no signal.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep the artifact, replace its predicate: the successor's list should be 'surfaces with no live source of truth in THIS bot', derived from the registry, not 'surfaces the old bot's capture harness could not record'.

strengths.claim: Exactly ONE guard in this class exists and it is the implementable template for the killing test — tests/unit/band6/test_band6_game_sections.py pins the hub roster against the sections registry in both directions, keys/emoji/labels/hub-refs, order included. honest_nulls: SAMPLE RESULT AND ITS LIMITS, stated first because the projection is the weakest thing in this lane. Of 29 sampled sb/domain files (systematic every-4th over the path-sorted 115 that carry the convention's vocabulary): 6 of 29 TRUE DEFECT (admin/cogmgr.py, community/panels.py, diagnostic/handlers.py, server_management/panels.py, ux_lab/panels.py, channel/visibility.py), 4 of 29 AMBIGUOUS (games/panels.py — has the literal-to-literal drift guard and live routes; btd6/store.py — describes a dead lane, not a live-state claim; ai/service.py and setup/handlers.py — golden-pinned empty-state and usage bytes I did not trace to a render), 19 of 29 LEGITIMATE (ported pure logic: governance/resolver.py, role/automation.py, fishing/energy.py, inventory/service.py; shipped display copy: setup/{cleanup,panels,roles,wizard}.py, rps/handlers.py, moderation/panels.py, games hub copy; provenance-only notes: creature/service.py, farm/ops.py, mining/panels.py, btd6/oracle_surface.py, fishing/panels.py; honest live/declared surfaces: diagnostic/process_state.py, utility/handlers.py, xp/rank_card.py). Naive projection 6/29 x 115 = ~24 files. DO NOT USE THAT NUMBER without these three limits: (i) the sample is systematic over a PATH-SORTED list, so it is clustered, not random — sb/domain/setup alone holds 19 of the 115 and is almost entirely legitimate shipped copy, which biases the estimate downward; (ii) a 29-draw binomial puts the true rate roughly between 8% and 40%, i.e. 9 to 46 files, which is too wide to plan against; (iii) file count is the wrong severity unit anyway — platform_views.py was NOT drawn into my sample and it alone backs 28 of the ~36 lying commands, so a file-count projection understates the surface impact by roughly an order of magnitude. Use the surface count (33 platform-group commands + check_database + coglist + adminmenu + 4 hub fields) rather than the file count.

Consequence: no row in this lane is PRODUCTION-PROVEN or LIVE-TESTED. Reachability is established from the compiled manifest (the artifact the runtime registers from), not from a live registration.

lanes.headline: The dominant vacuity shape in BOTH repos is not "the guard is wrong" — it is "the guard's correctness is proven over a synthetic model while its production population is empty, skipped, or never scanned." 19 of 77 executable guards are vacuous-capable by measurement. superbot-next's flagship navigation golden is doubly empty: the autouse conftest clears the registry, AND `register_hub()` has ZERO production call sites in all of sb/ (1 def, 3 test callers) — so `walk_navigation`'s `roots` is the empty set in a fully-booted process too, which refutes that docstring's promise that it "arms automatically as port bands register real panels." Its "verified live" gate is pinned to zero records by its own test. superbot, by contrast, ships the two mechanisms a successor must copy verbatim: a live-population negative control ("a vacuous check is worse than none") and a shrink-only ratchet with an anti-staleness test — and it does NOT apply them consistently to its own sibling ratchets.

strengths.claim: superbot's help-reachability invariant carries an explicit negative control that mutates the LIVE scheme (not a fixture) and asserts the detector fires — and it fails if the live population is empty, because it pytest.fail()s when 'blackjack' is not a child of any live section. Measured live population under a discord stub: 8 hub sections / 42 leaves / 34 children, 0 violations. This is the exact mechanism superbot-next's navigation golden lacks.

lanes.headline: The rebuild did not trade flexibility for purity uniformly — it traded DEPLOY-TIME and RUNTIME flexibility (no subsystem selection filter, no load/unload) for AUTHORING flexibility (one auto-discovered file vs 13 hand-coordinated touch-points), kept per-guild visibility intact, and then blocked the owner's stated cog-portability requirement for 29 of its own 49 subsystems by fencing `stores` out of the plugin contract: every stateful feature (fishing, mining, economy, xp, karma, moderation, ai, starboard) is structurally un-shippable as an out-of-tree plugin today.

strengths.claim: The extension loader isolates failures per cog: each of the 59 entries in INITIAL_EXTENSIONS is loaded inside its own try/except, a failure is recorded and the loop continues, and the affected subsystems are then downgraded to INTERNAL rather than crashing the process. 59 of 59 extensions ride this path.
strengths.contradicts: The framing that superbot is the pile of debt and superbot-next the clean rebuild: on boot-fault containment superbot is strictly better. superbot-next's load_live_manifests() (sb/app/main.py:99-104) has no try/except at all, so one broken manifest module aborts the whole boot.
strengths.prevents_failure: whole-bot outage caused by one broken feature module

strengths.claim: Runtime load/unload/reload of any of the 59 extensions exists, is audited, and has a protected-core guard. Two independent surfaces reach it (prefix commands in admin_cog.py:137/163, and the interactive Cog Manager panel), and _PROTECTED_COGS denies panel-unload of core cogs.

        meta = SUBSYSTEMS[name]
defects.contradicts: check_settings_reachability.py's own measured output at this pin — 'check_settings_reachability — 19 reachable · 3 exempt · 0 GAP', EXIT=0. It reports zero gaps while a shipped, user-configurable subsystem has no !settings route, because its population is SUBSYSTEMS and starboard is not in SUBSYSTEMS.
defects.failure_scenario: A server admin opens !settings to change the starboard threshold or ignore a channel. Starboard is not listed. The only route is the undiscoverable !starboard command. The repo's guard for exactly this failure reports 0 GAP, so nobody is told.
defects.new_failure_class: guard-population blindness: a registry-driven checker cannot see anything missing FROM the registry, so absence is indistinguishable from compliance
defects.successor_recommendation: Derive the guard's population from the loaded/declared feature set (the manifest corpus), never from a second hand-maintained registry; a feature that declares settings and has no route must be an error, and a feature absent from the registry must itself be the error.

defects.claim: The CI architecture gate sees 1 of 40 views->cogs coupling edges. Measured: the default/strict run lists exactly ONE views->cogs warning (views/games/blackjack_panel.py:30); --report-lazy-imports raises the total to 137 warnings including 101 lazy_layer_boundary findings, of which 39 are views->cogs; and lazy findings 'are always WARNINGS, never errors'. grep counts 47 'from cogs' statements across 19 files under views/.
defects.quote:
# IMPORTANT: Only MODULE-LEVEL imports are checked. Lazy function-body
# imports (from X import Y inside a def) are allowed throughout the
# codebase to avoid circular import problems — these are NOT flagged.
defects.contradicts: R3-S4's clean EXIT=0 and the 55-entry known_violations ledger, which records 18 views->cogs violations while the live run surfaces 1 — the other 17 moved into function bodies and left the gate's field of view without being fixed.
defects.failure_scenario: A developer adds `from cogs.deathmatch_cog import _Duel` at module level; CI errors. They move the same line inside the function (as views/games/deathmatch_panel.py already does at lines 212, 445, 518, 574). CI goes green. The coupling is now permanent and invisible, and later deleting or porting deathmatch_cog breaks the SHARED games hub panel at runtime, not at import time.
defects.new_failure_class: silent violation laundering — the documented escape hatch for circular imports doubles as an escape hatch from the gate
defects.successor_recommendation: Enforce import boundaries over ALL import statements including function-body ones, with an explicit per-edge allowlist for genuine cycle-breakers; never make the fix for a violation also the way to hide it.

defects.claim: The only CI-enforced architecture rule cannot constrain cog coupling at all: the cogs layer's may_import list contains every layer in the system including cogs itself. Measured consequence: 134 `from cogs.<x>` import statements inside cogs/, all fully legal under the rule.
defects.quote:
cogs:
    description: Discord command handlers and event listeners (top layer).
    path_prefix: cogs
    may_import: [utils, core, services, views, governance, cogs]
defects.contradicts: The repo's presentation of check_architecture as THE architecture guard. It guards every layer except the one the owner actually wants portable.
defects.failure_scenario: The owner tries to lift a cog into the successor 'slightly altered', as he asked for. Because cog->cog imports were never constrained, the cog he picks may sit anywhere in a 134-edge intra-cogs graph; he discovers the true closure only by pulling the thread at import time in the new bot.
defects.new_failure_class: unbounded top-layer coupling — the layer nearest the user is the one with no rule
defects.successor_recommendation: Give the feature layer a real ceiling: a feature module may import the platform/kernel and its OWN package, never another feature's internals. Make sibling-feature interaction go through a declared, countable seam.

defects.claim: A cog cannot be lifted out without governance and env config coming with it. Measured import chain, observed as a real traceback while running scripts/new_subsystem.py: core.runtime -> core.resources -> core/resources/role_service.py:30 -> governance/__init__.py -> governance/cleanup.py -> governance/resolver.py:14 -> config.py -> dotenv. 4 of the 5 sampled cogs import core.runtime (utility, starboard, server_management, ai).
defects.quote: from config import is_platform_owner
defects.contradicts: layers.yaml's stated contract 'core → utils (NOT services, NOT cogs — per arch doc)'. The declared core layer is not the actual core layer: at import time it reaches governance and the process-wide dotenv config.
defects.failure_scenario: The owner copies utility_cog.py (9 internal module imports, 0 migrations, 0 DB tables — the most portable cog sampled) into another bot. Its single line `from core.runtime.permission_checks import perms_or_owner` fails at import until he also brings governance/ (16 modules), config.py, and a populated .env. The simplest cog in the estate is not copy-portable.
defects.new_failure_class: import-time transitive closure far exceeding the declared dependency
defects.successor_recommendation: Feature modules must receive permission/config capability by injection at registration, never by importing a package whose __init__ eagerly wires the platform.

defects.claim: 29 of the successor's own 49 in-tree manifests declare at least one host-owned facet and therefore CANNOT be shipped as out-of-tree plugins under the v1 contract: 29 declare `stores`, 4 also declare `data_invariants` (economy, karma, treasury, xp), 1 also `wizard_sections` (setup). The 29 include fishing, mining, economy, xp, karma, moderation, ai, starboard, ticket, role, help, settings and governance itself. Measured by calling HOST_ONLY_FACETS against the live loaded manifests, EXIT=0.
defects.contradicts: The owner's stated requirement, verbatim: 'I should be able to add exiting cogs to it on demand, or be able to slightly alter an existing cog so that it works with this bot' (2026-08-23). Under the shipped plugin contract that is impossible for 59% of the bot's own feature set — every stateful one. The two shipped exemplars pass only because hello is stateless and idle persists through the settings KV lane instead of tables.
defects.failure_scenario: The owner packages the fishing subsystem as its own repo to install on demand, exactly as the plugin contract advertises. load_plugins() emits a facet violation naming `stores`, and because any violation is fatal the bot does not start at all — he loses all 49 subsystems, not just fishing.
defects.new_failure_class: portability contract that excludes the majority of the artifacts it is for
defects.successor_recommendation: Give plugins a first-class owned-schema lane (namespaced tables + their own migration chain) before calling anything cog-portable; without it the plugin host serves stateless UI only.

defects.claim: Any single plugin problem aborts the entire boot: load_plugins() collects violations from discovery, the facet fence, the pin check and the joint compile, and the composition root turns a non-empty list into _fail_startup('plugin_gate'). There is no per-plugin skip for a violating plugin — only for a PINNED-but-not-installed one.
defects.contradicts: superbot's per-extension try/except at bot1.py:721-731 (R3-S1). The successor is strictly less fault-tolerant than the bot it replaces, in the exact place the owner wants third-party code plugged in.
defects.failure_scenario: The owner runs `pip install -U superbot-idle-plugin` on the host and restarts. The new version's manifest hash no longer matches the committed plugins.lock.json, load_plugins() records 'manifest hash drift', and the bot refuses to start — moderation, xp, economy and 46 other subsystems are offline until he clones the host repo, runs tools/plugin_pin.py --write and commits.
defects.new_failure_class: total-outage blast radius from an optional third-party component
defects.successor_recommendation: Quarantine a violating plugin (log loudly, boot without it, surface it in a diagnostics panel) and reserve FAILED_STARTUP for in-tree corpus drift only.

defects.claim: There is no way to run a subset of the bot. load_live_manifests() imports every module in sb/manifest/ with the only skips being packages and underscore-prefixed names — all 49 load unconditionally, verified at pin d5f66dc2 (49 manifests reported by both manifest.snapshot.json and the live smoke run). Grep for SB_*SUBSYSTEM / ENABLED_SUBSYSTEM / DISABLED_SUBSYSTEM / MANIFEST_ALLOW / skip_manifest across the repo returns 0 hits; the 8 SB_* env vars that exist are about intents, data plane, sync guild and boot verification.
defects.contradicts: The 2026-08-05 live audit's claim as a hypothesis — re-verified independently at this pin and CONFIRMED, not merely repeated. It also contradicts the framing that superbot's INITIAL_EXTENSIONS list is pure legacy overhead: that list is also the only deployment-shaping knob either bot has ever had.
defects.failure_scenario: The owner wants a second, small deployment (the spider-bot scale: moderation + utility only) off the same codebase. There is no flag, env var or config file that will do it; he must delete manifest modules and regenerate manifest.snapshot.json or the boot gate fails leg A. Separately, because the import loop has no try/except, one syntax error in any one of the 49 modules stops the whole bot from starting.
defects.new_failure_class: all-or-nothing composition — no deployment profile, and no per-module import isolation
defects.successor_recommendation: Keep pkgutil auto-discovery (it is the good half) but add a declarative profile (an allow/deny list resolved at boot, compiled into the snapshot) so one codebase can ship several bot shapes; wrap each module import so a broken feature degrades instead of blocking the process.

defects.claim: The Cog Manager panel was ported as a dead end: its Load / Unload / Reload buttons are wired to a pending_handler that states the capability does not exist, and the source records this as final. The panel's select and pagination are live, so the surface looks functional.
defects.quote:
* Load / Unload / Reload reloaded discord.py extensions IN-PROCESS —
  deploy-ops, DELIBERATELY not ported (docs/decisions.md: extension
  management has no analog in the compiled architecture — subsystems
  are manifests, not runtime-loadable cogs); the clicks land on the
  declared BY-DESIGN terminal whose copy states exactly that (the
  hub's Reload All precedent). This is the surface's end state, not a
  pending port.
defects.contradicts: superbot's working, audited, protected-set implementation at cogs/admin/cog_manager.py:176-218 (R3-S2). This is a capability the owner has today and would not have after the cut — and the successor's own source calls it the end state.
defects.failure_scenario: A subsystem starts spamming a channel or erroring on every interaction. On the current bot the owner opens the Cog Manager, picks it, clicks Unload, and the noise stops in seconds with an audit row. On the successor he clicks the same button, gets '📋 Extension load/unload/reload is deploy-ops in the compiled architecture', and the only remedy is a redeploy of the whole process.
defects.new_failure_class: surface-present/capability-absent — a panel that renders as operable and terminates
defects.successor_recommendation: Put this decision to the owner explicitly. A middle path exists and costs little: keep manifests compile-time, but let the per-guild visibility lane (R3-S9) be driven from an operator panel so a subsystem can be switched off live without a redeploy.

defects.claim: The rebuild has zero import-boundary enforcement. 35 checkers exist under tools/ (check_namespace, check_egress, check_escape_hatches, check_no_skip, ...) and none enforces layering; there is no layers.yaml analog anywhere in the repo. The kernel's 0-domain-import property (R3-S7) is therefore held by convention alone.
defects.quote: #!/usr/bin/env python3
defects.contradicts: The rebuild's premise — 'a bot without architectural debt ... everything should be planned and connected from the start so it remains manageable'. superbot, the repo being replaced FOR its debt, has a CI-required layer ratchet; its replacement has none. The clean kernel/domain split is currently unguarded and will erode the same way superbot's did, by the same mechanism, with no signal.
defects.failure_scenario: A future session adds `from sb.domain.fishing.store import ...` to sb/kernel/panels/engine.py to fix a rendering bug quickly. Every gate stays green (namespace, smoke, goldens all pass — none inspects imports). The kernel is now coupled to one game; the next subsystem author inherits it, and the property that made adding a manifest cheap is gone with nothing recording when it went.
defects.new_failure_class: unguarded invariant — the rebuild's central structural claim has no instrument
defects.successor_recommendation: Port superbot's check_architecture.py as the FIRST guard in the successor, with an empty known_violations list on day one, and fix R3-D2 while porting: check function-body imports too.

defects.claim: The file that calls itself the single source of truth holds 43 real subsystem keys (50 entries minus 7 diagnostic sentinels) against 59 cog modules; 16 cog modules have no same-named key: ai_review, bootstrap_access, btd6_events, btd6_ops, btd6_reference, btd6_strategy, creature_battle, health_maintenance, hermes, media_maintenance, mining_relay, paragon, quicksetup, role_grants, setup, starboard. extension_crosswalk.py --check passes (EXIT=0) because it verifies role classification, not registry membership.
defects.quote: This file is the single source of truth for all subsystem definitions.
defects.contradicts: extension_crosswalk.py's clean EXIT=0 and architecture_rules/extension_roles.yaml's stated purpose 'to enforce ... that **every** extension is classified — so the gap can never silently re-grow'. Classification coverage is complete; registry coverage is not, and no checker measures the second.
defects.failure_scenario: An admin uses the governance surface to hide or restrict a feature per guild. Governance resolves policy by subsystem key, so any of the 16 unkeyed features (starboard included) has no policy row to set — the control simply has no entry for them, with no error explaining why.
defects.new_failure_class: two registries, one guarded
defects.successor_recommendation: One declaration per feature, discovered not listed (the successor's manifest model already does this) — and any guard that reads it must fail when a loaded feature is missing from it, not merely when a listed feature is unclassified.

defects.claim: The executable integration standard is never swept. scripts/new_subsystem.py checks exactly one subsystem key, passed by hand on the command line; there is no --all mode and no test that iterates the 59 cog modules. The 6 enumeration tests it names as the verify step check registry<->docs<->source agreement for entries that EXIST, not for cogs missing from the registry. Its effective population is 0 unless a human types a key.
defects.quote: * ``check``    — verify every touch-point for a subsystem key; exit 1 on gaps.
defects.contradicts: R3-S10's own value. The tool works — it correctly found 6 missing touch-points for starboard on first invocation in this session — which means the gap has been findable in one command for however long starboard has shipped, and was never found because nothing runs it.
defects.failure_scenario: A session adds a new cog and, being told the integration standard is enforced, ships it. Nobody passes the new key to new_subsystem.py. CI is green (the crosswalk only checks classification; the reachability guard only walks the registry). The cog loads, works via its own command, and is absent from help, settings and governance — exactly starboard's state today.
defects.new_failure_class: on-demand guard with a default population of zero
defects.successor_recommendation: Any completeness guard must derive its population from the artifacts that actually load (the manifest corpus / the extension list), iterate all of them, and be CI-required — never take the subject as an argument.

defects.area: authoring cost, honest counterweight to R3-S6
defects.claim: The 'one file, no registry edit' gain is partly repaid at the snapshot: leg A of the boot gate recompiles the manifest corpus in-process and compares it by stable_hash to the committed manifest.snapshot.json (49 subsystems, 318 field_roles), and any divergence is FAILED_STARTUP. So adding a subsystem is one new file PLUS a regenerated, committed 49-subsystem snapshot artifact.
defects.quote:
A — recompile-parity: committed snapshot == in-process `compile_manifests()`
      re-run (all of P1..P9, by stable_hash). Boot: FAILED_STARTUP on divergence.
defects.contradicts: A one-sided reading of R3-S6. The touch-point count went from 13 hand-coordinated edits to 1 file + 1 regenerated artifact — a large real win, but not zero, and the failure mode of forgetting is harsher (the bot does not start at all, versus superbot where a forgotten INITIAL_EXTENSIONS entry only makes the new cog silently absent).
defects.failure_scenario: A contributor adds sb/manifest/newfeature.py, tests it locally with the smoke checker regenerated in place, but commits without the regenerated manifest.snapshot.json. Deploy: leg A hash divergence, FAILED_STARTUP, the whole bot is down rather than just missing the new feature.
defects.new_failure_class: committed-artifact drift converting an omission into an outage
defects.successor_recommendation: Keep the parity gate — it is the reason the compiled architecture can be trusted — but add a pre-commit/CI regeneration check that fails the PR (loudly, in seconds) rather than letting the divergence reach a boot.

honest_nulls: I could NOT establish that the plugin path works for an actually pip-installed third-party distribution. No plugin is installed in this checkout, and the only real-artifact proof (tests/unit/app/test_plugin_boot_real_exemplar.py) states in its own docstring that it runs 'minus a pip install' and fakes the importlib.metadata transport via a _RealDist shim. discover_plugins() over genuine entry points is therefore unexercised anywhere I could find. Everything downstream of discovery (pin verify, facet fence, joint compile, panel registration) IS proven on real artifacts.

I did NOT observe either bot running. Both clones are read-only, discord.py/asyncpg/dotenv are absent (I stubbed them), and there is no token or Postgres here. Every claim I marked PRODUCTION-PROVEN for superbot rests on the frozen source being the code behind the live bot, not on watching the live bot behave.

I could not count DB tables for utility_cog and server_management_cog. Both matched 0 migration files by filename, but they may read or write shared tables through utils/db, which I did not trace. Their portability scores (9 and 3 internal module imports respectively) therefore understate DB coupling by an unknown amount.

I did NOT verify whether the other 15 cog modules missing from SUBSYSTEMS are intentional sub-surfaces or genuine gaps. Several plainly are sub-surfaces (btd6_events/ops/reference/strategy under btd6, role_grants under role, creature_battle under creature). Only starboard was verified end-to-end as a standalone feature with real user-facing settings and no !settings route.

I did NOT test whether scripts/check_command_reachability.py has the same registry-population blindness as its settings sibling. The two are described in-repo as analogs, so it is a live suspicion, not a measurement — I ran out of budget before running it. Do not report it as found.

I did not establish how long starboard has been missing from SUBSYSTEMS, or whether it was ever there. That needs git archaeology I did not spend budget on; the defect stands on the current pin regardless.
I did not measure spider-bot at all — out of lane by the prompt's own scoping, and I did not borrow it as a comparison point.

I could not run either repo's full pytest suite. My stubs are sufficient for the stdlib-ish checkers and for superbot-next's plugin test (which needs no discord), but superbot's unit tests import real discord.py. So every superbot test-based claim in these rows is source-read, and I classified none of them TEST-PROVEN.

I dropped no verified row for space. Two candidate rows were dropped for being code smells rather than concrete failures, per the survival rule: (a) superbot's ai_cog registering into 4 separate runtime registries at cog_load with interaction_router having no unregister() API — real and documented at cogs/ai_cog.py:308-311 and 351-356, but I could not construct a user-visible failure from it since cog_load is idempotent by guard; (b) the 5 raw_sql warnings outside utils/db/, which are layering debt with no reachable user consequence I could name.

lanes.lane: R4 — bootstrap, degraded states and recovery, compared (superbot @5e3a667b vs superbot-next @d5f66dc2)
