challenges.headline: The "too much history / too many trials and errors" framing is a claim about the docs, not the runtime: only 12 of 883 modules and 1,695 of 243,961 lines (0.69%) of superbot's code is unreachable from its composition root and there is exactly ONE TODO marker in the whole tree, while the doc corpus is 863 files / 185,658 lines with 176 files / 39,605 lines already machine-labelled `historical`/`archive` — so the minimal honest cleanup is a doc harvest plus two named lazy back-edges (views.navigation→cogs.help_cog, core.runtime.persistent_views→views.base/navigation) that weld a 148-module shared floor onto every cog, and the rebuild is being paid for instead even though it makes the marginal cost of a subsystem 3.0x heavier (10,149 vs 3,389 LOC).

strengths.area: code health / dead-mass census — the central test of the 'trials and errors' framing
strengths.claim: superbot's runtime carries essentially no abandoned code. Transitive AST import-walk from the composition root (bot1, config, healthserver, control_api, guild_lifecycle + all 59 AST-parsed config.INITIAL_EXTENSIONS entries, following module-level AND function-body imports, marking package ancestors) reaches 871 of 883 modules and 242,266 of 243,961 lines. DEAD = 12 modules / 1,695 LOC = 0.69%, and 2 of those 12 are package __init__ shims. Corroborating density measures on the same tree: exactly 1 TODO/FIXME/HACK/XXX marker in 243,961 lines (disbot/services/ai_tools.py:201, an issue-numbered forward reference), and 2 files whose NAME carries a legacy/version marker (services/parsers/steam_btd6_news.py, views/ux_lab/layout_v2.py). Strict module-level-only exact-resolution SCC analysis finds 4 cycles covering 42 modules and every one is a documented package-facade re-export (utils.db + its 34 submodules; utils.fishing; core.runtime.ai; views.casino) — zero genuine dependency tangles.
strengths.quote:
Ownership rule
--------------
Submodules import primitives via ``from utils.db import pool`` and call
``pool.get() / pool.fetchone() / pool.fetchall() / pool.execute()`` so
production callers and tests that monkeypatch ``utils.db.pool.X`` both
target the same attribute.
strengths.contradicts: The owner's own framing (2026-08-28) that superbot is 'filled with too much history, too many trials and errors' — as a statement about the CODE it is refuted by measurement: 99.31% of disbot's lines are reachable from the composition root, and the largest single SCC is a deliberately documented re-export facade, not a tangle. It also contradicts the estate's implicit reading that a 243,961-line tree must be accreted debris.
strengths.guard_population: All 883 .py files under disbot/ at 5e3a667b. Cannot be empty: the seed set is config.INITIAL_EXTENSIONS, AST-counted at exactly 59 entries, and tests/unit/invariants/test_extension_integrity.py imports every one of those 59 inside the required code-quality check. The walker is mine, not the repo's — the repo has no dead-code guard, which is why enforcement here is the extension-import tier rather than a purpose-built checker.
strengths.simpler_than_counterpart: superbot-next has no equivalent measurement and no dead-code guard either; its own R1 lane found 12 files of frozen capture-world literals shipped as live surfaces, which is a defect class superbot's tree does not carry.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Stop budgeting for 'clearing out the trials and errors'. There are 1,695 lines of them. Budget instead for the two structural seams in A-S09/A-D03 and the owner content decision in A-D02.

strengths.area: enforcement architecture — what actually blocks a merge
strengths.claim: superbot's enforcement is not thin, it is CONCENTRATED, and I verified the concentration live rather than inferring it from workflow files. GET /repos/menno420/superbot/rules/branches/main returns exactly ONE required status check context — `code-quality` — and that context is the job key `code-quality:` in .github/workflows/code-quality.yml, whose final step runs `pytest tests/ -v -n auto --tb=short` over 1,060 test files / 11,668 test functions (both counted). check_architecture --mode strict, check_consistency --mode strict, ruff and mypy are steps in that SAME required job with no continue-on-error. So the estate reading 'only 14 of 45 checkers run in CI' is a statement about workflow step lines, not about enforcement: the checkers are libraries driven from tests/, and tests/ is the gate.
strengths.quote:
- name: Run pytest
        if: steps.changes.outputs.code == 'true'
        # pytest is the dominant per-run cost (was ~109s serial for the 9.4k-test
        # suite). `-n auto` (pytest-xdist) spreads it across the runner's cores for a
        # ~3x speedup (~35s on the 4-core runner).
strengths.contradicts: M5-D09 ('45 scripts/check_*.py exist; only 14 are invoked from any file in .github/workflows/' presented as an enforcement-coverage defect) and the many honest nulls across the digest that say required-status-check state for superbot could not be established. It IS establishable and I established it: one required context, and it runs the whole suite. It also inverts the count comparison the estate leans on — superbot has 1 required check to superbot-next's 7, but superbot's one check executes 11,668 tests while superbot-next's seven execute 3,648.
strengths.prevents_failure: a checker-detectable regression (layer boundary, write boundary, unmanaged task, silent auto-create, reachability ratchet) reaching main
strengths.guard_population: 1,060 test files / 11,668 test functions under tests/. NOT emptiable in the ordinary case — but see A-D01: the whole pytest step is conditioned on steps.changes.outputs.code == 'true', so on a docs-only PR the population is zero and the required check still reports success.
strengths.simpler_than_counterpart: One required context that runs everything, versus superbot-next's seven contexts of which R2-D04/R2-D05 measured two that exit 0 with zero tests executed.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep the pattern: checkers as importable libraries, one blocking suite. Do NOT copy superbot-next's fan-out into many named contexts without first proving each one's population is non-empty.

strengths.area: anti-vacuity — the managed-task guard tested with an injected positive AND a clean control
strengths.claim: The estate's highest-yield question answered for superbot's flagship write-boundary guard, both directions, by me: tests/unit/invariants/test_no_unmanaged_create_task.py sweeps every .py under disbot/ (883 files, __pycache__ and tests excluded by its own _iter_disbot_py_files) with a 2-entry count-pinned allowlist. Injecting `asyncio.create_task(other())` into a synthetic services/evil_service.py made it FIRE ('Unmanaged asyncio.create_task callsite(s):'); a control tree containing only the real allowlisted files plus a tasks.spawn caller did NOT fire. The allowlist pins a COUNT per file, so adding a second bare create_task to an already-allowlisted file still reds.
strengths.quote:
# Allowlist: (relative_path, expected_callsite_count).  Each entry must

If the owner wants a size ceiling, it needs to be a ratchet over the real per-feature line count (superbot's test_cog_size.py measures only the top-level *_cog.py file, which is why it reads clean while the feature behind it is 50,000 lines), and it applies equally to whichever tree ships.

defects.area: provisioning confirmation gate — worse than the estate recorded
defects.claim: disbot/services/readiness_repair.py, 462 lines, is the LARGEST statically-orphaned module in the tree: zero production importers. `grep -rn 'readiness_repair' --include='*.py' disbot tests scripts tools` returns 6 hits inside disbot/ and every one of them is a docstring or comment mention (resource_provisioning.py:62, setup_operations.py:1000, setup_draft.py:38, setup_access.py:5 and :143, views/setup/draft_render.py:15) plus one real test file. Yet it contains a live `ResourceProvisioningPipeline().provision(..., confirmed=True)` call at lines 382-387, and the estate digest counts it as one of the '3 of 3 production call sites' that bypass the confirmation gate.
defects.quote:
result = await ResourceProvisioningPipeline().provision(
        guild,
        request,
        actor,
        confirmed=True,
    )
defects.contradicts: M1-D02 directly: 'all 3 of 3 production call sites of ResourceProvisioningPipeline().provision() hardcode confirmed=True — services/readiness_repair.py:382-387, services/automation_executor.py:427-432, services/setup_operations.py:1352-1358'. One of those three is not a production call site — nothing under disbot/ imports the module it lives in, so it is unreachable at runtime. The real production count is 2 of 2, and the module is dead weight that also inflates the recorded severity of the gate defect.
defects.failure_scenario: A session acts on M1-D02 and audits all three call sites to fix the confirmation-gate bypass, spending a third of the work on readiness_repair.py — code no user can reach. Worse in the other direction: readiness_repair.py is unit-tested (tests/unit/services/test_readiness_repair.py, 270+ lines), so the suite reports it green and a reader concludes the repair path works, when nothing invokes it. Preview -> repair is a documented setup capability the operator does not actually have.
defects.successor_recommendation: Delete readiness_repair.py and its test, or wire it, but decide. Then re-scope M1-D02 to the 2 reachable call sites. This is also the template for the other 11 orphans: each is small, each has a decision attached, and the whole set is 1,695 lines.

defects.area: the rebuild made the per-feature increment three times heavier
defects.claim: Measured on the same walker with matched thresholds, superbot-next's marginal cost per subsystem is 52 modules / 10,149 LOC (median over the 48 of 49 domain subsystems whose closure exceeds 30 modules) against superbot's 15 modules / 3,389 LOC per cog. Its shared floor is only 12 modules / 2,050 LOC (7 kernel + 5 spec), so almost the entire closure of a subsystem is non-shared code. The fattest are cleanup 161 modules / 41,078 LOC, setup 125 / 34,057, ai 110 / 24,923; even the leanest real ones (automation 27 / 3,959, image_moderation 27 / 5,188) match or exceed superbot's MEDIAN cog.
defects.contradicts: The owner's stated goal for the successor, verbatim: 'Everything should be planned and connected from the start so it remains manageable and able to grow indefinitely.' A design where each additional subsystem drags a median 10,149 lines of non-shared code, on a 12-module shared floor, is the opposite of an indefinitely-growable one — growth is linear in a large constant. It also contradicts R3-S6's 'authoring cost' win, which counts touch-points and not code.
defects.failure_scenario: The owner adds the 50th subsystem to the successor as he intends to keep doing. It costs him a median 10,149 lines of subsystem-local code because there is almost no shared floor to lean on — 12 modules — so panel rendering, ops, service and manifest logic are re-authored per subsystem rather than shared. By the 60th subsystem the tree is larger than the bot it replaced, with the same accretion the rebuild was meant to prevent, and no import-boundary checker (R3-D9) to notice the layers decaying.
defects.new_failure_class: per-subsystem code duplication in place of a shared platform floor — the accretion mode the rebuild was commissioned to prevent
defects.successor_recommendation: Before any more porting, decide the successor's target shape on THIS axis: a deliberately large shared floor with a small per-feature marginal (superbot's shape, 30,925 + 3,389) or a small floor with a large marginal (superbot-next's, 2,050 + 10,149). The first grows indefinitely; the second grows linearly in 10k-line units. The owner asked for the first and the rebuild built the second.

honest_nulls: I did NOT run either bot. Both clones are read-only, discord.py/asyncpg/aiohttp/dotenv are absent (I stubbed all four), and there is no token or Postgres here. Every claim marked LIVE-TESTED means I executed a checker, a test, an API call or my own analysis on this machine — never that I observed production behaviour.

My reachability walker (A-S01, A-D07) follows ast.walk over ALL Import/ImportFrom nodes, so it counts function-body and TYPE_CHECKING imports as edges. That makes it CONSERVATIVE for the dead-code claim (a module reached only lazily still counts as reached, so 0.69% is an upper bound on liveness, i.e. real dead code is <= 1,695 LOC) but it means the 148-module 'shared floor' in A-S08/A-D03 is a RUNTIME closure, not a module-load closure. My separate strict module-level-only pass found only 4 SCCs / 42 modules in superbot. Both numbers are in the method note; do not quote one as the other.

I could NOT reproduce a clean run of superbot's FULL test suite — only the invariants tier (466 tests, 439 passed). tests/unit/invariants/test_lifecycle_observability_contract.py cannot be collected with my stubs (AttributeError: '_SuperBot' object has no attribute 'event') and I ignored it. The 27 failures in test_extension_integrity.py and test_cog_load_smoke.py are stub artifacts (my commands.command/group decorators return the bare function), NOT repo findings — but I did not prove that by fixing the stub, I inferred it from the exception shape. A-S02's live ruleset read establishes that `code-quality` is the ONE required context on menno420/superbot main TODAY. I did NOT check whether it was required at the 5e3a667b pin, nor whether the repository ruleset (id 18556417 / 7388191) has bypass actors configured — I read the effective /rules/branches/main endpoint, which reports applicable rules, not bypass lists.

challenges.lane: CHALLENGE B — defend superbot-next: which abstractions a successor would be foolish to re-derive

challenges.headline: superbot-next's real inheritance is not its panel/manifest/parity layer at all — it is that authority, audit, send-egress and member-data erasure were moved from per-surface convention (superbot: 166 decorators, 49 hand-written audit calls, 18 of 915 sends setting allowed_mentions, 31 hand-written teardown helpers against 84 guild-scoped columns) into REQUIRED FIELDS and REGISTRY-DERIVED WALKS that a new feature cannot forget, and re-deriving those four seams from scratch is the single most expensive thing a successor could choose to do.

strengths.area: workflow engine / audit as a constructor requirement
strengths.claim: Audit cannot be forgotten because it is a REQUIRED no-default field on a frozen dataclass, and there is exactly ONE writer. Measured live: 175 of 175 registered CompoundOpSpecs carry a non-empty audit_verb (100%); `audit_verb: str` sits inside the spec's own '--- required (no default) ---' block, so a CompoundOpSpec cannot be constructed without naming a mutation_type; `emit_central_audit` has ONE production call site (engine.py:272), inside the step-4 transaction; and zero sb/domain modules write audit_log (grep for 'audit_log' outside sb/kernel/workflow returns only binding_audit_log, comments and panel copy). superbot's counterpart is 49 hand-written emit_audit_action call sites across 28 files.
strengths.quote:
# --- required (no default) ---
    op_key: str                                # [S] namespace-reserved workflow key; the once() namespace
    domain: str                                # [S] audit subsystem
    lane: WorkflowLane                         # [S]
    authority_ref: str                         # [S] resolved as leg-0 (K6)
    legs: tuple[LegSpec, ...]                  # [S] ordered; DB legs in-txn first, EFFECT after commit
    idempotency: IdempotencyPosture            # [S] T2-21
    dedup_key: DedupKeySpec | None             # [S] REQUIRED iff DURABLE_ONCE (else None)
    audit_verb: str                            # [S] mutation_type for the ONE central row
strengths.contradicts: M4-D5 and R6-D03 record superbot's audit seam as convention policed by an advisory checker (check_audit_seam is continue-on-error and clears 85 of 193 write-signal functions by NAME MATCH, M5-D02). The digest reads audit as a shared weakness of both repos; on this axis they are not comparable — one is a required constructor argument, the other is a habit with a warn-only linter.
strengths.prevents_failure: unaudited state mutation ships (an operator cannot answer 'who changed this and when' for a subsystem whose author forgot the audit call)
strengths.guard_population: The 'guard' is the Python type system over the 175 registered ops — it cannot be empty while any op exists, and it is the real artifact (the same registry the engine dispatches from), not a model. Its limit: it forces a verb STRING, not that the string is meaningful.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port CompoundOpSpec's required-field discipline verbatim (audit_verb, authority_ref, idempotency in the no-default block). Cheapest structural win in either repo: one dataclass, and an entire class of review burden disappears.

strengths.area: authority attached to the operation, not the surface
strengths.claim: Authority is a property of the MUTATION, resolved as leg-0 by the engine before any leg runs, so every surface that reaches an op inherits the check. Measured live: 175 of 175 ops carry authority_ref; 146 name an explicit tier (user 96, staff 26, administrator 20, moderator 4) and 29 default to '' = the administrator floor; resolve_authority is fail-closed on a non-member actor and on an unconfigured ROLE_SET binding. superbot puts authority on the SURFACE instead: 166 permission decorators in disbot/cogs, 3 in disbot/views, ZERO in disbot/services — and of the 93 view modules that import a service, only 19 contain any authority token at all.
strengths.contradicts: M5-D01/M5-D06 (superbot's governance runs at ONE seam that discord.py applies to prefix commands only; 31 app_commands never reach it; 35 of 43 subsystems fail OPEN when the gate throws). Also contradicts the fleet framing that superbot-next merely 'restated' superbot's patterns — superbot has no equivalent of an authority declaration on a mutation, only on a command.
strengths.prevents_failure: second-surface authority bypass: an existing mutation reached from a new surface (panel button, modal, automation, AI tool, another cog) with no permission check, because the check lived on the old entry point
strengths.guard_population: 175 registered ops — the real dispatch population, never empty. Honest limit: the compiler's P4 authority pass is FORMAT-only at this pin (reserved_capabilities=None => 'no corpus available'), and '' is always valid, so the compiler checks shape, not membership.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep authority on the op spec and resolve it inside the mutation engine. superbot's 166-decorator approach is exactly what made its slash surface (M5-D01) and its !setupadvanced door (M1-D07) diverge from each other.

strengths.claim: The @everyone mass-ping class is closed BY CONSTRUCTION and the fence fires. One module constructs discord.AllowedMentions (adapters/discord/egress.py; UNTRUSTED => AllowedMentions.none() + markdown escape); tools/check_egress.py AST-asserts that no send/reply/Discord-state-mutation call exists outside sb/adapters. Measured: bare run EXIT=0 'check_egress: clean'; an injected `await channel.send(...)` in sb/domain/economy/ produced EXIT=1 with the exact violation; removing it restored EXIT=0. The checker runs at named-gates.yml:94, in the `architecture` job — one of the 7 required contexts. superbot's equivalent surface: 915 `.send(` call sites, 18 `allowed_mentions` occurrences across 5 files, and NO allowed_mentions on the Bot constructor (disbot/bot1.py:98-112 read in full).
strengths.quote:
- SEND (service-initiated ``channel.send`` — the X-1 mass-ping vector,
    reachable by NO frozen primitive until now): THIS port. Every
    service-initiated send routes through ONE ``ChannelEmitter.send``;
    the concrete ``DiscordChannelEmitter`` (adapters/discord/egress.py) is
    the ONLY module that constructs ``discord.AllowedMentions`` — UNTRUSTED
    ⇒ ``AllowedMentions.none()`` + markdown escape, so ``@everyone`` from
    user-authored template text is STRUCTURALLY impossible.
strengths.contradicts: The whole-fleet reading in which superbot is the production-proven bot and superbot-next the unproven rebuild. On the single highest-blast-radius Discord failure mode the PRODUCTION bot has no control at all, and the parked rebuild has a fence I fired on an injected positive.
strengths.prevents_failure: a bot-authored message re-pinging @everyone/@here or a role because it echoed user-supplied text (X-1 mass-ping)
strengths.guard_population: Every .py file under sb/ (634+ at this pin) — the real shipped tree, not a snapshot or a model, and it cannot be empty. Verified non-vacuous by injected positive (EXIT=1).
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port the ChannelEmitter port, the (trust, allow_mentions) -> AllowedMentions function and check_egress together. Re-deriving this after a live incident is the expensive order.

strengths.claim: Every table declares what class of personal data it holds, how long it keeps it, and the audited workflow that erases it — and a checker enforces the pairing over the REAL registry. Measured live: 81 registered StoreSpecs; 52 carry member data (48 MEMBER_ID + 4 MEMBER_PII) and 52 of 52 carry BOTH a non-empty retention window AND an erasure_ref; 29 are DataClass.NONE. `python3 tools/check_data_lifecycle.py` -> 'clean (81 store(s))' EXIT=0, and injecting one MEMBER_PII store with no retention and no erasure_ref produced 2 distinct violations in-process. superbot has no analogue: 92 CREATE TABLE statements in disbot/migrations and 9 total occurrences of erasure/retention vocabulary in disbot/, one of which is a docstring calling erasure 'Reserved'.
strengths.quote:
Over EVERY registered StoreSpec (kernel constants + manifest `stores`
facets):
  (a) every `data_class != NONE` store carries a non-empty `retention` AND a
      non-empty `erasure_ref`;
  (b) every cache declares a `cache_scope`, and a member-data cache is
      GUILD-scoped (closes the B#34/X-3 cross-guild bleed by construction);
  (c) the `erasure_ref` is a WorkflowRef (a bare HandlerRef bypassing the
      audited seam is a SEMANTIC_VIOLATION — erasure IS an auditable
      mutation).
strengths.contradicts: R2's headline that superbot-next's guards characteristically run over empty or modelled populations. This one runs over 81 real registered stores, 52 of them load-bearing, and I fired it on an injected positive. It also contradicts the estate reading that the rebuild only re-expressed what superbot already had — superbot has nothing here.
strengths.prevents_failure: personal data with no declared retention and no erasure path accumulating in a new table that nobody remembers when a deletion request or a retention question arrives
strengths.guard_population: The 81 StoreSpecs registered by kernel constants + the 49 manifests' `stores` facets; 52 of 81 are the biting population. Non-empty, real artifact. Weakness recorded as B-D04: the checker is NOT one of the 7 required contexts, and erasure_ref defaults to None in the dataclass, so the field itself does not force the pairing.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port StoreSpec's data_class/retention/erasure_ref triple and the checker, AND promote the checker into the required set (one line of workflow YAML).

strengths.area: erasure completeness derived from the registry, not a hand list
strengths.claim: The member-erasure executor ENUMERATES the registered store inventory rather than carrying a hand-maintained table list, so a store added tomorrow is erased without anyone editing the eraser; each store's leg runs through run_ref (audited) and is idempotency-keyed so a crash mid-walk resumes; and a store it could not reach is reported as complete=False + unreached rather than silently skipped. Contrast the same problem in superbot: guild_lifecycle.teardown is 31 hand-written `_teardown_*` helpers against 84 guild_id BIGINT column declarations in disbot/migrations, under a docstring asserting the list is complete.
strengths.quote:
Completeness is STRUCTURAL, not audited by inspection:
(1) ENUMERATE — the registered StoreSpec inventory (sb.spec.versioning
    register_store — kernel constants now, manifest `stores` facets at the
    port bands), filtered `data_class != NONE`. check_data_lifecycle CI-reds
    any member-data store lacking data_class + erasure_ref, so no member-data
    store exists OUTSIDE this walk.
strengths.contradicts: M1-S06, which files superbot's teardown as a strength for preserving the forensic audit trail. That is true and orthogonal: the same file's COMPLETENESS claim ('Every module that owns guild-scoped in-process state must be represented here') is a hand list, measured by M1-D06 at 23 helpers vs 74 tables and by me at 31 helpers vs 84 guild_id column declarations — different numbers from the same defect, and I record the discrepancy rather than adopting theirs.
strengths.prevents_failure: a table added after the purge routine was written keeps a departed member's or guild's data forever, because the purge is a list somebody has to remember to extend
strengths.guard_population: Derived at runtime from registered_stores() filtered to data_class != NONE — 52 stores at this pin. It CANNOT be empty while any member-data store is registered, which is exactly the property the hand-list version lacks. Proven by tests/unit/privacy/test_s11_mechanics.py:170 ('walks_every_member_store_and_proves_complete') — but over an in-memory fixture, not a real database.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve the enumerate-the-registry shape even if the erasure product is deferred: it is the difference between a purge that ages well and one that rots. But see B-D01 — at this pin the executor has zero production callers and none of its 48 named erasure workflows is a registered op.

strengths.claim: The rebuild's verification layer runs where the donor's cannot. MEASURED on this machine with neither discord.py nor asyncpg installed: `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q --collect-only` in superbot-next -> '3678 tests collected in 2.02s', EXIT=0; the same command in superbot -> '5402 tests collected, 632 errors in 26.23s', EXIT=2, 'Interrupted: 632 errors during collection'. That is 632 of ~1060 test files unable to even import. This lane, and by the digest's own honest nulls at least four sibling lanes, could not execute a single superbot test — the donor's 9.4k-test verification story is unavailable to any reviewer, CI job or contributor without a fully provisioned environment.
strengths.line_span: 5-7 (kernel port isolation); measured property is whole-tree
strengths.quote: One kernel runtime interprets every grammar-expressible PanelSpec
strengths.contradicts: R6-D10, which ranks superbot ahead on the verification axis by COUNT (1060 test files vs 273, 863 docs vs 92). Counted differently — tests that can actually be run in a bare checkout — the ranking inverts completely: 3678 collectable vs 632 collection errors. Both numbers are true; only one of them is a property you can use.
strengths.prevents_failure: a verification estate that silently degrades to skip-green (or dies at collection) in every environment that is not fully provisioned — the mechanism behind R2-D04/R2-D05's 14-skipped and 11-skipped required CI legs
strengths.guard_population: 3678 collected test items over the real sb/ tree with the vendor SDKs absent. Real artifact; empty only if the suite is deleted.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep the ports-and-adapters split that makes this true (discord types only under sb/adapters). It is the precondition for a reviewer, a CI runner and an auditing agent all being able to run the same checks.

strengths.area: Discord surface containment / one admission order
strengths.claim: Every Discord entry point is confined to 37 files in 3 declared directories (sb/kernel/interaction/adapters 7, sb/adapters/discord 20, sb/app 10), each of the 6 kernel surface adapters ends in one `await resolve(req)`, and resolve() applies ONE fixed order — admission -> authority -> validate -> cooldown -> ACK -> audit -> dispatch -> render — across all 8 declared Surfaces (SLASH, PREFIX, COMPONENT, MODAL, NL_INTENT, NL_ORCHESTRATION, MAINTENANCE, SETUP). The containment half is CI-enforced and I fired it: an injected @bot.command calling a domain handler directly produced EXIT=1 with 3 violations in sb/domain/economy/. check_no_skip runs at named-gates.yml:88, in the required `architecture` job. superbot's counterpart is 54 files free to register a command or listener, behind three partial gates with different coverage and different failure postures.
strengths.quote:
1. **Surface-registration containment** — the tokens that register a Discord
   entry point (`@bot.event`, `@bot.command`, `@commands.command`,
   `@tree.command`, `@app_commands.command`, `tree.interaction_check`,
   `bot.add_view`, `@bot.listen`) may appear ONLY under the sanctioned
   composition layers: `sb/kernel/interaction/adapters/`,
   `sb/adapters/discord/`, `sb/app/`. Anywhere else = a bypassing path.
strengths.contradicts: Its own success message and docstring, which claim the stronger property ('there is NO path from a Discord surface to a handler except through resolve()'). I measured that the SKIP half is unenforced inside the 3 sanctioned dirs — see B-D02. The containment half is real; the funnel half is convention.
strengths.prevents_failure: a new cog quietly registering its own listener and dispatching straight to a mutation, outside governance, cooldown and audit — the shape behind superbot's 31 governance-free app_commands
strengths.guard_population: All .py under sb/ (634+ files). Non-empty, real artifact; injected positive returns EXIT=1. The blind spot is the 37 files of the sanctioned dirs, which the guard by design does not inspect.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port the fence AND close its blind spot with a second rule asserting that every function inside the sanctioned dirs that touches a handler ref reaches resolve() — a ~30-line AST addition, not a redesign.

strengths.claim: Component ids are minted once into a single static table with a RAISING collision fence — `_mint` raises PanelCompileError('custom_id_collision') if a custom_id is already bound to a different binding, and register_hub raises PanelCompileError('hub_redefined') on reassignment. superbot's equivalent is 280 hand-written `custom_id=` literals across 86 files, routed by the prefix before the first colon, with a register() that LOGS A WARNING and silently overwrites the previous handler (4 register call sites total).
strengths.contradicts: The reading in which superbot's persistent-panel machinery is the mature one. On identity collision the shipped bot degrades silently ('Overwriting existing handler for prefix %r') while the rebuild refuses to boot.
strengths.prevents_failure: two subsystems minting the same custom_id (or router prefix) so a user's button click is handled by the wrong subsystem, or one subsystem's buttons stop working after an unrelated load-order change
strengths.guard_population: The 863 table entries minted when all 314 panels register (827 ComponentBinding + 36 NavBinding, per M9-S02, re-read here in source). The population is the real registration path used at boot; empty only if no panel registers.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve minting-with-a-raise. Six lines, and it removes an entire debugging genre.

strengths.claim: Every environment variable is declared once as a typed ConfigSpec and read through cfg, with an AST fence banning os.getenv/os.environ outside sb/kernel/config/ (2 allowlist entries), running in the REQUIRED `architecture` job at named-gates.yml:90. Measured: 53 ConfigSpec entries (`python3 -c 'from sb.spec.config import CONFIG_FIELDS; print(len(CONFIG_FIELDS))'` -> 53). superbot's counterpart is 61 os.getenv/os.environ reads scattered across 24 files, several parsing their own defaults inline (e.g. `int(os.getenv("BTD6_INGESTION_STARTUP_DELAY_S", "60"))`).
strengths.quote: ONE place every env var is declared: `CONFIG_FIELDS`.
strengths.contradicts: M8-S03 and M10-S1 report 38 and 44 declared fields respectively; I measure 53 by importing CONFIG_FIELDS and taking len() at the same pin. Two prior lanes and I disagree on the size of the very thing we are all praising — the shape of the claim survives, the number in the digest does not.
strengths.prevents_failure: an undeclared env var read deep in a service, discovered only when production boots with it unset (superbot's BTD6/automation/YouTube flags are exactly this shape)
strengths.guard_population: All .py under sb/ minus 2 allowlisted paths — the real tree, verified non-vacuous by another lane's injected positives (M8-S03: os.getenv injected into sb/kernel and sb/domain both EXIT=1).
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port CONFIG_FIELDS + check_config_usage before writing the first feature; retrofitting 61 scattered reads is the expensive order.

strengths.claim: The rebuild has a kernel answer to the exact bug class superbot could only allowlist. sb/kernel/scheduler/due_queue.py makes a timer fire ONE scheduler-owned transaction — deterministic once() key (task_id:fire_epoch), the audited run_ref, and mark_fired/advance committing together, 'no crash window in either direction' — and its three declared consumers are proof_channel's LOCK_RECONCILE_TASK, role's GRANTS_EXPIRY_TASK and games' SESSION_GC_TASK. superbot's known instances of the same class are an in-memory asyncio.sleep with no persisted deadline (security raid-lockdown _hold_then_lift, M2-D2, allowlisted with a written user-visible caveat) and proof_channel_cog._auto_unlock — which are literally the 2 of 2 functions superbot's check_deferred_recovery can even see (M5-D03).
strengths.quote:
The whole fire is ONE scheduler-owned txn: ``once()`` (deterministic
``task_id:fire_epoch`` — the fix for the shipped uuid4-defeated claim) +
K7 ``run_ref(ref, ctx, conn=conn)`` (pure-DB legs + central audit +
AT_LEAST_ONCE enqueue on MY conn) + ``mark_fired``/advance commit together —
no crash window in either direction.
strengths.contradicts: M2-S6, which files superbot's allowlist entry for the raid-lockdown restart gap as a strength ('a real instance of never write down a limitation'). Documenting a restart gap honestly is better than hiding it — but the successor should know the rebuild carries the mechanism that removes the gap, wired to that same subsystem (proof_channel).
strengths.prevents_failure: a deferred one-shot (raid slowmode lift, temp-role expiry, reminder, session GC) lost across a restart or deploy, leaving a channel or member in the temporary state permanently
strengths.guard_population: 12 tests in tests/unit/scheduler/test_due_queue.py assert arm/claim/fire-exactly-once, quiet hours, condition polls, failure routing and boot reconcile — but over conftest.py's FakeSchedulerDb, an IN-MEMORY MODEL of sb_due_queue, not a real Postgres. The real-DB tier skips green here. The design is source-verified; the DB behaviour is not.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve the due-queue primitive and its 'one txn covers fire + mark_fired' rule; do NOT preserve the belief that it is database-proven until the integration tier actually runs.

strengths.claim: superbot-next has an actual out-of-tree plugin contract; superbot has none. plugin_host declares which manifest facets an installed distribution may own (commands, panels, settings, events, capabilities) and which stay host-owned (stores, data_invariants, wizard_sections), pins each plugin by manifest hash (proven both ways in M8-S07: a zeroed hash and a deleted pin each produced EXIT=1), and boots 2 real exemplars through the production load path inside check_runtime_smoke. superbot's only extension mechanism is bot.load_extension over hand-listed in-tree module paths (6 call sites, all in admin cogs).
strengths.quote:
#: v1 contract: the SubsystemManifest facets an out-of-tree plugin may
#: declare / the facets that stay host-owned (docs/game-plugin-contract.md).
ALLOWED_FACETS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "commands", "panels", "settings", "events", "capabilities",
)
HOST_ONLY_FACETS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "stores", "data_invariants", "wizard_sections",
)
strengths.contradicts: R3-D5 reads this same fence as the thing that BLOCKS the owner's cog-portability requirement (29 of 49 in-tree manifests declare stores and so could not ship as plugins). Both are true, and the digest carries only the negative half: superbot cannot ship an out-of-tree extension AT ALL (R3-D4 measured that lifting one of its cogs drags governance and config with it). The successor's choice is not 'this contract vs superbot's better one' — it is 'this contract, widened, vs nothing'.
strengths.prevents_failure: an extension silently taking ownership of host-owned state (tables, data invariants) so the host can no longer reason about who writes what
strengths.guard_population: The installed-distribution set discovered via the sb.plugins entry point — which M8-D04 measured can degrade to the EMPTY SET and stay green (`mv examples /tmp` -> EXIT=0). The FENCE is source-real; the GATE proving plugins boot is emptiable. Both facts belong in a successor's plan.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep the contract; widen HOST_ONLY_FACETS to allow a plugin-owned store namespace — the owner's requirement is adding EXISTING cogs, and 29 of 49 of the repo's own subsystems fail the current fence.

strengths.claim: Mutating store functions cannot be called without a transaction handle the engine owns: in sb/domain/economy/store.py every mutator (credit_coins, try_debit_coins, insert_economy_audit, set_daily_claim, set_last_worked, increment_job, try_grant_unique_item, and the four erase_/tombstone_ functions) takes `conn` as its first positional argument, while every read accessor (get_coins, read_economy, get_inventory, has_item) defaults conn=None. Measured on the only cross-domain consumer I traced: all 10 imports of sb.domain.economy.store from outside sb/domain/economy (fishing service/panels/ops, 3 files) import `get_coins` — a read. Nothing outside the subsystem imports a mutator.
strengths.quote:
async def get_coins(user_id: int, guild_id: int, conn: Any = None) -> int:

async def credit_coins(conn: Any, *, user_id: int, guild_id: int,
strengths.contradicts: M10-D2, which records that the 'raw conn.execute banned outside sb/kernel/db' rule is enforced by nothing. That is correct about ENFORCEMENT; this row records that the SIGNATURE convention nonetheless holds where I traced it, so the digest's implied conclusion (that writes are loose in practice) is not what the code shows in the one domain I checked end to end.
strengths.prevents_failure: a panel or handler mutating money outside the audited transaction because the store function was importable and self-contained
strengths.guard_population: Not a guard — a signature convention, unchecked by any tool. I traced ONE subsystem (economy) of 49. Do not read this as a repo-wide property; read it as the shape a successor should make machine-checked (a checker asserting every mutating store function takes conn as arg 0 is ~40 lines).
strengths.successor_recommendation: Promote the convention to a checker before the tree grows; it is the cheap half of M10-D2's missing sole_writer enforcement.

defects.area: erasure — a complete declaration with no implementation behind it
defects.claim: The erasure spine is declared over 52 stores and executes NOTHING. Measured live: of the 48 distinct erasure_ref names, ZERO are registered CompoundOpSpec op_keys (the walk calls run_ref, which needs one); 42 resolve to some callable through sb.spec.refs.resolve but 6 do not resolve at all — kernel.ai.scrub_decision_audit, kernel.audit.tombstone_subject, kernel.outbox.scrub_subject, kernel.idempotency.prune_subject, kernel.draft.discard_subject_drafts, kernel.scheduler.erase_subject_timers. And `grep -rn run_erasure` over the whole repo returns the definition, the __all__ entry, one docstring and 6 test lines — ZERO production callers. check_data_lifecycle stays EXIT=0 throughout, because it checks that erasure_ref is non-empty and is a WorkflowRef, never that it resolves.
defects.quote: Completeness is STRUCTURAL, not audited by inspection:
defects.contradicts: B-S05, my own strongest 'superbot never solved this' row, and the module's own header. The registry-derived WALK is the right abstraction and I still recommend preserving it — but the successor must not inherit the belief that erasure works. It also contradicts check_data_lifecycle's clean EXIT=0, which certifies a promise, not a capability.
defects.failure_scenario: A member asks the owner to delete their data (or leaves and the guild owner asks for a purge). An operator tries to invoke the erasure path — there is none to invoke, because run_erasure has no command, no button and no guild-leave hook. If it is wired later exactly as written, the walk still cannot erase the six kernel stores whose refs do not resolve, so the member's user_id remains in audit_log (retention 'permanent'), event_outbox, ai_decision_audit, sb_drafts, idempotency_keys and sb_due_queue after a run the executor reports on.
defects.new_failure_class: A declaration-complete, implementation-empty subsystem that passes its own CI gate: the gate checks the shape of the promise, not the existence of the promised code.
defects.successor_recommendation: Extend the ref-resolution gate (check_runtime_smoke / check_orphan_pendings already walk 936 handler refs) to cover erasure_ref and require each to be a registered op. One loop, and 48 promises become 48 checked obligations.

defects.claim: check_no_skip prints 'every surface funnels through resolve()' while being structurally unable to see a surface that skips resolve(). MEASURED with a copied tree: a file registering `@bot.command(name="freecoins")` and awaiting a domain handler directly — no resolve(), no authority, no audit — produced EXIT=1 with 3 violations when placed in sb/domain/economy/, and EXIT=0 with the message 'check_no_skip: clean (every surface funnels through resolve())' when placed in sb/adapters/discord/. The fence checks CONTAINMENT to 3 directories (37 files); the skip half of its own contract has an effective population of ZERO.
defects.quote:
check_no_skip — the K8 AST no-skip fence (frozen L0 spec 02 §7, arms at
S9): there is NO path from a Discord surface to a handler except through
`sb.kernel.interaction.resolve.resolve()`.
defects.contradicts: R5-S04 and R6-S02, which both state the strong form ('an AST fence over the whole sb/ tree asserting there is NO path from a Discord surface to a handler except through resolve()') as if the checker enforced it. It enforces containment only. My injected positive inside sb/adapters/discord returned EXIT=0.
defects.failure_scenario: A contributor adds a fast path to sb/adapters/discord/ (the natural home for anything Discord-shaped — 20 files already live there) that calls a domain handler directly to avoid resolve() overhead on a hot component. Authority leg-0, the cooldown, the dispatch trace and the transparency audit are all skipped for that path; every required CI gate stays green, and the checker's own success line asserts the opposite.
defects.new_failure_class: A guard whose success MESSAGE states a stronger property than the guard's rules — so a reader who greps CI output learns something false.
defects.successor_recommendation: Either add the missing rule (inside the sanctioned dirs, a call to a resolved handler ref must be lexically downstream of resolve()) or change the success line to 'surface registration contained to N files'. The message is doing damage on its own.

defects.claim: The double-submit protection the engine is built around never runs. Measured live over the 175 registered ops: idempotency posture is NATURAL_KEY on 174 and NONE_JUSTIFIED on 1 — ZERO DURABLE_ONCE. Consequently `key` at engine.py:227 is None for every op, the once()/_reproduce dedup branch at step 4a is unreachable, and the 'This action was already completed.' replay path cannot be produced by any shipped operation. Zero ops declare single_flight_scope, so the _single_flight_locks table is likewise unused; 0 of 175 carry a dedup_key.
defects.contradicts: M9-S07's contradiction note reads the unused saga machinery as the problem (165 of 175 ops single-leg). The sharper measurement is here: it is the IDEMPOTENCY posture, a required field, that is unanimously set to the one value which disables the mechanism — and the idempotency_keys table (migration 0001) therefore receives no rows from the compound-op path at all.
defects.failure_scenario: A member double-clicks 'Claim daily' or a moderator double-clicks 'Ban' on a slow panel. Both interactions reach the engine, both mint a fresh uuid4 mutation_id, both run their DB legs, and both write an audit_log row — the guard designed to collapse the second into 'This action was already completed.' is armed for no operation in the bot.
defects.new_failure_class: A required constructor field satisfied unanimously by the ONE value that disables the mechanism the field exists to select.
defects.successor_recommendation: Make DURABLE_ONCE the default for any op with a user-clickable trigger, or add a compiler predicate asserting that a panel-action-reachable op is not NATURAL_KEY. As shipped, the posture field records an intention nobody exercises.

defects.claim: The 52-store retention/erasure guarantee rests on a NON-REQUIRED check plus a field that defaults to None. check_data_lifecycle appears in exactly one workflow line — ci.yml:51, inside the `checkers` job — and never in named-gates.yml, so it is not among the 7 required contexts on main (code-quality, manifest-validate, architecture, sim-gate, golden-parity, check_compat_frozen, pip-audit). In sb/spec/versioning.py the field is `erasure_ref: WorkflowRef | None = None`, i.e. omitting it is legal Python. Contrast the three fences that ARE required (check_no_skip, check_egress, check_config_usage at named-gates.yml:88/94/90).
defects.quote:
data_class: DataClass = DataClass.NONE            # [S]
    erasure_ref: WorkflowRef | None = None            # [S] REQUIRED iff data_class != NONE (AUDITED K7 hook)
defects.contradicts: My own B-S04, which files the data-lifecycle guard as LIVE-TESTED and source-enforced. It is both of those and NOT blocking — M11-D11 counted 12 of 24 checkers in the same non-required job; this is one of them, and it happens to be the one guarding personal data.
defects.failure_scenario: A contributor adds a store holding member ids, sets data_class=MEMBER_ID and leaves erasure_ref at its default. check_data_lifecycle reds — in a job that does not block the merge — and the PR lands. The table is now inside the registry-derived erasure walk's filter but names no erasure workflow, and the walk reports the subject as unreached forever after.
defects.successor_recommendation: One line: move check_data_lifecycle into the required architecture job alongside its three siblings. The comment already says 'REQUIRED iff' — make the CI agree with the comment.

defects.claim: Not one operation in the bot asks for confirmation. Measured live: 0 of 175 registered CompoundOpSpecs carry a ConfirmationSpec, so the ConfirmRequired branch at engine.py:219-221 is dead code; and 0 of 185 legs declare IRREVERSIBLE (176 reversible, 9 compensatable), so the reversibility rollup never reaches the value the confirmation grammar exists to gate. This sits beside a whole shipped apparatus implying otherwise: sb/adapters/discord/confirm_view.py, ConfirmationSpec in sb/spec/confirmation.py, and the compiler's destructive_confirmation predicate, which M9-D04 measured runs over 2 of 640 panel actions.
defects.contradicts: M9-D04 reports destructive_confirmation's population as 2 of 640 panel ACTIONS and reads it as a thin but non-zero fence. Measured from the workflow side it is exactly ZERO: no compound op declares a ConfirmationSpec, so the engine-level backstop — the one that would catch an action reached from a non-panel surface — has never been armed for anything.
defects.failure_scenario: An operator opens the moderation panel and clicks Ban, or the settings panel and clicks Unbind, or Clear warnings. The mutation executes on the first click with no confirmation step anywhere in the path, because no operation declares one — including moderation.ban, moderation.kick, moderation.clearwarnings, settings.unbind and settings.clear_scalar, all enumerated from the live registry.
defects.new_failure_class: Three cooperating layers (spec grammar, engine branch, adapter view) all correct and all connected to a population of zero — the apparatus reads as a shipped feature to every reviewer who greps for it.
defects.successor_recommendation: Add a compiler predicate with a real denominator: every op reachable from a panel action whose legs are not all reversible must declare a ConfirmationSpec. Until then, treat 'the bot confirms destructive actions' as false.

defects.area: send egress — the live mass-ping vector
defects.claim: The PRODUCTION bot has no mention-containment control at any level. Measured at 5e3a667b: 915 `.send(` call sites in disbot/; 18 occurrences of `allowed_mentions` in the whole tree across 5 files (views/youtube_renderers.py, cogs/setup_cog.py, cogs/ai_review_cog.py, core/runtime/ai/natural_language_stage.py, core/runtime/ai/response_renderer_registry.py); and the Bot constructor at disbot/bot1.py:98-112 passes command_prefix, intents, help_command, max_messages and case_insensitive — and no allowed_mentions, so discord.py's permissive default applies process-wide. No checker, invariant test or architecture rule in the repo mentions allowed_mentions.
defects.quote:
bot = _SuperBot(
    command_prefix=config.PREFIX,
    intents=intents,
    help_command=None,
defects.contradicts: The estate's treatment of superbot as the production-hardened donor whose safety patterns should be ported forward. Its AI subsystem carries a carefully-built prompt-injection envelope (M4-S11) while its ordinary message path — 915 sends — has no mention containment at all. spider-bot's BUG-0019 fix (M12-S03) shows this family of bug is live and known in the estate.
defects.failure_scenario: A member types a command whose reply echoes their input — a ticket subject, a poll question (`!poll` renders raw options, M2-D5), a starboard quote, a karma reason, an AI answer quoting the channel. The bot's own message contains @everyone, and because the bot holds Mention Everyone in that channel the ping is delivered server-wide, from the bot, un-deletable by the member who caused it.
defects.successor_recommendation: Port superbot-next's ChannelEmitter/(trust, allow_mentions) port and check_egress. This is the one place in the whole two-repo comparison where the frozen production bot carries an unmitigated high-blast-radius defect and the parked rebuild carries the closed form.

defects.area: authority lives on the surface, not the mutation
defects.claim: Authority in superbot is 166 decorators in disbot/cogs, 3 in disbot/views, 8 in core, 2 in utils and ZERO in disbot/services — while 190 service modules hold the mutations. Of the 93 view modules that import a service, only 19 contain any authority token at all (guild_permissions / admin_or_owner / is_setup_admin / is_owner / can_apply_setup / manage_guild / administrator); 74 do not. There is no place in the codebase where a mutation itself declares who may run it.
defects.quote: services: 0
defects.contradicts: M1-S03/M1-S04, which file setup_access.py's two-tier line and the hub's live administrator re-check as patterns to port almost verbatim. They are good — and they are 2 careful surfaces out of 93 service-importing view modules. Porting the pattern reproduces the coverage problem; porting superbot-next's op-level declaration does not.
defects.failure_scenario: A new panel button is added that calls an existing mutation service — the normal way features grow here, since 93 view modules already import services. The author adds no permission check because the service does not ask for one and 74 sibling view modules do not have one either. Any member who can open that panel now runs an operator mutation. This is the general form of the two shipped instances already measured: !setupadvanced with no permission decorator (M1-D07) and the 31 app_commands that never reach the governance seam (M5-D01).
defects.successor_recommendation: Do not port the decorator pattern. Port CompoundOpSpec.authority_ref (B-S02) — the same information, stored where it cannot be lost.

defects.claim: guild_lifecycle.py asserts total coverage and implements a hand list. Measured: 31 `_teardown_*` helper definitions against 84 `guild_id ... BIGINT` column declarations across disbot/migrations/*.sql (92 CREATE TABLE statements in total). The module docstring states the completeness rule as an obligation on every future author, which is the definition of a list that goes stale.
defects.quote:
Centralises all cleanup that must happen when the bot leaves a guild, so that
no module accumulates permanent per-guild state indefinitely.

Every module that owns guild-scoped in-process state must be represented here.
defects.contradicts: M1-D06 counts 23 helpers against 74 guild-scoped tables; I count 31 helper definitions against 84 guild_id BIGINT column declarations. Different counting rules, same defect — recorded rather than smoothed, because a planner quoting either number without re-measuring will be quoting a figure two lanes could not reproduce from each other.
defects.failure_scenario: A guild removes the bot and later re-invites it. State written to any guild-scoped table that never got a _teardown_ helper is still there and is read as current — the shape M1-D01 already confirmed for setup_draft_operations, where a staged setup operation from before the removal is re-read on re-invite and can be applied to the new configuration.
defects.successor_recommendation: Replace with superbot-next's shape: derive the purge population from the store registry (B-S05) so a new table joins the walk by existing, not by being remembered.

defects.claim: Duplicate component-prefix registration is a warning and a silent overwrite. interaction_router.register() logs 'Overwriting existing handler for prefix %r' and then replaces the entry; dispatch routes on the substring before the first ':' in custom_id. There are 280 hand-written `custom_id=` literals across 86 files and no checker anywhere in scripts/ or tests/unit/invariants/ that inspects them for prefix collisions (scripts/check_command_collisions.py covers command names, not custom_ids).
defects.contradicts: M5-S04, which reads interaction_router as a considered design with an observable fail posture. Its DENY/ALLOW posture is indeed observable; its IDENTITY layer is not — a collision is one WARNING line at boot and a permanently misrouted button.
defects.failure_scenario: Two subsystems register the same custom_id prefix (or one subsystem's ids collide with another's after a rename). The second registration wins, the first subsystem's buttons start dispatching into the wrong handler, and the only evidence is one WARNING at boot. Which subsystem loses depends on INITIAL_EXTENSIONS order, so the symptom moves when an unrelated cog is added.
defects.successor_recommendation: Port superbot-next's minting-with-a-raise (B-S08). A collision should be a boot failure, not a log line.

defects.area: the verification estate is unrunnable without the vendor SDK
defects.claim: superbot's test suite cannot be collected, let alone run, in an environment without discord.py: `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q --collect-only` -> '5402 tests collected, 632 errors in 26.23s', 'Interrupted: 632 errors during collection', EXIT=2. superbot-next's collects clean in the same environment (3678 collected, EXIT=0). The digest's own honest nulls record at least five sibling lanes independently failing to execute superbot's tests ('COULD NOT RUN superbot's invariant tier', '352 errors', 'Three attempts, real exit codes EXIT=2/1/1').
defects.line_span: whole tree; 632 of ~1060 test files error at collection
defects.quote: 5402 tests collected, 632 errors in 26.23s
defects.contradicts: R6-S01, which locates superbot's real enforcement in pytest (44 of 45 checkers driven from tests/ as libraries behind blocking invariant tests). That is architecturally elegant and it means the enforcement layer inherits the collection fragility measured here: in any environment where 632 test files cannot import, the checkers behind them do not run either.
defects.failure_scenario: Anyone verifying a change — a contributor, a reviewer, an auditing agent, or a CI job whose dependency install partially fails — cannot run the checks that are supposed to protect the code. This already happened repeatedly during this audit: the guards the estate cites as superbot's strength (14 AST write-boundary invariants, the help-reachability negative control, the managed-task sweep) went unexercised by every lane that tried, and their green status is inherited from an environment nobody in this review could reproduce.
defects.new_failure_class: Verification that exists only inside one provisioned environment: not vacuous, but unavailable — which produces the same practical result as vacuous whenever that environment is absent.
defects.successor_recommendation: Adopt the ports split that makes the kernel importable without discord.py. It is the precondition for every other guard in this comparison actually being run by the person who needs the answer.

defects.area: saga machinery vs the work it does
defects.claim: The multi-leg saga apparatus carries almost no load. Measured live across the 175 registered ops: 185 legs total, of which 173 are LegKind.DB and 12 are LegKind.EFFECT; leg reversibility is 176 reversible + 9 compensatable + 0 irreversible. So the compensator/PARTIAL/IRREVERSIBLE machinery in sb/kernel/workflow (LegSpec.compensator, the compensation path at engine.py:349, the reversibility rollup) exists for 12 EFFECT legs spread across 175 operations, and the average op has 1.06 legs.
defects.quote: compensator: WorkflowRef | None = None     # [S] REQUIRED iff kind==EFFECT and COMPENSATABLE
defects.contradicts: My own B-S01/B-S02, which recommend porting the engine's contract. The contract is worth porting; the 1,340-LOC engine that implements it is over-built for its own workload by roughly an order of magnitude, and a successor that ports the file instead of the contract inherits the wrong half. M9-S07 reached the same reading from the op side; the leg-level counts here are the sharper form.
defects.failure_scenario: A planner reading sb/kernel/workflow decides the successor needs the saga machinery on day one, ports 1,340 LOC of engine, and then maintains compensator plumbing for operations that are, at this pin, 173-of-185 single-transaction DB writes. The concrete cost is not a runtime bug — it is that the successor's mutation engine starts an order of magnitude more complex than its own workload has ever justified, which is precisely the architectural debt the owner said he wants designed out.
defects.successor_recommendation: Port the ENGINE's contract (authority leg-0, in-txn audit, one seam) and start with DB legs only; add EFFECT legs and compensators when the first operation genuinely needs an undoable post-commit Discord side effect.

defects.claim: A missing authority declaration is indistinguishable from a deliberate one. validate_authority_ref treats '' as ALWAYS valid ('the ADMIN-floor carve-out'), classify_authority_ref('') returns Lane.CAPABILITY, and the CAPABILITY lane's required tier is ADMIN_FLOOR_TIER = 'administrator'. Measured: 29 of 175 ops carry ''. All 29 happen to be genuinely admin-tier today (moderation.*, settings.*, setup.*, routing.set_policy, automation.add_rule, cleanup.*, proof_channel.record_unlock_row, role.expire_temp_role), so the default is currently fail-SAFE — but nothing distinguishes 'I chose the admin floor' from 'I forgot the field', and the compiler's P4 pass is format-only at this pin (reserved_capabilities=None => 'compile passes P4 with format checks only').
defects.quote: validate_authority_ref(ref)  # "" is ALWAYS valid (ADMIN-floor carve-out)
defects.contradicts: My own B-S02, which counts authority_ref as a required field satisfied 175/175. It is required as a NAME and optional as a VALUE, and I found no shipped instance of the failure — all 29 empty refs are correctly admin-tier — so this row is a structural hazard, not an observed bug, and should be read at that strength.
defects.failure_scenario: An author adds a member-facing operation (a daily claim, a game join, a leaderboard opt-in) and omits authority_ref, because the field's requiredness is satisfied by the empty string used in 29 surrounding examples. The op silently acquires the administrator floor: every ordinary member clicking the button gets an authority denial, the compiler is green, no test covers it, and the symptom looks like a guild permissions misconfiguration rather than a missing character in a spec.
defects.new_failure_class: A required field whose sentinel value means something specific and legitimate — so 'required' stops distinguishing declared from defaulted.
defects.successor_recommendation: Make the admin floor an explicit enum member (AuthorityRef.ADMIN_FLOOR) so '' becomes a compile error, and thread the reservation corpus into P4 so a typo'd capability ref reds instead of format-passing.

honest_nulls: I did NOT boot either bot, and did not run superbot-next's full pytest (only --collect-only, EXIT=0, 3678 items). The digest's two prior full runs (3648 passed / 44 skipped) are cited, not reproduced.

I could NOT prove that any domain write bypasses the audited engine, and I record this as a REFUTATION of my own working hypothesis. I measured 202 mutation-SQL statements across 33 sb/domain modules against 172 distinct DB leg handlers hosted in 32 modules, and found 28 of the 33 mutation modules host no leg handler — but they are all `*_store.py` files, which is the intended ops.py/store.py split, and I did not trace call graphs to see whether any store mutator is called outside a leg. The 202-vs-172 gap is NOT evidence of a bypass and must not be quoted as one.

The durable due-queue (B-S10) is proven only against tests/unit/scheduler/conftest.py's FakeSchedulerDb, an in-memory MODEL of the sb_due_queue table. The real-Postgres tier that would exercise the actual transaction skips green (R2-D04). 'Restart-safe timers' is therefore a source-and-model claim here, never a database-observed one.

I did not verify that the `architecture` JOB in named-gates.yml maps to the required CONTEXT literally named 'architecture' in the live ruleset. I inherited that mapping from M11-S01/M8-S08, which read the rulesets API live; I read only the workflow files. If the mapping is wrong, B-S03/B-S07/B-S09's enforcement_locus drops from required-CI to advisory-CI.

CONFIG_FIELDS measures 53 at this pin by len(CONFIG_FIELDS). M8-S03 says 38 env vars and M10-S1 says 44 fields. I did not reconcile the three numbers. Same class of discrepancy: I count 31 `_teardown_` helper definitions where M1-D06 counts 23, and 84 guild_id BIGINT column declarations where they count 74 tables. A planner should re-measure before quoting any of these.

I did not examine sb/kernel/versioning/ (179 LOC), sb/kernel/invariants/ (420 LOC), sb/kernel/credentials/ (341 LOC), sb/kernel/render/ (566 LOC), sb/kernel/observability/ or sb/kernel/draft/ beyond file listings. Four of those are plausible additional 'superbot never solved this' candidates — credential rotation especially, since superbot has no rotation concept at all — and this lane makes NO claim about them. That is a coverage gap in my own defence, not evidence they are weak.

I did not test whether check_egress can be bypassed by dynamic dispatch (getattr(channel, 'send')(...)); I only fired the static `.send(` form. M8-D09 proved exactly that bypass exists for check_no_skip's discord-import rule via importlib, so the same weakness is likely here and I did not measure it.

I did not verify that superbot's 915 `.send(` sites actually echo untrusted content anywhere. B-D06's failure scenario names plausible echo paths (ticket subject, poll options, starboard quote, karma reason) drawn from the digest's own feature inventory; I traced none of them end to end into a message body. What is MEASURED is the absence of any allowed_mentions control at bot level and its presence in only 5 of the tree's files.

I dropped no verified row for space; the 12/12 caps were not binding on strengths (I filed 12 by choice, and B-S12 is the weakest — a one-subsystem trace, marked as such). Two candidate rows were dropped for failing the survival rule rather than for space: (a) the compiler's P4 authority pass, because it is format-only with no reservation corpus threaded, and (b) the interaction funnel's fixed admission ORDER, folded into B-S07 because I could not evidence it independently of the containment fence.

My challenge's premise — that reviewers underrated superbot-next because it produced the wrong product — survives only in a specific form, and I state the limit plainly: I found NOTHING that rehabilitates the panel/manifest/parity layer, which is where the digest's damage is concentrated and where my own measurements (0 confirmations, 0 DURABLE_ONCE, 12 EFFECT legs of 185, 48 unimplemented erasure workflows) add more damage, not less. The defensible inheritance is a much smaller and more specific object than 'superbot-next': roughly sb/kernel/workflow's spec contract, sb/kernel/authority, sb/kernel/interaction's funnel plus the three required AST fences, sb/spec/config, sb/spec/versioning's store grammar, and sb/kernel/privacy's enumerate-the-registry walk — on the order of 4-6k LOC of the 20,486-LOC kernel, not the 150k-LOC repo.

challenges.lane: CHALLENGE C — REJECT BOTH (name the historical constraint each design encodes, why it no longer binds, what the third design is)
