challenges.headline: Both bots are prefix-command bots in modern clothing — superbot-next, the ground-up rebuild, declares 386 of 413 commands as prefix-only (27 reachable by slash) and freezes those 413 names + 135 aliases into a REQUIRED CI check, while the two gates guarding the modern surface (the 100/25 slash-cap budget and intent-survivability) are non-required and run over 18 and 4 commands — so the third bot's single highest-leverage decision is to make one grouped slash tree the invocation surface and demote prefix to a declared alias whose loss degrades nothing.

strengths.area: interaction kernel / the constraint that does NOT expire (3s ack)
strengths.claim: The one platform constraint no Discord release will ever relax — an interaction must be acknowledged inside 3 seconds — is encoded ONCE and derived from the surface, not from the author: `_surface_default_defer` returns AUTO for SLASH and COMPONENT and NONE for PREFIX/MODAL/NL, so 399 of 413 CommandSpecs leave defer_mode unset (measured) and still get the right ack. This is why a prefix->slash conversion in the third design is a one-field change: flip `kind`, and the ack, the visibility commit and the modal fence follow automatically.
strengths.contradicts: My own lane's premise that everything surface-shaped in superbot-next is prefix-era debt. This seam is the opposite: it is already slash-native and is the cheapest migration path either repo offers. It also contradicts the reading of `defer_mode: None` on 399 of 413 commands as an omission — None means surface-derived (sb/spec/commands.py:104), which is correct.
strengths.prevents_failure: Discord error 10062 'Unknown interaction' — an interaction not acked within 3s, the single most common way a slash/component bot appears broken to users
strengths.guard_population: Not itself a guard. The fence that keeps resolve() the ONLY path from a Discord surface to a handler is tools/check_no_skip.py, an AST pass over the whole sb/ tree — a real, non-empty population, not a model. Its known hole: it is name-based on ast.Import/ImportFrom and is bypassed by importlib.import_module (independently measured by lane M8).
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port this function verbatim into the third bot and add the two surfaces both repos lack (USER_CONTEXT, MESSAGE_CONTEXT) as new enum members with AUTO defer. The table is the whole migration cost.

strengths.area: process-global state / the guard superbot-next dropped
strengths.claim: superbot answers the 'who classifies the process globals?' question with an executable guard over the real tree: test_global_state_isolation.py rglobs every .py under disbot/, discovers every module defining `_reset_for_tests`/`reset_for_tests` (36 modules at this pin, measured by re-running its own regex), and FAILS if any is missing from tests/_isolation.py's GLOBAL_RESET_HOOKS / PER_FILE_RESET_HOOKS. superbot-next has 92 such hooks (measured) and NO analog: grep -rn 'GLOBAL_RESET|_isolation' over superbot-next/tests returns no classification module.
strengths.quote:
def test_every_reset_hook_is_classified() -> None:
    """No reset hook may be unclassified — a new one forces a GLOBAL/PER_FILE call."""
    discovered = _discover_reset_hooks()
    classified = classified_modules()

    unclassified = discovered - classified
strengths.contradicts: The estate reading that superbot is the debt repo and superbot-next the disciplined rebuild. On process-global hygiene the ranking inverts: superbot has 36 hooks and a meta-guard forcing a deliberate GLOBAL/PER_FILE decision on every new one; superbot-next has 92 hooks, 7 conftests that clear them by hand, and no guard — which is precisely how tests/unit/navigation_golden ended up green over a registry its own autouse conftest clears.
strengths.prevents_failure: the PR #815 class named in the file's own docstring — a module-level global mutated by one test and read by another under `pytest -n auto`, failing a different subset each parallel run
strengths.guard_population: Every .py under disbot/ that ALREADY defines a reset hook — 36 modules, measured by re-running the checker's own regex. Real artifact, not a model, and cannot be empty in practice. Its honest blind spot: a module holding process-global state that never defines a hook is invisible to it, so the population is 'globals that opted in', not 'globals'.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Do not port this guard — port the design that makes it unnecessary (see C-D06). If module-level registration survives into the third bot at all, this guard is the minimum price of admission.

strengths.claim: sb/spec/governance.py is the ONLY place in either repo where Discord's application-command caps exist as executable constants rather than prose: SLASH_CAP_TOP_LEVEL = 100, SLASH_CAP_PER_GROUP = 25, SLASH_CAP_MAX_DEPTH enforcing one level of nesting, with tools/check_slash_cap.py wiring them to a CI job. This is the exact budget a slash-first third design must run against, and it already exists — it is simply pointed at a surface the bot barely uses (18 of 413 commands; see C-D03).
strengths.contradicts: My own lane's opening hypothesis, stated loudly: I predicted neither repo named Discord's 100-global-command cap at all. That is false — superbot-next encodes it as law and superbot's 2026-07-03 analysis names it verbatim. The defect is not ignorance, it is that the law governs 4.4% of the command corpus.
strengths.prevents_failure: a global command tree that exceeds Discord's 100-top-level / 25-per-group caps and is rejected at tree.sync(), leaving the bot with no slash surface at all
strengths.guard_population: MEASURED, and this is the row's whole point: slash_cap_violations skips every command whose surface != 'slash' (governance.py:112-113), so the population is 18 of 413 CommandSpecs (4.4%) — while the checker's OK line prints '413 command(s)'. In a slash-first third design the same function would run over ~413 and would RED immediately; that is the correct behaviour and the reason to preserve it.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep the constants and the function; make it a REQUIRED check (today it is only in ci.yml's non-required `checkers` job) and fix the surface filter to include kind='both' before the third bot declares a single command.

strengths.area: intent survivability as a build gate
strengths.claim: superbot-next is the only bot in the estate that makes 'which capabilities die when Discord denies a privileged intent' an executable CI question rather than an ops incident: check_manifest_survival reds a capability tagged slash_common whose only registrations are PREFIX CommandSpecs. Ran it bare: EXIT=0, '49 manifest(s) walked'. The CONTRACT is exactly what a third design needs; only its population and its reachability predicate are wrong (C-D05).
strengths.quote:
capability with the slash_common tag set must have >=1
    interaction-delivered entry point — a SLASH-surface CommandSpec, or any
    PanelActionSpec/SelectorSpec (presence = survivable). A slash-common
    capability whose only registrations are PREFIX CommandSpecs is red.
strengths.contradicts: R6-S04, which records this gate as a working strength on the strength of its EXIT=0 alone. Measured: only 4 of 413 CommandSpecs carry slash_common=True, so 'essential' is a 4-row set (diagnostics, help, settings, setup) and the green exit says nothing about the other 409.
strengths.prevents_failure: an essential operator capability that is reachable only by a prefix command and therefore goes dark the moment Discord denies or revokes message_content — the exact class superbot has no defence against at all (bot1.py:76-78 requests both privileged intents unconditionally)
strengths.guard_population: MEASURED: the gate walks all 49 manifests, but its ESSENTIAL set is whatever carries slash_common=True — 4 of 413 commands. The population is not empty, but it is 1% of the corpus and is opt-in per author, which is the same shape as an allowlist that nobody adds to.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Invert the default: in the third bot every capability is essential unless explicitly tagged expendable, so the gate's population is the corpus and the tag records the exceptions.

strengths.area: the escape route, already shipped once in production
strengths.claim: The third design is not speculative — superbot already built it, at the owner's own request, for one subsystem: cogs/btd6/_unified.py collapses five prefix groups (btd6 / btd6ref / btd6ops / btd6strat / btd6events) into a single `/btd6` tree with flat leaves plus one level of nesting, explicitly budgeted against Discord's caps, keeping the old prefixes as aliases. It ships in the live bot. It was applied to 1 subsystem; superbot still registers 406 prefix commands against 30 app_commands (measured).
strengths.quote:
Owner request (2026-06-24): collapse the five separate BTD6 command groups
(``btd6`` / ``btd6ref`` / ``btd6ops`` / ``btd6strat`` / ``btd6events``) into a
single ``/btd6`` so users no longer have to remember which prefix owns which
action.
...
Discord allows a top-level command to mix flat subcommands with nested
subcommand-groups (max 25 per level, one level of nesting), so this is valid.
strengths.contradicts: superbot-next's own outcome. This pattern shipped 2026-06-24, two weeks before superbot-next's first commit (de36d28, 2026-07-08), and the rebuild did not generalise it: the successor's prefix-only count went UP, from the 2026-07-03 analysis's measured 225 to 386.
strengths.prevents_failure: the owner-named failure in the file's own first paragraph — 'users no longer have to remember which prefix owns which action', i.e. an unnavigable flat verb space
strengths.successor_recommendation: Make this the DEFAULT, not the exception: one slash group per subsystem key, leaves flat, one nesting level, prefix names retained as aliases on the same declaration. superbot's own file already documents why it must be a module-level tree rather than a cog (discord.py cannot share an app_commands.Group across cogs).

strengths.claim: The MECHANISM by which the successor protects a user-visible surface from silent drift is correct and worth keeping: compat/compat-frozen.json pins the surface (measured: 46 subsystems, 413 command rows, 135 aliases, 265 legacy custom_ids, 49 subsystem keys), tools/check_compat_frozen.py re-derives the same set from manifest.snapshot.json and reds on any difference, and the pin file is CODEOWNERS-routed so amending it structurally carries owner sign-off. A third bot needs exactly this shape — a frozen, owner-signed, CI-checked surface contract.
strengths.quote:
The pin lives at ``compat/compat-frozen.json``. ANY drift is red until the
pin is regenerated (``--write``) in the same PR — and the pin file is
CODEOWNERS-routed, so amending the §5.3 contract structurally carries the
owner-sign-off requirement (the ruleset makes this a required check; this
tool only reports).
strengths.contradicts: Its own contents, and this is the sting: what the required check freezes is 413 PREFIX command names and 135 aliases — a 2020-era invocation vocabulary — while the two checkers that guard the modern surface (check_slash_cap, check_intent_survival) appear only at ci.yml:53 and ci.yml:59, in the non-required `checkers` job. CI blocks a merge that renames a prefix command and does not block one that blows the slash budget.
strengths.prevents_failure: a silent rename of a live command, alias or custom_id that breaks every user's muscle memory and every persisted component id, with no owner sign-off
strengths.guard_population: The pin's 413 rows + the recompiled manifest snapshot — a large, non-empty, real artifact on both sides. This is a genuine artifact-vs-artifact diff, not a model, which is why it deserves to survive the rejection.
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep the pin, the CODEOWNERS route and the required check; change what it pins. In the third bot the frozen contract should be the slash tree paths + component custom_id roots + event payload field sets. Prefix aliases, if kept at all, belong in the pin as an explicitly-labelled compatibility appendix that is allowed to shrink.

defects.area: invocation surface / the historical constraint the rebuild inherited whole
defects.claim: THE HEADLINE, measured in-process at pin d5f66dc2: of 413 CommandSpecs across 49 manifests, kind is prefix for 386, slash for 18 and both for 9 — so 27 of 413 (6.5%) are reachable without the message_content privileged intent. The repo's own written justification for choosing DEGRADE over refuse-to-boot says refusing 'darked the WHOLE bot when every slash command still serves'; 'every slash command' is 27, and those 27 open 12 of the 314 registered panels directly. The historical constraint: in discord.py's commands.Bot a prefix command costs one decorator, has no registration round-trip, no name budget and supports aliases, while a slash command costs a tree sync, fits inside Discord's 100-top-level/25-per-group caps and cannot have aliases — and superbot was seeded on 2025-08-10 from two pre-existing prefix bots (initial commit trees: disbot, minebot, superbot-start). That constraint stopped binding when slash commands went GA and message_content became privileged; it is now inverted — the prefix surface is the one that can be taken away.
defects.quote:
INTENT_CONTRACT: tuple[IntentSpec, ...] = (
    # S15 seam correction (spec 14 §2.B / PG-2 ruled DEGRADE): required
    # True→False — refuse-to-boot on a routine message_content denial darked
    # the WHOLE bot when every slash command still serves; the fail-closed
    # rule's real goal (no SILENT reliance) is met by the EXPLICIT degrade.
    IntentSpec("message_content", privileged=True, required=False,
               approval_env="SB_INTENT_MSGCONTENT_OK",
               posture=IntentPosture.DEGRADE,
               degrades=("prefix", "fuzzy", "triggers", "nl_message",
                         "passive_onmessage")),
defects.contradicts: sb/spec/config.py:252-255's own rationale, by a factor of 15. It also contradicts R4-D01 in a complementary direction: that lane showed the slash tree is never synced at all (main.py:616 hardcodes enabled=False), so even the 27 are unreachable in production today; my measurement is independent of sync and shows that the DECLARED slash surface would be 6.5% even if sync worked.
defects.failure_scenario: Discord denies or revokes the message_content intent for the successor's application — the routine outcome for any bot that crosses 100 guilds without an approved verification, and the exact event superbot-next wrote an IntentSpec for. The bot boots and reports itself healthy (readiness is gateway+DB only). A user types !mine, !karma, !ticket open, !blackjack, !starboard, !economy pay or any of the other 386 prefix-only commands and gets total silence — no error, because the message never reaches the bot with content. 27 commands answer. The operator reads the degrade notice, which names five capability CLASSES ('prefix','fuzzy','triggers','nl_message','passive_onmessage') and no count, and has no way to learn from the running bot that 93.5% of the command surface just went away.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: the grouped slash tree is the invocation surface and the only one the product contract mentions. One top-level slash command per subsystem key (49 today, well inside the 100 cap), leaves flat, one level of nesting, 25-per-level budget enforced by the checker that already exists (C-S03). Prefix names survive as a declared alias table on the same CommandSpec, served by an adapter that is allowed to be absent; losing message_content then degrades nothing but the alias convenience and the two features that genuinely need to read bystander messages. Make 'kind' a derived field, not an author choice, so a new command cannot be born prefix-only.

defects.area: the escape was analysed and then not taken
defects.claim: superbot's own rebuild-discovery analysis, dated 2026-07-03 — FIVE DAYS before superbot-next's first commit (de36d28, 2026-07-08) — measured the split, named Discord's caps as 'the mechanical oracle the computation must budget against', and recommended the fix in two places. Its measured baseline was '225 @commands.command + 19 groups vs 31 app_commands.command, 0 hybrid'. At superbot-next's pin the same census is 386 prefix / 18 slash / 9 both: the prefix-only count went UP by 161 and the slash count went DOWN by 13.
defects.quote:
discord.py `app_commands.Group`: the substrate whose caps (100 top-level / 25 sub / 1 nest / lowercase `^[\w-]{1,32}$`) are the mechanical oracle the computation must budget against.
...
(d) slash **command groups** to live under Discord's ~100-global cap vs ~244 commands.
defects.contradicts: The estate's framing of superbot-next as the design-led rebuild and superbot as the accreted one. On the single most consequential surface decision, superbot's analysis layer got the answer right and superbot's own product shipped the counter-example (_unified.py, C-S05); the rebuild carried the problem forward and enlarged it. It also contradicts the same document's stated goal 'to erase the 225/31/0-hybrid split' — the split was not erased, it was re-frozen into a required CI pin.
defects.failure_scenario: The owner asks the third bot's planner 'we already studied this, why did nothing change?' and the answer is that the finding lived in an analysis document with no mechanism behind it. Concretely: a session opens superbot-next to add a new subsystem, copies the neighbouring manifest (386 of 413 precedents are prefix-only), declares CommandSpec(kind=prefix) for every verb, and all 7 required checks pass — because the only checker that would object (check_slash_cap) skips non-slash commands and is not a required context.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: promote the 2026-07-03 recommendation from prose to a compiler pass. The manifest compiler should REFUSE a CommandSpec that declares no interaction-delivered path, and the cap budget should run over the whole corpus at compile time, so 'the analysis said so' and 'the build enforces it' are the same artifact.

defects.area: guard population — the cap gate governs 4.4% of the corpus
defects.claim: tools/check_slash_cap.py reports 'OK (49 manifest(s), 413 command(s))' and EXIT=0, but slash_cap_violations discards every command whose surface is not exactly 'slash' — so its real population is 18 of 413 (4.4%), and it excludes the 9 kind='both' commands even though check_manifest_survival, 30 lines earlier IN THE SAME FILE, states that 'both' registers a slash surface. The checker's own output line overstates its population by 23x.
defects.contradicts: The same file at lines 82-84: '# `both` registers a slash surface too (G-6 kind partition), so / # it is interaction-delivered and survives an intent denial.' Two functions in one module disagree about whether kind='both' is a slash command; the survivability half says yes, the cap-budget half says no.
defects.failure_scenario: A session converts a batch of prefix commands to kind='both' — the natural, recommended migration step and the one the third design requires — and every one of them is invisible to the cap budget. The tree crosses 100 top-level commands with check_slash_cap still printing OK, and the failure surfaces at production boot as a rejected tree.sync(), i.e. the whole slash surface disappears at once. Because check_slash_cap runs only in ci.yml's `checkers` job and not in the 7 required contexts, no merge is blocked on the way there.
defects.new_failure_class: a cap-budget gate that is green precisely because the surface it budgets is unused, and that goes blind at the exact moment the surface starts being used
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: the budget runs over the SYNCED tree, computed the same way the adapter computes it, not over a kind filter — one function shared by the checker and the tree builder. And it is a required status check from the first command, because it is the only gate whose failure mode is 'the bot has no commands at all'.

defects.area: CI freezes the historical surface and does not gate the modern one
defects.claim: The required-check set protects exactly the wrong contract. compat/compat-frozen.json pins 413 prefix command names + 135 aliases across 46 subsystems and check_compat_frozen is one of the 7 required contexts (named-gates.yml:156). check_slash_cap and check_intent_survival — the two gates that would notice a surface the third design must move to — appear ONLY at .github/workflows/ci.yml:53 and :59, inside the `checkers` job, which is not among the required contexts.
defects.quote:
check_escape_hatches check_intent_survival check_lockfile_fresh \
...
            check_sim_gate check_slash_cap check_symbol_shadowing \
defects.contradicts: The reading of compat-frozen as a neutral anti-drift device. It is not neutral: it makes the 2020-era prefix vocabulary the one part of the surface a merge cannot change without owner sign-off, while the slash budget and intent survivability can be broken silently. It also sharpens M11-D11/M8-D07 (half the checker fleet decorates rather than blocks) with the specific consequence for this lane.
defects.failure_scenario: A session lands the third bot's first real slash migration. It renames a prefix command as part of grouping it (!btd6ops readiness -> /btd6 ops readiness) and check_compat_frozen REDS and blocks the merge, so the historical name is defended by CI. In the same PR the tree crosses the 100-command cap and check_slash_cap's failure is invisible because its job is not required. The merge is blocked on the wrong signal and lets the fatal one through.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: the required set is (a) the compiled surface pin, whose contents are slash paths + custom_id roots + event payloads, (b) the cap budget, (c) intent survivability. Prefix aliases live in a non-blocking appendix that is allowed to shrink without owner sign-off — the exact inverse of today.

defects.area: survivability predicate — reachability is not asserted
defects.claim: check_manifest_survival credits a capability as surviving an intent denial if ANY PanelActionSpec or SelectorSpec declares it ('presence = survivable'), without asking whether the panel that hosts it can be OPENED without message_content. Measured: 58 distinct panels are opened directly by a command, and 46 of those 58 (79%) have a prefix-only entry command. The gate's essential population is separately tiny — 4 of 413 CommandSpecs carry slash_common=True.
defects.contradicts: MY OWN MEASUREMENT, recorded loudly rather than smoothed: I expected the panel surface to collapse with the command surface and it does not. A transitive walk of static PanelRef edges gives 100 panels reachable from the 12 slash-opened hubs versus 117 from all command roots — so only 17 panels are lost to a message_content denial, not hundreds. The predicate is still wrong in principle (it never checks reachability at all), but the blast radius I predicted is refuted by my own probe, and R6-S04's reading of this gate as a working strength is closer to right on panels than I assumed.
defects.failure_scenario: A subsystem is tagged slash_common because it is essential; its only command entry is a prefix command that opens a hub panel; the hub's buttons carry the capability. check_intent_survival passes (the buttons are interaction-delivered) and EXIT=0. Under a message_content denial the operator cannot open the hub, so the capability is dark while the gate that exists to detect exactly that says the surface survives.
defects.new_failure_class: a survivability gate that measures the affordance and not the path to it
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: survivability is computed over the REACHABILITY GRAPH, not over declaration presence — a capability survives iff there is a path from an interaction-delivered ENTRY POINT (slash command or context menu) to it. The graph already exists; my probe built it in 40 lines from the manifests. Make it the gate.

defects.area: import-time registration — the constraint whose cause was removed and whose consequence was kept
defects.claim: superbot-next kept discord.py's 'a module is imported for its side effects' contract after deleting the extension loader that required it: load_live_manifests() pkgutil-imports every sb/manifest module and the docstring states the import IS the registration. The cost is 92 module-level clear_*/reset_*_for_tests functions (measured across sb/) with no classification guard, versus superbot's 36 hooks with one (C-S02). This is the mechanism behind the estate's flagship vacuous guard: tests/unit/navigation_golden's autouse conftest clears the global panel registry, so the completeness golden walks nothing.
defects.contradicts: The rebuild's own premise of escaping architectural debt. The historical constraint is discord.py's load_extension/setup(bot) contract, which forces import-for-side-effect; superbot-next has NO extension loader — it discovers modules by pkgutil and returns MANIFEST objects it could have consumed as pure data — and kept the side effects anyway. It also contradicts the naive grep reading (92 vs 1) that superbot is worse here: superbot has 36 hook modules and, unlike superbot-next, a guard forcing each to be classified.
defects.failure_scenario: A session adds a completeness or reachability test for a new subsystem and puts it in a directory whose conftest clears the relevant registry (7 conftests in superbot-next wire for_tests clears). The test passes over the empty set, is committed as proof, and the subsystem ships with an unreachable panel — which is exactly what happened to tests/unit/navigation_golden and what R2-D01 and M11-D02 independently re-confirmed. Nothing in CI can notice, because there is no artifact listing which globals exist or which tests clear them.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: manifest modules are pure data — `MANIFEST = SubsystemManifest(...)` and nothing else; a composition function `build_runtime(manifests) -> Runtime` constructs the panel registry, the custom_id table, the handler index and the subscriber roster and RETURNS them. A test builds a Runtime and asserts over it; there is nothing to clear, no autouse fixture can empty it, and a completeness golden is structurally incapable of running over zero panels. This also gives the third bot per-guild or per-shard runtimes for free, which module globals forbid.

defects.area: choice over large sets — autocomplete declared 'dormant'
defects.claim: Neither bot uses application-command autocomplete. Measured: the token 'autocomplete' appears once in superbot/disbot (a comment) and twice in superbot-next/sb, both times saying it is NOT implemented — 'autocomplete (wire 4) stays a dormant successor'. Meanwhile superbot carries 991 LOC of paginated-select machinery (views/paginated_select.py + views/selectors/) whose stated reason is Discord's 25-option select cap, and superbot-next ported the same idea into the kernel (sb/kernel/panels/browserview.py filter->sort->paginate, render.py:559 `options = options[: min(cspec.page_size, 25)]`).
defects.quote:
Application-command interactions belong to the command tree's callbacks;
autocomplete (wire 4) stays a dormant successor.
defects.contradicts: superbot's own 2026-07-03 analysis, which names the escape in one clause — 'slash avoids typos via autocomplete' — in the same document that recommended grouping. The pagination machinery is a workaround for a cap that only binds on the component surface; on the slash surface Discord has shipped the answer since 2021.
defects.failure_scenario: A user wants to look up one of ~180 BTD6 towers, or one of 74 store tables, or a role from a 60-role server. The bot renders a 25-option select with page-turn buttons; the user clicks Next four times and reads 100 labels looking for the one they already knew the name of. Every page turn is an interaction round trip that must be acked in 3 seconds, and every page is a message edit against the per-channel edit throttle. With autocomplete the same lookup is one keystroke sequence with server-side filtering and no components at all.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: add AUTOCOMPLETE as a first-class Surface in the interaction kernel and a `choices_provider` field on the command grammar; any option whose candidate set can exceed 25 MUST declare one, enforced at compile time. Keep the paginated select only for component-only flows where there is no slash option to attach to.

defects.area: per-message affordances — reactions kept, context menus never built
defects.claim: Both bots' per-object affordance is a reaction listener, and neither has ever used a Discord context menu: grep for ContextMenu / context_menu / app_commands.context returns ZERO hits across superbot/disbot and superbot-next/sb. superbot has reaction listeners in 6 cog files (karma, starboard, blackjack, rps_tournament, role, ai_review) and superbot-next ported the pattern (20 raw_reaction references, including a register_reaction_consumer seam). The kernel's Surface enum is closed at 8 members and none of them is a context menu, so adding one is a kernel edit plus a new ack row.
defects.quote:
class Surface(enum.Enum):
    SLASH = "slash"
    PREFIX = "prefix"
    COMPONENT = "component"
    MODAL = "modal"
    NL_INTENT = "nl_intent"
    NL_ORCHESTRATION = "nl_orchestration"
    MAINTENANCE = "maintenance"     # PIN-4/RC-19 — the ONE background member
    SETUP = "setup"                 # the wizard render surface (02 §3.3 fold-in)
defects.contradicts: The successor's claim to be a ground-up design. Its surface vocabulary is a faithful enumeration of what a 2020 discord.py bot could do plus the two AI lanes; the two surfaces Discord added in 2021 for exactly these jobs (user and message context menus, and autocomplete) are absent from the enum entirely.
defects.failure_scenario: A moderator wants to warn the author of a specific message, or a user wants to karma a specific message, or an operator wants to star one. Today: react with the right emoji from an undiscoverable vocabulary and hope the listener is armed, or copy the message id and type a prefix command with it. The emoji route needs a raw-reaction listener per feature and cannot be permission-scoped per user; the id route needs message_content. A message context menu does both jobs with no listener, no intent, an authority check at dispatch, and a discoverable right-click entry — and cannot be expressed at all because Surface has no member for it.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: Surface gains USER_CONTEXT and MESSAGE_CONTEXT, both AUTO-defer, both routed through the same resolve() chokepoint (C-S01). Every per-message action in the corpus (warn, timeout, star, karma, report, pin-to-board) declares a context-menu entry; reaction listeners survive only where the reaction itself is the product (starboard's public vote count), not as an invocation mechanism.

defects.area: the fuzzy typo rung — a subsystem that exists only because invocation is free text
defects.claim: superbot ships a difflib typo resolver (utils/command_resolution.py 174 LOC + utils/synonyms.py 69 LOC) wired into the CommandNotFound path with a documented infinite-loop history (BUG-0014), an AUTO/SUGGEST/NONE outcome model, a hand-maintained DESTRUCTIVE_COMMANDS carve-out and an ambiguity delta. superbot-next did not drop it — it PROMOTED it into the kernel as sb/kernel/interaction/adapters/fuzzy.py (150 LOC), whose own docstring binds AUTO-run safety to a manifest `effect` field that lane M9 measured as present on ZERO of 3,552 spec objects.
defects.quote:
"""The fuzzy adapter (spec 02 §3.7): a `CommandNotFound` raw token → K1
fuzzy match → AUTO (safe corrections re-enter `resolve()` — never a
`process_commands` re-dispatch) / SUGGEST / NONE.
...
AUTO-run safety derives from the manifest `effect` field
(02 §9 deferral): only `effect == "read"` targets auto-run."""
defects.contradicts: M9-D02, which measured that ZERO of 3,552 walked spec objects carry an `effect` attribute — so the safety predicate this kernel adapter names as its AUTO-run gate reads a field that does not exist. And it contradicts the successor's own kernel-purity story: a workaround for mistyped free text is not a kernel concern.
defects.failure_scenario: A user types !bal instead of !balance. The fuzzy rung matches, checks a safety predicate keyed on a manifest field that no spec defines, and either auto-runs the wrong command or emits a public 'did you mean' message. superbot's version already produced an infinite dispatch loop in production (BUG-0014, loop-breaker still in bot1.py). None of this can happen on a slash command: the picker completes the name before the user submits, so the entire failure class — and both implementations — exist solely to patch free-text invocation.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: delete the rung. The synonym/alias table survives as alias entries on the slash declaration (an alias is a real tree entry, discoverable and unmistypeable). If prefix aliases are kept for the owner's muscle memory, an unmatched prefix token is answered with silence, not a guess — which is what every modern bot does and what removes the loop class outright.

defects.area: panel engine — documents and interfaces are the same object
defects.claim: Measured over the live registry: 115 of 314 registered PanelSpecs (37%) declare ZERO actions and ZERO selectors. They are documents. Each still consumes a panel_id in a process-global registry, a session_lifecycle flag (223 of 314 are True), an anchor policy, a timeout, engine-injected navigation, and a renderer_override in 48 cases. The historical constraint: before ephemeral interaction responses and buttons, a bot's only output was a channel message, so 'a screen' and 'a printed answer' were necessarily the same object with the same lifecycle.
defects.line_span: 305-318 (PanelSpec fields: anchor_policy, timeout_s, actions, selectors, session_lifecycle, renderer_override)
defects.quote: defer_mode: DeferMode = DeferMode.AUTO      # [S]
defects.contradicts: My own second hypothesis, refuted by measurement and recorded here rather than dropped: I expected the successor to be dominated by persistent channel-anchored panels inherited from the pre-ephemeral era. It is not — 308 of 314 declare AnchorPolicy.REPLY and only 6 declare CHANNEL_ANCHOR. The pre-ephemeral inheritance shows up not as anchoring but as every read-only card carrying a stateful panel's whole apparatus.
defects.failure_scenario: A session adds a one-screen read-only status card — the most common thing anyone adds to this bot. It must mint a panel_id in the global registry (which every test must then remember to clear, C-D06), pick an anchor policy and a timeout it does not need, decide a session_lifecycle it does not have, and inherit engine-injected Help/Home/Back navigation. It then owes a golden and a sim-gate assignment. The 153-of-314 zero-action figure the estate keeps re-confirming is not a content problem — it is this type error, counted.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: two types. `Card` — a pure function from data to an ephemeral rendered reply, no id, no registry entry, no session, no navigation injection, provable by calling it. `Panel` — stateful, registered, custom_id-bearing, session-backed, worth the apparatus. Today's 115 zero-action panels become Cards on day one, which removes 37% of the panel registry, 37% of the custom_id minting and 37% of the navigation-golden surface without losing a single user-visible screen.

defects.area: acceptance oracle — byte-parity to a bot the owner has rejected
defects.claim: The successor's acceptance oracle is the running old bot, byte for byte: parity/README.md states it in four words. The owner stated on 2026-08-28 that 'the current build is nothing like the desired product' and that superbot itself is 'filled with too much history, too many trials and errors'. So the rebuild's pass/fail criterion is agreement with an artifact its owner has ruled out — and the mechanism by which that became binding is concrete and measurable: the 413 prefix names and 135 aliases the oracle observed are now frozen in compat/compat-frozen.json behind a REQUIRED status check.
defects.quote:
**The current bot is the oracle.** The harness observes it verbatim and
never changes its behavior; a rebuilt bot replays the same cases against the
same goldens and is **red until parity**
defects.contradicts: The estate's reading of golden-parity as neutral regression insurance (R5, M11 both treat the corpus as an oracle with coverage problems). My angle is upstream of coverage: even a PERFECT golden corpus would have produced this outcome, because the oracle's job description is 'reproduce the predecessor', and the predecessor's invocation surface is the single thing the owner most needs changed. The corpus did not fail to prove the port; it succeeded at proving the wrong thing.
defects.failure_scenario: The third bot is planned. A session reaches for the 533-golden corpus as the acceptance layer, because it is the estate's largest verification asset and it is green. Every golden's expected bytes were produced by a bot invoked with `!`, so the third bot must ship 413 prefix commands to stay green — reproducing the exact defect C-D01 names, with CI enforcing it. The owner then asks why the third bot also needs `!` for everything.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: the oracle is the spec, not the predecessor. Acceptance is an EFFECT contract minted from the manifest — for each capability: the DB row delta, the emitted event with its payload fields, the authority decision, and the audit row — asserted through the real presenter. The old bot's goldens are retained as a corpus of PRODUCT DECISIONS (what the feature does, what the copy says, what the limits are) and are never again a byte oracle. That change alone frees the invocation surface, the panel/document split (C-D10) and the frozen alias vocabulary (C-D04) in one move.

defects.area: the AI product is a message-pipeline stage and therefore dies with the intent
defects.claim: In both bots the conversational AI is a stage on the on_message pipeline rather than an invocable capability. superbot registers the natural-language stage into message_pipeline at cog setup (ai_cog.py:299) alongside 8 other stages; superbot-next's INTENT_CONTRACT lists 'nl_message' and 'passive_onmessage' among the five capability classes that degrade with message_content. So the whole AI vertical — superbot's 24 ai_* services plus core/runtime/ai/, and superbot-next's 30-file sb/kernel/ai/ — hangs off the one privileged intent.
defects.quote:
from core.runtime import message_pipeline
        from core.runtime.ai.natural_language_stage import get_stage

        message_pipeline.register(get_stage())
defects.contradicts: M4-S5's framing of the ordered message pipeline as an architectural strength ('AI is the LAST tier of a single ordered message pipeline'). The ordering IS good; the substrate is not — every stage in it, deterministic and AI alike, is only reachable while Discord delivers message content. The strength and this defect are the same design read at two altitudes.
defects.failure_scenario: message_content is denied or revoked. The AI product — the estate's largest engineering investment by any measure — becomes completely unreachable in one step, with no slash entry point to fall back to (superbot-next declares 27 slash commands and none of them is an AI ask; the four slash_common capabilities are diagnostics, help, settings, setup). Auto-moderation, rewards and the counting/karma listeners go with it, since all 9 stages ride the same feed.
defects.successor_recommendation: THIRD DESIGN: split the AI surface by what it needs. (a) An `/ask` slash command plus a message context menu — invocable, permission-scoped, ack-bounded, needing no privileged intent. (b) A direct-mention and DM path, which Discord delivers with content even without the intent (spider-bot already keys its reply on `message.mentions` at spiderbot/cogs/chat.py:111-113). (c) 'Initiative' — reading bystander messages the bot was not addressed in — is the ONE feature that genuinely costs message_content, and it should be the only thing declared against that intent, so the degrade notice reads 'initiative off' instead of taking the product with it.

honest_nulls: REFUTED MY OWN CENTRAL SUB-HYPOTHESIS, recorded first because it is the weakest point of C-D01/C-D05. I predicted a message_content denial would collapse the CLICK surface as well as the command surface. Measured by transitively walking static PanelRef edges from every command-opened panel: 100 of 314 panels are reachable from the 12 slash/both-opened hubs, 117 from all command roots — so only 17 panels are lost. The COMMAND surface collapses (386 of 413); the panel surface largely survives. My rows say so.

REFUTED a second hypothesis: I expected superbot-next to be dominated by pre-ephemeral persistent channel-anchored panels. Measured: anchor_policy is REPLY on 308 of 314 PanelSpecs and CHANNEL_ANCHOR on 6. The successor already defaults to reply-scoped panels; I dropped the intended 'anchored-panel machinery is historical' row entirely rather than argue it on 6 instances.

CORRECTED my own naive grep before filing C-D06: `grep -c 'def (clear|reset)_[a-z_]*_for_tests'` gives superbot-next 92 and superbot 1, which reads as a 92x regression. It is wrong — superbot names its hooks `_reset_for_tests` and has 36 such modules (I re-ran superbot's own discovery regex to get the number). The real difference is the classification guard, not the count, and the row says that.

I could NOT verify Discord's platform rules against the vendor: no network probe of Discord's documentation was made. Every platform number in my rows comes from the repos' own source — SLASH_CAP_TOP_LEVEL = 100 and SLASH_CAP_PER_GROUP = 25 at sb/spec/governance.py:45-46, the '100 top-level / 25 sub / 1 nest' clause in superbot's 2026-07-03 analysis, and the 25-option select comments in superbot's view modules. In particular the claim underpinning C-D12(b) — that Discord delivers message content for messages that MENTION the bot and for DMs even without the message_content intent — is NOT measured here; it is the standard platform rule and spider-bot's mention-keyed path is consistent with it, but treat it as the one assumption a planner should re-check before betting on it.

I did NOT read the live branch ruleset myself. C-D04's 'required contexts' half rests on the sibling lanes' live read (M8-S08, M11-S01: code-quality, manifest-validate, architecture, sim-gate, golden-parity, check_compat_frozen, pip-audit). What I measured myself is only that check_slash_cap and check_intent_survival appear ONLY in ci.yml's `checkers` job and that check_compat_frozen is a named job in named-gates.yml.

I did NOT establish what the 218 renderer_override callables render, so C-D10's Card/Panel split is argued from the 115 zero-action-zero-selector count, not from what the overrides do. 48 of the 115 also carry an override — those are the ones most likely to be pure documents, but I did not open them.

197 of 314 panels are reachable from NO command root via static PanelRef edges. I did not establish whether they are reachable at runtime through handler-returned PanelRefs (my walker only follows refs declared inside PanelSpecs), so I made no claim about them.

I ran neither bot and installed nothing: discord.py, asyncpg and python-dotenv are absent and I deliberately built no stubs — every probe here imports sb.manifest/sb.spec only, which is stdlib-clean, and every superbot claim is a source or git measurement. So there is no LIVE-TESTED evidence in this lane at all; my strongest classes are MEASURED and SOURCE-ENFORCED.

I did not measure spider-bot beyond two greps (its intents block at spiderbot/bot.py:29-31 and the mention check at spiderbot/cogs/chat.py:105-120). Note against C-D12: spider-bot DOES enable message_content, for 'AI initiative' — i.e. the estate's newest bot independently chose the same trade, which is evidence that the third design must make 'initiative' an explicit, separately-declared cost rather than assuming nobody wants it.

DROPPED for row budget, both verified: (a) superbot's ux_lab is 5,016 LOC of admin-only fake-UI gallery and superbot-next ported 344 LOC of it — a component catalogue that exists because there was no design system, which is content weight and an owner call, already covered by M3-D6; (b) the single global static `!` prefix with no per-guild or callable form in either bot. Neither is dropped for being wrong.

I did not test the C-D06 successor recommendation (pure-data manifests + build_runtime) against the successor's actual coupling. sb/manifest/xp.py's own docstring says 'IMPORTING THIS MANIFEST FILLS THE BAND-3 WAITING PORTS' — i.e. some manifests install cross-subsystem ports at import today, so the port-installation seam would have to move into the composition function as well. I name the obstacle rather than claim the refactor is free.

challenges.lane: CHALLENGE D — PRODUCT-FIRST CRITIC (superbot @5e3a667b vs superbot-next @d5f66dc2): is the successor pleasant and useful in Discord for a member, a first-time server owner, and a 2am operator?

challenges.headline: A rebuild that inherits superbot-next's shape would be a bot that says NOTHING when a member mistypes a command — measured: `!helpp` and `!seting` produce total silence, and so does every unrecognised token — which is the exact "command vanished" UX that superbot's own composition root (disbot/bot1.py:540-546) names as a root-cause bug it already fixed with an always-answer fallback; the successor deleted the fallback and made the only working surface (prefix, since global slash sync is hardcoded off) the one surface with no ephemerality, no self-deleting replies, and no not-found reply at all.

strengths.claim: superbot's prefix bot ALWAYS answers a failed command, from ONE global @bot.event handler covering all 243 counted prefix commands, across 7 branches (MissingPermissions, BotMissingPermissions, CommandNotFound with a 3-outcome typo ladder, MissingRequiredArgument, BadArgument, CommandOnCooldown, and a catch-all), and every reply self-deletes. There is no silent path: the CommandNotFound chain's final else still sends a not-found line naming `!help`.
strengths.contradicts: The estate framing that superbot is the debt pile and superbot-next the clean rebuild. On the single most basic member-facing property — does the bot answer at all — superbot is complete and superbot-next has a measured silent path (D-D01).
strengths.prevents_failure: the 'command vanished' class — a member types something the bot does not know and gets no feedback, so cannot tell whether the bot is down, lacks permission, or they typed it wrong
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port the always-answer contract as a kernel invariant of the message surface, not a handler someone remembers to register: every inbound token starting with the prefix that does not resolve MUST produce exactly one user-visible line. Make the not-found reply the default return of the typo ladder, never None.
strengths.simpler_than_counterpart: One registered event handler with a flat if/elif table; superbot-next spreads the same job across message_feed.py, fuzzy.py and error_handlers.py and loses the fallback in the seams.

strengths.claim: superbot self-cleans its own transient noise: 113 counted `delete_after=` sends in disbot/cogs/ (131 across disbot/), at 8 distinct durations tuned to the message class — 10s for denials and errors (63 uses), 8s for cooldowns and auto-corrections (17), 5s for acknowledgements (16), 15s for did-you-mean (9), 60s for a full help embed (2). Error and denial traffic therefore leaves no residue in a busy channel.
strengths.contradicts: superbot-next's SurfaceResponder protocol, which has no vocabulary for a transient reply at all (sb/kernel/interaction/request.py:121 `async def deny(self, message: str, *, ephemeral: bool) -> None: ...`) — the successor kept the ephemeral axis, which does not exist on the surface it actually runs on, and dropped the axis that does.
strengths.prevents_failure: a busy public channel accumulating permanent bot error/denial embeds until it is unreadable, which is the single most common reason server owners uninstall a prefix bot
strengths.successor_recommendation: Put `ttl_seconds` on the reply contract next to `visibility`, so the message surface has a real privacy analogue instead of silently degrading EPHEMERAL to a permanent public post. One default per message class (denial/error/ack/help), set in the kernel.

strengths.area: member UX / error copy as a kernel property
strengths.claim: superbot-next's user-facing error copy is ONE 28-line table in the kernel, not per-handler strings: `from_exception` is the only ErrorEnvelope constructor (sb/kernel/interaction/errors.py:27 `__all__ = ["ErrorEnvelope", "ValidatorError", "from_exception"]`), it has 2 counted production consumers (sb/app/error_handlers.py:24 SLASH and :38 PREFIX) plus resolve()'s own denial path, and the copy is genuinely good: it names the missing Discord permission, points at `!help <cmd>` for a bad argument, and in the setup wizard appends the two recoveries by name.
strengths.contradicts: superbot's equivalent, which is split between disbot/bot1.py:548-621 (user-facing) and disbot/services/webhook_reporter.py:504-600 (operator-facing) with the two tables independently maintained — the successor genuinely improved this and the improvement is invisible in every prior lane's rows.
strengths.prevents_failure: a raw Python exception name, or nothing, being shown to a Discord member when a handler throws
strengths.successor_recommendation: Keep verbatim. Then close the one gap: `f"`!help {cmd}` for usage." hardcodes `!` while BOT_PREFIX is a declared config field (sb/spec/config.py:126), so a server that changes its prefix is told to type a command that does not exist.

strengths.claim: Deferral is a kernel default keyed on the SURFACE, not a per-command choice: 399 of 413 counted commands declare `defer_mode: null` and inherit AUTO on SLASH (non-panel routes) and on COMPONENT, so the Discord 3-second acknowledgement deadline cannot be missed by an author forgetting to defer. Only 1 command declares `auto` explicitly and 13 declare `none`.
strengths.prevents_failure: Discord's 'The application did not respond' error — the single most visible bot failure a member ever sees — appearing because one slow handler forgot to defer
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve. Note the one soft spot: SLASH+PanelRef defaults to NONE, so a panel whose data providers hit the DB has the full 3s budget and no defer; sb/kernel/panels/render.py:282-296 swallows a failing provider and renders anyway, so a slow provider degrades to a wrong-looking panel rather than a visible timeout.

strengths.claim: The invoker lock is a kernel property with plain-language denial copy, applied to 238 of 314 counted panels (audience=invoker) and enforced at 2 counted call sites (sb/adapters/discord/panel_view.py:176 view-side, sb/adapters/discord/component_feed.py:116 feed-side). After a restart the session is gone and the lock opens rather than bricking the panel, with authority still re-resolved per click.
strengths.quote:
def may_interact(session: PanelSession | None, user_id: int | None) -> bool:
    """The invoker lock (audience=invoker ⇒ only the opener may click).
    No session (e.g. a persistent panel after restart) ⇒ open access —
    authority is still re-resolved per click by resolve()."""
    if session is None or session.invoker_id is None:
        return True
    return session.invoker_id == user_id
strengths.contradicts: Its own value on the surface the bot actually runs on: see D-D02 — on the prefix surface the panel is sent PUBLICLY, so the lock converts a shared-looking message into one that answers 'This panel belongs to someone else' to everyone but one person.
strengths.prevents_failure: another member clicking your open inventory/economy/setup panel and mutating your state, or reading a private list you opened
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve the lock and the copy. Bind it to visibility: a panel declared audience=invoker must be DELIVERED privately on every surface, and if the surface cannot deliver privately the open must be refused with a reason, not downgraded to public.

strengths.claim: A server owner never has to know a command exists: on_guild_join creates a private #superbot-setup channel, posts the setup launcher there with an owner ping, and degrades through two named fallbacks (post_launcher picks the safest existing channel, then DMs the owner) before starting a persisted setup session. Both repos carry it — superbot in production, superbot-next via the ported guild-join feed armed at sb/app/main.py:715-723 with a registered launcher consumer (sb/manifest/setup.py:228 `_launcher.register_guild_join_launcher()`).
strengths.quote:
Tries to auto-create a private ``#superbot-setup`` channel and
        post the launcher there with an owner ping. If the bot lacks
        Manage Channels (or the create fails), falls back to
        :func:`post_launcher` which picks the safest existing channel
        or DMs the owner.
strengths.prevents_failure: the invite-and-nothing-happens failure: an owner adds the bot, sees no message, does not know the prefix or that !setup exists, and removes it
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve including the three-tier fallback ladder — it is the only piece of either bot that works for an owner who has read nothing. Extend it: the launcher message should also state the prefix and offer the slash alternative, since D-D08 shows a member has no other way to learn either.

strengths.claim: Help is 8 counted top-level categories (Games, BTD6 Assistant, Project Moon, Economy, Moderation & Safety, Community, Utility, Server & Admin) behind ONE dropdown that swaps the message in place and appends a Back-to-Help button, with the legacy flat 'All Commands' browser deliberately deleted once every subsystem was homed. Governance is re-resolved at CLICK time, not at render time, so a member who lost a role between renders sees the current set. superbot-next ported the map verbatim (sb/domain/help/categories.py:53+) and the goldens pin a 6-category member view against the 8-category operator view.
strengths.quote:
The legacy paginated "All Commands / Advanced" browser (``HelpPanelView``)
was removed once every subsystem was homed into a hub — it only re-listed
the hub hosts, redundant with this index (owner decision, 2026-06-22, PR
#1294). Every feature is reachable through its hub in ≤2 clicks.
strengths.prevents_failure: a 243-to-413-command bot presenting a member with a flat, unsorted command list they cannot navigate
strengths.guard_population: parity/goldens/help/help_panel_open.json (member view) and sweep_help.json (operator view) — a real, non-empty population of 2 rendered category sets, not a model; but only the OPENING render is pinned, so the ≤2-clicks claim itself is unguarded
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve the 8-category index and the click-time governance re-resolve. Do NOT preserve the category CONTENT unexamined — see D-D11: 'BTD6 Assistant' is a permanent top-level category in every server.

strengths.claim: A member who is warned, timed out, kicked or banned gets a DM naming the action, the server and the reason, and the operator can template it with {guild}/{action}/{reason}/{user}. The substitution is plain token replacement, explicitly never str.format, so a brace or attribute expression typed by an operator can neither raise nor leak object internals into a member's DM.
strengths.quote:
``{guild}`` / ``{action}`` / ``{reason}`` / ``{user}`` substituted (plain
    token replacement — never ``str.format``, so a stray brace or attribute
    expression in operator input can't raise or leak).
strengths.prevents_failure: a member being silently punished with no notification and no stated reason, and the second-order failure of an operator's templating typo crashing the notice or leaking a Python repr into a stranger's DM
strengths.successor_recommendation: Preserve verbatim, including the never-str.format rule. Extend the template vocabulary rather than the mechanism (appeal link, duration) — the pure, no-I/O renderer is exactly the right seam.

strengths.claim: superbot subscribes Discord's own audit-log gateway event and mirrors every administrative action — by ANY actor, including humans in the web client and other bots — into the configured log channel with the actor named, and it surfaces the missing View Audit Log permission in `!logging status` rather than failing silently. superbot-next has ZERO occurrences of on_audit_log_entry_create; it is one of 21 counted gateway listeners in superbot against 5 armed in superbot-next.
strengths.quote:
# The v2 layer. ``on_audit_log_entry_create`` is a single gateway event
    # that surfaces every administrative action Discord records — by anyone,
    # with the actor named — so the log finally matches what a mature logging
    # bot (Dyno) shows: bans/kicks/timeouts, channel/role/server changes,
    # invites, emojis, webhooks.
strengths.contradicts: The estate's reading of superbot-next as the operationally stronger bot. On the one question an operator actually asks at 2am — who changed this — superbot answers from Discord's own record and superbot-next has no listener and no read surface (D-D09).
strengths.prevents_failure: an operator woken at 2am by 'a channel is gone / everyone lost a role' having no way to find out who did it or when, because the bot only records actions it performed itself
strengths.successor_recommendation: Port this before porting any of the 33 !platform introspection cards. It is one listener and one router, it covers actions the bot did not perform, and it is worth more to a 2am operator than the entire frozen platform-card surface.

defects.area: member UX / the bot says nothing
defects.claim: superbot-next answers NOTHING to an unrecognised prefix command. The message feed's only not-found path is the typo ladder, and `prefix_typo_reply` returns None on BOTH of its two miss branches — no close match (fuzzy.py:72-73) and a close match that is AUTO on a read target (fuzzy.py:75-76) — after which message_feed.py:121 `if copy:` sends nothing. The discord.py fallback that would have caught it is explicitly disabled at sb/app/error_handlers.py:35-37. MEASURED with the repo's own AUTO_CUTOFF=0.85 over its own 61 panel-routed prefix names: `!helpp`→`help` ratio 0.889, `!seting`→`settings` 0.857, `!seetings`→`settings` 0.875, `!fishng`→`fishing` 0.923, `!tickt`→`ticket` 0.909 — 5 of 5 SILENT. Only tokens landing in the narrow 0.6–0.85 band against a NON-panel command produce any reply at all.
defects.contradicts: superbot's own composition root, disbot/bot1.py:540-546 verbatim: 'The legacy ``in_allowed = ctx.channel.id in ALLOWED_CHANNELS`` gate that suppressed replies outside hardcoded channel IDs was the root cause of the "command vanished" UX — operators in fresh guilds saw nothing when a command failed.' superbot fixed this bug and shipped an always-answer fallback at bot1.py:600-604; the successor re-introduced the same user-visible symptom by a different mechanism. It also contradicts fuzzy.py:52-58's own framing of this module as 'the shipped CommandNotFound SUGGEST surface (bot1.py:541-586)' — it ported one of the shipped ladder's three outcomes and dropped the other two.
defects.failure_scenario: A new member joins a server, is told 'the bot uses !', and types `!helpp` — a 1-character slip. superbot-next computes similarity 0.889 to `help`, classifies AUTO, sees `help` routes to a PanelRef so is_read is True, returns None, and sends nothing at all. The member sees a bot that ignored them. They try `!seting`, `!fishng`, `!tickt` — silence every time. Because global slash sync is hardcoded off (sb/app/main.py:616 `sync_remote(bot, committed, enabled=False)`), typing `/` shows them nothing either. There is no path from 'I do not know a command' to 'I know one'.
defects.new_failure_class: silent-miss: the successor can be indistinguishable from an offline bot to a member who has not memorised a command name
defects.successor_recommendation: Make 'exactly one user-visible reply per prefix token' a kernel invariant of the message surface with a test that drives every branch of the ladder and asserts a non-empty reply. Restore all three shipped outcomes: AUTO (correct, run, and SAY so), SUGGEST (did-you-mean), NOT-FOUND (name !help). None of the three may return None.

defects.area: member UX / panels on the only working surface
defects.claim: 238 of 314 counted panels declare audience=invoker, and the presenter computes `ephemeral` from exactly that at panel_view.py:326 — then DROPS it on the prefix branch. The message path at panel_view.py:367-368 calls `origin.reply(embed=..., view=...)` with no ephemeral argument and no delete_after, so an invoker-only panel is posted as a permanent PUBLIC channel message. The invoker lock (D-S05) then answers every other member 'This panel belongs to someone else — open your own.' The responder makes the loss explicit: MessageResponder's docstring at responders.py:166-167 states 'ephemerality does not exist on the message surface — EPHEMERAL renders as a normal reply', and its deny at :182-183 is a bare `await self._ctx.reply(message)`.
defects.quote:
elif hasattr(origin, "reply"):
            message = await origin.reply(embed=embed, view=view, **file_kwargs)
defects.contradicts: superbot, which uses ephemeral interaction responses across 142 counted view files under disbot/views/ and self-deletes transient channel sends 113 times (D-S02). The successor kept the privacy AXIS that its live surface cannot express and dropped the one it can.
defects.failure_scenario: Five members in #general each type `!mining`. Five permanent embeds full of buttons appear in the channel. Each member can click only their own; clicking anyone else's produces an ephemeral 'This panel belongs to someone else'. The channel now carries five dead interactive panels that never expire from view, and the conversation is pushed off-screen. Because global slash sync is off, there is no ephemeral alternative to reach for.
defects.new_failure_class: public-panel litter: the invoker lock plus a public delivery surface turns every private panel into channel debris addressed to one person
defects.successor_recommendation: Make delivery visibility a property the surface must SATISFY, not one it may ignore: audience=invoker on a surface with no private channel should either (a) DM/thread the panel, (b) send it with a TTL, or (c) refuse with a reason. Add `ttl_seconds` to SurfaceResponder so the message surface has a real privacy analogue.

defects.claim: 13 of the 14 commands that declare reply_visibility=ephemeral are kind=slash (the 14th, `setup`, is kind=both), and global slash sync is hardcoded off at sb/app/main.py:616 with the only other sync leg gated on an explicit test-guild target. So at this pin the entire declared-ephemeral surface of the bot is unreachable, and the one command that survives — `!setup` — reaches the member surface, where ephemerality does not exist (D-D02).
defects.quote: outcome = await sync_remote(bot, committed, enabled=False)
defects.contradicts: sb/manifest/setup.py:76-175, which declares ReplyVisibility.EPHEMERAL on 8 setup commands — a stated privacy intent that the composition root's own sync decision makes unreachable for 7 of the 8 and that the prefix responder discards for the 8th.
defects.failure_scenario: A server owner types `!setup` in whatever channel they were reading — commonly #general. The wizard posts publicly: the first golden (parity/goldens/setup/sweep_setup.json) shows the opening step sending a select whose options are the server's moderation presets with their descriptions, and later sections bind channels by listing them. Every member watching sees which channels are about to become mod-log and audit targets, and reads the server's moderation posture before it is applied. The owner has no ephemeral alternative because the slash twins are not registered with Discord.
defects.new_failure_class: declared-but-unreachable privacy: a visibility contract that compiles, passes every gate, and has no runtime
defects.successor_recommendation: Treat 'a command declaring EPHEMERAL is reachable on a surface that can deliver it' as a boot-gate assertion, not a manifest field. Until slash is synced, `!setup` should open in a DM or the private setup channel it already knows how to create (D-S06), never in the invoking channel.

defects.area: server owner / a feature that is ON and cannot run
defects.claim: The welcome greeting is ON by default and can never fire. `welcome_join_enabled` has activation on_by_default and default True, with a default join_message, and `!welcome` renders '👋 **Greet on join** — ✅' straight from the setting with no indication the trigger is absent. Measured: superbot-next arms 5 gateway listeners (on_guild_join, on_interaction, on_message, on_raw_reaction_add, on_raw_reaction_remove) against 21 distinct listeners in superbot; `grep -rn member_join sb/ --include=*.py | grep -v test` returns 5 hits, none an event bridge — 3 are automation templates and one (sb/domain/automation/__init__.py:12-13) says so out loud.
defects.quote:
f"👋 **Greet on join** — {_flag(policy.join_enabled)}",
        f"🚪 **Farewell on leave** — {_flag(policy.leave_enabled)}",
        f"✉️ **DM on join** — {_flag(policy.dm_enabled)}",
defects.contradicts: sb/domain/welcome/service.py:5-9 is honest in the DOCSTRING — 'The v1 slice is READ-ONLY ... the member-join/leave feeds (greeting send, entry-role grant, DM) arm with the member band' — but the PANEL a server owner reads says the opposite, in a green check. This is the R1 lane's 'live-misleading' class in a file R1 did not scan (its sample covered diagnostic/, admin/, settings/, ux_lab/).
defects.failure_scenario: A server owner opens `!welcome`, sees 'Greet on join — ✅' and a welcome message template, and edits the template to match their server's tone. They then watch three new members join in silence. They re-open `!welcome`, which still shows ✅. They have no way to discover that no on_member_join listener exists, so they conclude the bot is broken at random and file a bug that cannot be reproduced from the settings.
defects.new_failure_class: armed-looking dead feature: a policy card that reports enablement without reporting reachability
defects.successor_recommendation: A capability card must report the WEAKEST link, not the setting: render 'Greet on join — ✅ (configured) · ⛔ not armed: member-join feed not installed'. Generalise it — declare each subsystem's required gateway events in its manifest and have the boot gate mark any subsystem whose events are unarmed, so every status surface can say so without per-feature code.

defects.area: 2am operator / help text that is frozen state
defects.claim: The help description of a diagnostic command IS the frozen capture-guild card title. sb/manifest/diagnostic.py:66 sets each of the 33 counted `platform` subcommands' summary to `view.title`, and sb/domain/help/service.py:220-221 renders that summary verbatim in the help listing. Measured over the compiled snapshot: 3 of the 33 summaries carry a state value or an unsubstituted token — 'Command Access — <#{ch}>', 'Platform consistency · WARNING', 'Setup Readiness — 0%'.
defects.contradicts: The R1 lane's scoping of the frozen-literal class as a problem with what the 28 CARDS render. The freeze also propagates into the HELP INDEX through the manifest's summary field — a second, unnoticed rendering surface for the same literals, reached without opening any card.
defects.failure_scenario: An operator at 2am opens help for the diagnostic group to find the right command. The listing tells them 'consistency — 🛡 Platform consistency · WARNING' and 'setup-readiness — 🛰 Setup Readiness — 0%'. They read those as their server's current state and start chasing a consistency warning and a zero-percent setup that do not exist; both strings are constants from a different guild captured weeks earlier. A third row reads 'command-access — ✅ Command Access — <#{ch}>', an unrendered template token, which tells them the bot's own help is broken and undermines the other 32 rows they were about to trust.
defects.new_failure_class: state-as-documentation: a value that changes with the world used as a command's permanent description
defects.successor_recommendation: A command's summary must be authored prose about what the command DOES, never derived from a rendered artifact. Add a compile-time predicate: reject any CommandSpec.summary containing a substitution token or matching a rendered card title. This one is cheap and would have red-lined all three today.

defects.area: server owner / the setup wizard speaks implementation
defects.claim: The setup wizard's top-level navigation — the ten labels a first-time owner reads before anything else — names 2 of 10 sections after internal mechanisms: 'Cleanup inheritance' (a resolver precedence chain) and 'Cog routing' (a discord.py extension term). Both were carried over deliberately: sb/domain/setup/sections.py:42 says 'shipped values verbatim'. Running superbot's OWN extractor over both trees: 133 operator-facing jargon strings in disbot/views/setup vs 84 in sb/domain/setup, top terms bind×25, stage×16, preset×15, final review×14, tier×12. superbot at least has a guard (scripts/check_setup_copy.py, warn-only, baseline 133); superbot-next has none — `grep -rl 'jargon\|plain.language' tools/` returns 0 files.
defects.quote:
WizardSectionSpec(slug="cleanup", label="Cleanup inheritance",
                      emoji="🧹", order=60,
                      op_kinds=("set_cleanup_policy",)),
    WizardSectionSpec(slug="moderation", label="Moderation",
                      emoji="🛡️", order=65),
    WizardSectionSpec(slug="cog_routing", label="Cog routing",
                      emoji="🧭", order=70,
                      op_kinds=("set_cog_routing",)),
defects.contradicts: scripts/check_setup_copy.py:6-11, which states the plan's 'Law 2 is "zero jargon" — a non-technical server owner walking ``!setup`` must never read a Discord/bot internal term (draft, operation, bind, cog, subsystem, scope, resolver, threshold, seam, pipeline, routing, tier, guild, preset, …)'. Both repos violate Law 2 in the wizard's own section titles, which are the least escapable copy in the product. The guard's own promise — 'once it reaches zero the guard graduates to --mode strict in CI' — is unmet at 133 and the guard did not survive the port.
defects.failure_scenario: A server owner running !setup for the first time reaches step 6 of 10 and reads '🧹 Cleanup inheritance', whose body (sb/domain/setup/cleanup.py:380) says 'Configure cleanup behaviour at three scopes. The resolver walks thread → channel → server'. They do not know what a scope is, what inherits, or what happens if they skip. They skip it, and every subsequent message-cleanup complaint traces to a step they were structurally unable to evaluate. Step 8 reads '🧭 Cog routing' — a word from discord.py's extension API that has no meaning to anyone who has not written a bot.
defects.successor_recommendation: Name every wizard section after the OWNER'S GOAL, not the mechanism: 'How long messages stay' and 'Where each feature works'. Then port superbot's check_setup_copy.py as a strict gate on the successor's setup and help surfaces from day one — it is 200 lines of stdlib AST, it already works, and the baseline for a new tree is genuinely zero.

defects.area: copy quality frozen by the acceptance oracle
defects.claim: 128 of 2,102 counted distinct user-facing strings pinned across the 534 golden files contain internal jargon, so improving that copy reds golden-parity — one of the 7 live-required status checks. The worst single instance is shown to a server admin in the AI settings page: it cites a source directory path in the OLD repository's tree and then prints the subsystem's registry key and visibility tier as if they were product vocabulary.
defects.quote:
_SETTINGS_DESCRIPTION = (
    "_Read-only AI gateway diagnostics: provider state, feature flags, "
    "task routing, and request/failure counters. Does not own AI provider "
    "logic — that lives in core/runtime/ai/._\n"
    "visibility tier: `administrator`  ·  subsystem key: `ai`"
)
defects.contradicts: The owner's stated goal for the successor — 'a bot without architectural debt … everything should be planned and connected from the start'. Choosing byte-parity as the acceptance oracle converted the predecessor's copy debt into a CI-enforced contract: 128 pinned strings cannot be improved without re-minting goldens, and the one rule the estate has for this (check_setup_copy) was not ported.
defects.failure_scenario: A server admin opens the AI settings page to turn the assistant on. The page tells them the feature 'does not own AI provider logic — that lives in core/runtime/ai/', a filesystem path inside a repository they have never seen, and then labels itself 'visibility tier: administrator · subsystem key: ai'. They cannot tell whether they are looking at a settings page or a developer console, and they do not learn what any control does. A maintainer who tries to fix the sentence reds parity/goldens/ai/sweep_ai_settings.json and the required golden-parity check.
defects.new_failure_class: oracle-frozen copy: user-facing prose promoted to a CI contract, so quality work costs a re-mint
defects.successor_recommendation: Split the oracle: pin EFFECTS (db_delta, outbound method + target, event names) and never pin prose. Human-readable copy belongs behind a copy lint and human review, not a byte diff. Concretely, add a disposition class 'copy' to sb/adapters/parity/dispositions.py that strips embed description/label/placeholder text from BOTH documents, exactly as the three existing classes do.

defects.area: discoverability / prefix-first in a slash-first Discord
defects.claim: Both bots are prefix-first and neither has a real slash surface. superbot: 243 counted `@commands.command|group` against 30 `@app_commands.command` and ZERO hybrid commands. superbot-next: of 413 compiled commands, 386 are kind=prefix, 18 slash, 9 both — 27 of 413 (6.5%) reachable by slash, and only 4 declare slash_common, the flag check_intent_survival uses to decide what must survive an intent denial. superbot-next's global sync is then hardcoded off (main.py:616), so the effective slash surface at this pin is empty.
defects.line_span: subsystems[*].commands (413 entries, parsed with python3 json — not read as text)
defects.contradicts: sb/spec/config.py:256-265's INTENT_CONTRACT, which treats message_content as a degradable capability and sb/spec/config.py:252-255 which justifies DEGRADE over refuse-to-boot because 'every slash command still serves'. With 27 of 413 commands declared slash and none synced globally, a message_content denial does not degrade this bot — it silences it. The R4 lane found the sync half of this; the command-surface ratio that makes it fatal is measured here.
defects.failure_scenario: A member who has never read a manual joins a server, sees the bot in the member list, and types `/` — Discord's only built-in discovery affordance. In superbot they are shown 30 of 243 features. In superbot-next they are shown nothing, because the global command set was never synced. They have no way to learn the prefix (`!`) or any command name, and typing a guess produces silence (D-D01). Separately, Discord gates message_content for verified bots: the day that approval lapses, 386 of 413 commands stop existing with no fallback.
defects.successor_recommendation: Decide the surface FIRST and make it structural: declare every command as hybrid by default and let a manifest field opt OUT, so slash coverage is the default state rather than 27 hand-declared exceptions. Then make 'the synced global set equals the declared slash set' a boot-gate assertion, so the sync switch cannot sit at False through 100 commits unnoticed.

defects.area: 2am operator / no read surface for its own audit spine
defects.claim: superbot-next writes one audit_log row inside the mutation transaction for every one of its 175 registered compound ops — its central architectural claim — and provides no way to READ them from Discord. The only SELECT against audit_log in the whole tree is the workflow engine's dedup-replay lookup by idempotency key. A manifest scan of all 413 commands for audit/history/who/recent surfaces returns per-feature logs only (modlogs, strategy-audit, why-no-response, fishlog); none reads the central spine.
defects.quote: """Spec 07 §3.7 — the deduped-replay result: re-read the audit_log row by
defects.contradicts: M9-S03, which files the audit spine as a top strength ('Audit is a property of the mutation engine, not a call authors must remember … 175 of 175 registered CompoundOpSpecs carry a non-empty audit_verb'). The write side is real; the operator value is zero until something reads it. It also contradicts superbot's own posture — superbot streams Discord's native audit log into a channel (D-S09), which superbot-next dropped, so the successor lost the read surface it HAD and did not build one for the spine it GAINED.
defects.failure_scenario: At 02:00 a moderator reports that the games feature stopped working in three channels. The operator wants 'who changed governance for this guild in the last 6 hours'. Every one of those changes wrote an audit_log row with actor, verb, prev_value and new_value — and there is no command that shows them. The operator must open Postgres from a laptop, find the connection string, and write SQL. Meanwhile the in-process finding buffer that might have hinted at it is a deque(maxlen=256) that the restart they are about to perform will erase.
defects.new_failure_class: write-only audit: a perfectly instrumented mutation spine with no consumer
defects.successor_recommendation: Ship the reader with the writer. One paginated `!audit [actor|verb|since]` panel over audit_log, gated to the operator tier, is a few hundred lines and turns 175 already-written audit verbs into the highest-value operator surface in the bot — more valuable than the 33 !platform introspection cards combined.

defects.area: member UX / no channel hygiene on the surface that runs
defects.claim: There is exactly ONE `delete_after` send in superbot-next's entire runtime (sb/adapters/discord/message_feed.py:123, the typo suggestion), against 113 counted in superbot's cogs alone. Every other prefix-surface reply — every denial, every error envelope, every result — is a permanent public message, because MessageResponder.deny and MessageResponder.render both call `self._ctx.reply(...)` with no TTL and the SurfaceResponder protocol has no TTL parameter to pass.
defects.quote:
class MessageResponder:
    """Wraps a `commands.Context` / `discord.Message` (prefix surface).
    `ack` is a no-op; nothing is ever committed (ephemerality does not exist
    on the message surface — EPHEMERAL renders as a normal reply)."""
